full_text_sections.other: IntroductionSeasonal and pandemic influenza viruses continue to pose significant global health challenges, contributing to millions of cases of severe respiratory illness and hundreds of thousands of deaths each year (1). Although vaccines and antiviral medications are available, their efficacy varies by strain and season. Disease severity during influenza virus infection is determined not only by viral pathogenicity, but also by the magnitude and regulation of host immune responses. While early innate antiviral signaling and interferon production are essential for viral clearance, excessive or prolonged inflammation can result in lung injury, impaired viral resolution, and severe disease (2). Identifying host pathways that balance protective versus pathogenic antiviral immunity is therefore critical for understanding susceptibility to severe influenza virus infection.Vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent worldwide and has been associated with increased susceptibility to respiratory infections, including influenza virus infection (3). Observational studies have demonstrated inverse correlations between circulating serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and incidence of upper respiratory tract infections in both children and adults (4, 5). Furthermore, a large meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials demonstrated that vitamin D supplementation significantly reduced the risk of acute respiratory infections, particularly in individuals with profound vitamin D deficiency (6). However, clinical studies examining vitamin D supplementation during viral respiratory infections have produced inconsistent results, suggesting that the mechanisms by which vitamin D regulates antiviral immunity remain incompletely understood (7).The biological effects of vitamin D are mediated through the vitamin D receptor (VDR), a nuclear receptor expressed in epithelial cells and multiple immune cell populations, including macrophages, dendritic cells, and activated T lymphocytes (8). The effect of VDR KO on host resistance to infection has been studied for bacterial and parasitic infections, but not viruses (9–12). Immune cells from VDR KO mice have been shown to overproduce inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-6, IFN-β1, IL-1β, IL-12, and IFN-γ that contribute to susceptibility to colitis, infection and autoimmunity (9–12). T cells from VDR KO mice proliferate more quickly and over- produce IFN-γ and IL-17 (9, 10). Because of the critical role of IFN-γ on host resistance to influenza virus by promoting antiviral immunity and viral clearance (11, 12), the effect of high IFN-γ on the host response of VDR KO mice to influenza infection is difficult to predict.There is evidence that vitamin D may be a direct regulator of some viruses. Human bronchial epithelial cells have been shown to produce the vitamin D hydroxylase that produces the high affinity VDR binding compound, 1,25(OH)2D (13). 1,25(OH)2D treatment of human bronchial epithelial cells induced cathelicidin that suppressed respiratory syncytial virus replication in vitro (13). Although respiratory syncytial virus is a common respiratory illness that belongs to a different viral family than influenza virus, there is the possibility of direct effects of vitamin D on host responses that control viral replication.An additional and largely unexplored component of vitamin D biology during infection is its close endocrine relationship with parathyroid hormone (PTH). PTH, a calcium-regulating peptide hormone, is secreted in response to low vitamin D status. PTH induces the production of the vitamin D hydroxylase to increase the circulating levels of 1,25(OH)2D (14). In a feedback loop, 1,25(OH)2D production inhibits PTH and together regulates serum calcium and phosphorous levels (14). Vitamin D deficiency and VDR KO result in very high PTH levels (15) even when calcium is normalized by rescue diets (16). PTH has recently been shown to be an immune system regulator (17–19). Importantly, PTH signaling enhanced T cell proliferation, and inflammatory cytokine production (e.g., TNF-α, IL-17) (17–19). Elevated PTH levels may contribute to the enhanced inflammation and cytokine production present in VDR KO mice.VDR KO mice developed more severe and lethal influenza disease, characterized by heightened type I and II interferon production, with delayed viral clearance. Intermittent PTH treatment of WT mice exacerbated respiratory signs of influenza virus infection and resulted in higher viral M gene expression compared to vehicle-treated WT mice. PTH treated WT mice had greater IFN-γ production, elevated viral M gene and more severe clinical signs. Influenza infection of myeloid (M) specific, M-VDR KO mice, had impaired anti-viral responses and increased severity of symptoms. The increased susceptibility of the M-VDR KO mice demonstrates a critical role for myeloid cells as vitamin D targets in the host response to influenza. The combined effects of VDR KO and high PTH (16) result in excessive cytokine responses that are ineffective for host resistance to influenza viruses. Instead, the increased inflammation adds to the tissue injury. Interventions with vitamin D, would increase vitamin D status and reduce PTH, that potentially could reduce the impact of influenza virus infection. MiceC57BL/6 VDR KO (VDRCre+/+, KO) and (VDRCre-/-) WT littermates were used for experiments as previously described (20). For myeloid (M)-specific deletion studies, VDR floxed mice (VDRfl/fl) were crossed with LysM-Cre transgenic mice (B6.129P2-Lyz2tm1(cre)Ifo/J), Jackson Laboratory, stock #004781) to generate M-VDR KO (VDRfl/fl LysMCre+) and WT littermate controls. Genotyping primer sequences and expected PCR product sizes are provided in Supplementary Table S1. Experiments used 8–10 wk old mice of both sexes. There were no significant effects of sex on survival, body weight loss, and lethargy in WT and VDR KO mice and on respiratory symptoms in VDR KO mice following influenza infection (Supplementary Figure 1). There were significantly less respiratory symptoms in WT males late following the influenza infection than WT females (Supplementary Figure 1). Subsequent experiments were not powered to examine sex as a variable which is a limitation of the study. VDR KO and their WT littermates were fed vitamin D containing and high-lactose rescue diets (20% high lactose; Envigo, TD 96348, Madison, WI). All other experiments that used WT mice treated with PTH/vehicle or M-VDR KO and WT littermates used the same vitamin D containing diets but without the high-lactose (Envigo, TD 89124). All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the Pennsylvania State University (University Park, PA). papers.title_original: Myeloid cell expression of the VDR and parathyroid hormone control the host response to influenza infection in mice

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate the role of vitamin D receptor (VDR) and parathyroid hormone (PTH) in modulating the host response to influenza infection, particularly focusing on disease severity, mortality, and inflammatory cytokine responses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study used C57BL/6 VDR knockout (KO) and wild-type (WT) littermates to evaluate the effects of VDR and PTH on influenza infection. Mice were infected with H1N1 influenza virus, and their clinical symptoms, weight loss, and respiratory scores were monitored.
analysis.methods: The study involved genotyping using PCR with primers from Supplementary Table S1, serum calcium measurement via a colorimetric assay, RNA concentration and purity assessment using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) for influenza virus M gene quantitation. Infectious virus was measured using the TCID50 assay, and cell viability was assessed with a hemocytometer and trypan blue.
analysis.main_results: VDR KO mice showed 21% mortality, delayed viral clearance, more severe symptoms, and lung pathology compared to WT littermates. PTH treatment increased clinical scores, influenza M gene levels, and cytokine responses in WT mice compared to vehicle-treated controls.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted their findings as evidence of a novel paradigm where the vitamin D-PTH axis regulates host resistance to influenza virus disease by modulating inflammation and viral load in the lungs.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that VDR and PTH pathways could be important targets for understanding and potentially modulating host responses to influenza infection, offering insights into inflammation control and viral clearance mechanisms.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of mice as the model organism, which may not fully translate to human influenza infections. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on animal models and the absence of direct human clinical data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the role of the vitamin D-PTH axis in modulating the host response to influenza infection in mice. It investigates how VDR knockout (KO) and PTH treatments affect disease severity, mortality, and inflammatory cytokine responses. The research finds that VDR KO mice exhibit increased mortality, delayed viral clearance, and more severe symptoms compared to wild-type (WT) littermates. PTH treatment in WT mice enhances clinical scores, viral load, and cytokine responses. The study uses a combination of genetic models, qRT-PCR, and TCID50 assays to assess these effects. The findings suggest a novel mechanism by which the VDR-PTH axis influences host resistance to influenza, potentially offering new insights into inflammation and viral clearance. However, the study is limited to an animal model, which may affect the generalizability of results to human influenza. The evidence is moderate due to the experimental nature and lack of direct human data.

elements_en.methods: The study involved genotyping using PCR with primers from Supplementary Table S1, serum calcium measurement via a colorimetric assay, RNA concentration and purity assessment using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer, and quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) for influenza virus M gene quantitation. Infectious virus was measured using the TCID50 assay, and cell viability was assessed with a hemocytometer and trypan blue.
elements_en.main_results: VDR KO mice showed 21% mortality, delayed viral clearance, more severe symptoms, and lung pathology compared to WT littermates. PTH treatment increased clinical scores, influenza M gene levels, and cytokine responses in WT mice compared to vehicle-treated controls.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted their findings as evidence of a novel paradigm where the vitamin D-PTH axis regulates host resistance to influenza virus disease by modulating inflammation and viral load in the lungs.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that VDR and PTH pathways could be important targets for understanding and potentially modulating host responses to influenza infection, offering insights into inflammation control and viral clearance mechanisms.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its use of mice as the model organism, which may not fully translate to human influenza infections. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on animal models and the absence of direct human clinical data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在探讨维生素 D 受体 (VDR) 和甲状旁腺激素 (PTH) 在调节 宿主 对流感感染反应中的作用,特别关注疾病严重程度、宿主 和炎症细胞因子反应。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究使用 C57BL/6 VDR 敲除 (KO) 和野生型 (WT) 同窝小鼠来评估 VDR 和 PTH 对流感感染的影响。小鼠感染甲型H1N1流感病毒,监测其临床症状、体重减轻和呼吸评分。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究涉及使用补充表 S1 中引物的 PCR 进行基因分型、通过比色测定进行血清钙测量、使用 NanoDrop 分光光度计评估 RNA 浓度和纯度,以及用于流感病毒 M 基因定量的定量 PCR (qRT-PCR)。使用 TCID50 测定法测量感染性病毒,并使用血细胞计数器和台盼蓝评估细胞活力。
elements_zh.main_results: 与 WT 同窝小鼠相比,VDR KO 小鼠表现出 21% 的 死亡率、病毒清除延迟、更严重的症状和肺部病理。与媒介物处理的对照组相比,PTH 治疗 增加了 WT 小鼠的临床评分、流感 M 基因水平和细胞因子反应。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将他们的发现解释为一种新范例的证据,其中维生素 D-PTH 轴通过调节肺部炎症和病毒载量来调节 宿主 对流感病毒疾病的抵抗力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,VDR 和 PTH 通路可能是理解和潜在调节 宿主 对流感感染反应的重要靶点,为炎症控制和病毒清除机制提供见解。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性在于它使用小鼠作为模型生物,这可能无法完全转化为人类流感感染。由于依赖动物模型且缺乏直接的人体临床数据,证据强度中等。

Subsequent experiments were not powered to examine sex as a variable which is a limitation of the study. Relative gene expression levels were calculated using the 2^−ΔΔCT method, with GAPDH as the housekeeping gene. Infectious virus was quantified using the Tissue Culture Infectious Dose 50% (TCID50) assay, a standard method for determining the concentration of infectious virus based on cytopathic effect in cell culture. Values are the mean ± SEM and represent pooled results from two to three independent experiments (WT: n = 36; VDR KO: n = 28 total). IntroductionRespiratory infections caused by seasonal influenza viruses remain a major global health burden. Vitamin D receptor (VDR) signaling regulates immune responses, but the role of the VDR and its interaction with parathyroid hormone (PTH) in host resistance to H1N1 influenza infection is not understood.MethodsGlobal VDR knockout (KO) mice, or myeloid (M) deletion of the VDR (M-VDR KO) and the respective wildtype (WT) littermates were infected with H1N1 influenza virus. papers.title: A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1

source_records.title: A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1

papers.priority_tier_reason: 高相关性，且具备高等级研究设计、全文证据或较强数据库/引用支持
papers.full_text: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies. MATERIALS AND METHODSCells and virusesMadin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC), no. CRL-2936] were maintained in minimal essential medium (MEM) (Gibco, 11095080) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16000-044). Human embryonic kidney–293T (HEK-293T) cells (ATCC, no. CRL-3216) were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco, 11965092) supplemented with 10% FBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 16000-044). Both cell types were incubated at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator.The HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 isolate A/Canada Goose/ON/2025, referred to here as genotype D1.1 virus, was obtained from National Centre for Foreign Animal Disease, Canada. The HPAI H5N1 B3.13 genotype isolate A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-002/2024, referred to here as genotype B3.13 virus, was obtained from the US Department of Agriculture. Both viruses were propagated at a multiplicity of infection of 0.001 on MDCK cells until complete cytopathic effects (CPEs) were observed. Viral growth medium consisted of MEM supplemented with 0.2% bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich, A7030) with l-[(toluene-4-sulphonamido)-2-phenyl] ethyl chloromethyl ketone (1 μg/ml)–trypsin.Generation of vaccine virus by reverse geneticsThe sequences encoding HA and NA genes from the B3.13 H5N1 virus were cloned individually into pHW2000 plasmids. The multiple basic amino acids in the HA protein cleavage site were removed. The HA and NA plasmids, together with the six plasmids representing the rest of the gene segments from A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (PR8), were cotransfected into HEK-293T and MDCK cells to rescue the PR8 + B3.13 (6 + 2) virus (vaccine virus) using reverse genetics (37). Three days posttransfection, supernatant was harvested and used to inoculate 11-day-old embryonated chicken eggs, obtained from the University of Saskatchewan Poultry Teaching and Research Unit. At 3 DPI, allantoic fluid was harvested and inactivated with β-propiolactone at a final concentration of 0.1%, using our validated protocol (38). The inactivated virus was diluted in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Cytiva, SH30256.01) and prepared as a W/O/W vaccine emulsion using, MONTANIDE ISA 201 VG adjuvant (Seppic, Air Liquide Healthcare) following the manufacturer’s directions. One vaccine dose consisted of 1-ml total volume [55% adjuvant:45% antigen in PBS (v/v)] containing 1 × 106 TCID50.Biosafety and ethics statementAll work involving infectious HPAI H5N1 virus was performed in containment level 3 (CL3) laboratories and CL3 large animal facilities at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization (VIDO). Work was completed in compliance with the Canadian Biosafety Standard, third edition, under the authority of the Public Health Agency of Canada and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency. All animal experiments were completed at the University of Saskatchewan following guidelines provided by the Canadian Council on Animal Care and approved by the University Animal Care Committee (protocol no. 20240042).AnimalsTen Alpine dairy goats were sourced from a farm in Saskatchewan, Canada, and housed at the CL3 large animal facility at VIDO. Goats were fed an ad libitum diet consisting of alfalfa timothy hay cube pelleted ration (dairy ration, 16% protein) and water. Goats, milked once daily, were brought onto a milking stanchion (Sydell Inc.), and visible debris was removed from each teat using a WypAll general-purpose wipe saturated with an iodine-based disinfectant. Teats were manually stripped two to three times to allow milk let-down, followed by an additional wipe with the iodine disinfectant before sample collection. Milk from left and right glands was then manually stripped into individual specimen cups for sampling followed by the use of a portable milking machine to complete milk collection. The collection vessel containing the milk was weighed, and milk weights for each goat were recorded. One milking machine was dedicated to the vaccinated goat cohort and the other to the unvaccinated cohort. Individual claws on the machine were paired with designated teats (i.e., left and right) so that the claw was used on the same teat at every milking. After each daily milking, the machines were disinfected with hot water, detergent then sanitizer (12% sodium hypochlorite diluted to 200 parts per million). Gloves worn by personnel were disinfected with Prevail after handling the inoculated gland.Study design: Genotype D1.1 virus inoculationThree goats were acclimated for 7 days before viral challenge. Age and parity of all goats can be found in table S6. All three goats were inoculated in the right mammary gland with 104 TCID50 of HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 in MEM medium (Fig. 1A). The virus inoculum was back titrated to confirm dose. After milking, 1 ml of the viral inoculum was drawn into a sterile 3-ml syringe fitted with a sterile teat cannula. The teat orifice was disinfected using isopropyl alcohol wipes before infusion. The teat cannula was inserted its full length before depositing the solution into the teat canal. Firm pressure was applied to the base of the teat while the cannula was withdrawn and the teat was massaged upward to facilitate movement of the inoculum into the teat cistern. Before the study was initiated, one goat was preselected to be euthanized at 4 DPI (D4) during the period of peak viral shedding in milk, which had previously been identified in dairy cows (20). The remaining two goats were euthanized at 19 DPI (D19) by intravenous injection with Dorminal (20 ml per 45 kg of body weight; Rafter 8 Products Inc.) after resolution of infectious virus shedding in milk.Study design: Vaccination, B3.13 virus challenge, and rechallengeSeven goats were acclimated for 7 days. At D0 (prime) and D21 (boost), three goats were vaccinated subcutaneously in the neck with inactivated vaccine virus formulated with Montanide ISA 201 VG adjuvant (VACC group, n = 3), or with adjuvant alone (ADJ group, n = 3) (Fig. 4A). Groups were balanced in terms of age and parity of goats (table S6). One goat (goat #4) received neither vaccine nor adjuvant. full_text_sections.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 virus spillover into dairy cows represents the emergence of a mammalian host capable of sustaining a panzootic and creates a transmission pathway to humans. HPAI research involving dairy cows is constrained by the space requirements needed to house large animals in high biocontainment. A small ruminant model would enable larger sample sizes while reducing costs, improving safety, and lowering logistical barriers to conduct research. Here, we establish dairy goats as a model for HPAI mammary infection. Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and genotype B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. Parenteral vaccination with an inactivated virus induced antigen-specific antibodies in blood and milk, reduced clinical disease, limited virus shedding in milk, and mitigated milk production losses. HPAI H5N1 disease dynamics in dairy cows can be recapitulated in dairy goats, providing a relevant model for investigating pathogenesis and for supporting the development of control strategies.

full_text_sections.results: RESULTSClinical observations following inoculation with H5N1 genotype D1.1Three lactating goats were inoculated with 104 median tissue culture infectious dose (TCID50) of H5N1 genotype D1.1 virus in the right mammary gland through the teat canal; the left gland was untreated (Fig. 1A). Goat #2 was euthanized at 4 days postinoculation (DPI) [day 4 of study (D4)] to examine disease pathology, viral tissue distribution, and viral load. Goats #1 and #3 had elevated rectal temperatures at 2 DPI (D2) that returned to baseline by 5 DPI (D5), whereas rectal temperatures in goat #2 remained unchanged (Fig. 1B). Goats did not show any behavioral changes or clinical signs of respiratory distress after inoculation. Milk yield decreased by 50 to 70% in all three goats by 3 DPI (D3). Milk yield in goat #2 recovered completely by 4 DPI (D4). The other two goats rebounded to 80 to 100%, relative to day 0, by 2 to 3 weeks postinoculation (Fig. 1C). At 3 DPI (D3), right gland milk from goats #1 and #3 was discolored; no other clinical signs of mastitis nor changes in milk quality were noted throughout the remainder of the study (Fig. 1D and fig. One goat was euthanized at 4 DPI (D4) during peak virus shedding in milk to examine viral tissue distribution; the remaining two goats were euthanized at 19 DPI (D19). Created in BioRender. L. Aubrey (2026), https://BioRender.com/n56rps1. (B) Rectal temperatures for each goat (G1 to G3) postinoculation expressed as change (∆) relative to 0 DPI (D0). Mastitis severity was scored from 0 to 3 (0 = normal; 1 = abnormal milk: thick, clumped, and discolored; 2 = abnormal milk and visual udder edema, swelling, and redness; 3 = severe udder swelling, purple discoloration, systemic signs, and depression); x indicates no data were collected. Lesions involve up to ∼20% of the examined tissue. The left mammary gland demonstrated normal alveolar architecture consistent with unremarkable histology. The right mammary gland exhibited multifocal neutrophilic infiltration within the stroma but predominantly in the alveolar lumen, accompanied by necrotic cellular debris in the lumen and attenuation of luminal epithelial cells with vacuolation. On the sections examined, 20% of the areas were affected. full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONHPAI H5N1 has emerged as a novel mammary infection in dairy cows. The physical size of these animals is a major barrier for many laboratories to conduct HPAI research. This proof-of-concept study demonstrates that dairy goats represent a relevant model for HPAI H5N1 mammary infection, given their susceptibility to both D1.1 and B3.13 genotypes and their recapitulation of clinical and virological features similar to those observed in dairy cows (13, 19, 20). Field reports indicate that genotype D1.1 infection in dairy cows causes milder or subclinical disease compared with genotype B3.13 (32). Our preliminary observations suggest that this might be similar in dairy goats. Genotype D1.1 infection resulted in less severe mastitis, a smaller impact on milk yield, no observable changes in milk quality, and a more pronounced rebound in milk production (Fig. 1). The genotype D1.1 virus used in this study was isolated from Canada goose and has avian associated PB2 signatures 627E and 701D but lacks the mammalian-adaptive PB2 M631L substitution that is present in the genotype B3.13 bovine H5N1 isolate. Despite these genetic differences, viral shedding in milk was comparable between the genotypes, indicating that disease severity was influenced by factors beyond viral replication. This likely includes differences in other viral proteins that are known to contribute to pathogenicity, such as NS1, PB1-F2, and PA-X (33–35). Viremia was not evident for either genotype, although low levels of viral RNA were sporadically detected in blood. Genotype D1.1 remained localized to the inoculated right mammary gland with the one goat sacrificed at 4 DPI (D4), revealing that there was minimal spread to extramammary tissues and lymph nodes; by contrast, genotype B3.13 infection was associated with high viral RNA levels in multiple extramammary tissues in the one goat sacrificed at 5 DPC (D5) (table S1 and Fig. 3C). These observations are based on one animal per genotype at a single time point, warranting further validation to determine whether dissemination dynamics is a unique feature for these genotypes. Generally, dissemination of the virus to uninoculated mammary glands is rare in experimental intramammary H5N1 infection of cows, which is similarly observed in all goats, with exception of one goat in which genotype B3.13 infection was detected in both the inoculated and uninoculated mammary gland (Fig. 3, D and E) (19–21). Although the exact cause is unclear, possible explanations include exposure during animal handling, contamination during milking, or virus dissemination within the goat. This model facilitates HPAI H5N1 pathogenesis research in the mammary gland and offers a platform to investigate emerging and existing HPAI H5Nx strains of both avian and mammalian origin.Parenteral administration of the inactivated virus formulated with Montanide ISA 201 adjuvant had no negative effect on milk production in dairy goats. Overall, the vaccine conferred partial protection by reducing the severity of clinical mastitis and significantly limiting milk production losses following challenge (Fig. 5, A, B, and D). Immunization reduced the onset, duration, and amount of infectious virus shedding in milk when compared with the adjuvant alone group (Fig. 5F). We noted a discordance in infectious virus titers and viral RNA in milk of VACC goats, but not ADJ goats (Fig. 5, E and F). Viral titers converted from viral RNA levels were greater than infectious virus recovered in the VACC goats (Fig. 5, E and F), suggesting that H5N1 was replicating in the tissue, but either was subsequently bound by neutralizing antibodies in milk or that immune-mediated clearance of infected cells resulted in shedding of viral debris, including nucleic acids, into milk. Immunization induced VN and NP-specific antibodies as well as H5-specific IgG antibodies, although VN and NP-specific antibodies were undetectable in milk before challenge (Fig. 4). After challenge, VN titers were similar in right and left gland milk of VACC goats, whereas ADJ goats had lower titers in the uninoculated left gland milk compared with right gland milk (Fig. 4, D and E). Together, these data indicate that vaccination was safe and primed immune responses that mitigated clinical disease but did not confer sterilizing immunity. Our vaccine virus contained the hemagglutinin (HA; H5) and neuraminidase (NA; N1) proteins from the genotype B3.13 virus, but the internal protein-encoding genes were derived from the PR8 strain, which supports high yields of the vaccine virus in embryonated eggs. As immunodominant T cell epitopes are associated with internal influenza proteins, this mismatch with the genotype B3.13 strain might have limited T cell immunity and could be one reason why vaccination did not achieve complete protective immunity (36). Vaccine delivery route, together with dose and adjuvant optimization, requires further evaluation to determine which factors limited protective immunity in the udder. The dairy goat model established herein provides a platform for HPAI H5Nx vaccine development, screening, and assessing protective efficacy. In addition to improving vaccine design, consideration of cross-protection is necessary given the circulation of the two different H5N1 genotypes in cows. Natural immunity provides limited cross-protection in dairy cows, thus multivalent vaccine approaches are likely needed (21, 22). We propose that the dairy goat model can also be used to evaluate multivalent vaccine approaches given their susceptibility to both genotypes. The smaller stature of dairy goats, relative to dairy cows, allows for greater occupancy within high biocontainment agricultural rooms enabling researchers to use larger group sizes needed for robust group-level comparisons.Inactivated, DNA and mRNA H5N1 vaccines have previously been tested in cows. These vaccines prevented shedding of infectious virus in milk, although, in the absence of viral RNA detection, it is unclear whether sterilizing immunity was achieved (30, 31). Our data emphasize the importance of measuring both infectious virus and viral RNA to provide a complete picture of replication dynamics.In this study, infection-induced immunity in ADJ goats conferred protection against reinfection, consistent with our observations in dairy cows (20). Reexposing ADJ goats to H5N1 by inoculating into the left mammary gland did not result in clinical mastitis, milk production losses, or viral shedding; neither viral RNA nor infectious virus was detected. Before reexposing ADJ goats to H5N1, VN antibodies were not readily detected in left gland milk, yet all goats were protected from reinfection. However, anti-H5 IgG antibodies were detected in left gland milk of all ADJ goats, confirming the presence of antigen-specific antibodies in milk before rechallenge. This suggests that even low levels of antibodies correlate with protective immunity, similar to our observations in dairy cows, where low milk VN titers of 1:10 were associated with protection (20). Cell-mediated immunity in the udder likely plays an important role in immune protection, but to what extent remains to be determined. Defining the contribution of T cell–mediated responses to H5N1 infection is warranted to provide a complete understanding of host immunity.The emergence of HPAI H5N1 virus in dairy cows reveals a new mammalian host and tissue tropism that can trigger an avian influenza panzootic and introduces a novel pathway for zoonotic transmission to humans. This ongoing pandemic threat underscores the need for preparedness strategies that block cross-species transmission. Relevant H5N1 mammary infection models, such as the goat model, will become critically important for addressing key knowledge gaps and supporting the development of effective countermeasures to combat this public health threat.
full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONHighly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5Nx clade 2.3.4.4b has spread globally since 2020, resulting in extensive mortality in wild birds and commercial poultry (1–3). During its circulation, this clade has undergone extensive reassortment and expanded into an unusually broad host range, including many mammalian species (2, 4, 5). In 2024, HPAI H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13 was detected in dairy cows in the USA, introduced through a single transmission event from wild birds, followed by widespread cow-to-cow transmission within dairy herds in the USA (6). Historically, cattle were not affected by influenza A virus as evidenced by the rare occurrence of natural infections (7, 8). Since the initial HPAI H5N1 detection, three separate introductions to dairy cattle in the USA have been detected, all of clade 2.3.4.4b genotype D1.1, the dominant genotype in North American flyways (9, 10). Genotype B3.13 emerged in North America through reassortment between Eurasian 2.3.4.4.b lineage A1 viruses and circulating low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI), incorporating four segments from lineage A1 (PA, HA, NA, and M) and four segments from LPAI. Similarly, genotype D1.1 comprises four 2.3.4.4b A3 lineage segments (HA, PB1, M, and NS) and four from North American LPAI (11). To date, H5N1 has been confirmed in 1088 dairy cattle herds in 19 US states (12). Nearly all of these detections have been associated with genotype B3.13, whereas the genotype D1.1 spillovers have been reported in a small number of herds and were quickly contained (10). Experimental studies show that the virus primarily replicates in the bovine mammary gland, leading to acute mastitis and shedding of infectious virus in milk (13, 14). HPAI H5N1 outbreaks in dairy herds have major economic impacts for producers due to decreased milk yield that can persist for up to 2 months postinfection, increased culling due to reproductive issues and losses in productivity, and herd-replacement costs (14). HPAI H5N1 was likely introduced to other US dairy herds due to transport of infected cattle (6). Cow-to-cow transmission is thought to occur through the use of contaminated milking equipment, although this has not been recapitulated under experimental settings and additional transmission routes could be involved (6, 15). HPAI H5N1–infected dairy cows have been responsible for further transmission to nearby commercial poultry flocks, barn cats, humans working in close proximity to infected cows, and wildlife such as raccoons and birds, demonstrating that dairy cows can both sustain a panzootic and act as a new transmission pathway for HPAI H5N1 to humans (6, 13). In humans, previous HPAI H5N1 infections acquired from wild birds have been associated with high mortality rates; however, the 41 reported human cases linked to cattle exposure all resulted in mild respiratory-like illness and conjunctivitis (16–18). This increased circulation of HPAI in mammals always raises concerns of mammalian adaptations or reassortment with seasonal influenza viruses that can increase fitness and enable transmission in humans, potentially leading to a serious public health threat (19).We previously showed that experimental H5N1 infection of dairy cows induced natural immunity, which included virus-specific antibodies in milk that neutralized high titers of H5N1 and conferred protection against reinfection (20). Natural immunity in dairy cows persists for at least 1 year, as evidenced by protection against homologous experimental challenge, and is associated with neutralizing antibodies in milk (21, 22). These observations conceptually support that vaccines can be developed that elicit durable and protective immune responses in the udder (23).Conducting HPAI research in cows requires high biocontainment agricultural facilities, and the physical space requirements for these large ruminants exclude many laboratories from performing HPAI studies in the natural host. Goats are a small ruminant that are susceptible to HPAI and have mammary gland architecture comparable to dairy cows, therefore representing a potential surrogate model (24–27). In both species, immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibodies are transferred transepithelially from the blood to the milk and peripherally derived lymphocytes traffic to the mammary gland (28, 29). This supports that parenteral vaccination can generate immune responses that protect the mammary gland. In two separate studies, parenteral vaccination of dairy cows with either an mRNA, DNA, or inactivated virus vaccine induced serum and milk neutralizing antibodies, and no infectious virus was detected in milk following homologous intramammary challenge (30, 31). However, these studies did not report whether vaccination protected cows from milk production losses after challenge or measure viral RNA to confirm the absence of virus in milk. Further refinement of H5N1 vaccine strategies will benefit from a small ruminant surrogate model to support larger sample sizes and provides advantages in animal handling, costs, and safety when working with this high consequence pathogen.Here, we establish dairy goats as a relevant model for HPAI H5N1 mammary infection, bridging a major research gap between large ruminant animals and conventional laboratory models (i.e., mice and ferrets), which differ substantially in their mammary gland architecture. This model provides a biologically relevant species to interrogate existing and emerging H5Nx virus pathogenesis, host immune responses, and countermeasures. Goats #1 and #3 had elevated rectal temperatures at 2 DPI (D2) that returned to baseline by 5 DPI (D5), whereas rectal temperatures in goat #2 remained unchanged (Fig. 1B). Goats did not show any behavioral changes or clinical signs of respiratory distress after inoculation. Milk yield decreased by 50 to 70% in all three goats by 3 DPI (D3). Milk yield in goat #2 recovered completely by 4 DPI (D4). The other two goats rebounded to 80 to 100%, relative to day 0, by 2 to 3 weeks postinoculation (Fig. 1C). At 3 DPI (D3), right gland milk from goats #1 and #3 was discolored; no other clinical signs of mastitis nor changes in milk quality were noted throughout the remainder of the study (Fig. 1D and fig. papers.title_original: A caprine mammary infection model for highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop a caprine mammary infection model to investigate the pathogenesis and immune response to highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, addressing the need for a relevant animal model to study viral transmission and disease progression in livestock.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved seven goats acclimated for 7 days, with three vaccinated subcutaneously in the neck and three receiving adjuvant alone. One milking machine was dedicated to each vaccinated and unvaccinated cohort, and all procedures were conducted in CL3 laboratories.
analysis.methods: Goats were inoculated with HPAI H5N1 genotypes D1.1 and B3.13, and viral load was measured using TCID50 assays. Serum and milk samples were collected for virus neutralization and ELISA tests, with clinical scoring based on rectal temperatures and signs of respiration, depression, and mastitis.
analysis.main_results: Intramammary inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotype D1.1 and B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding in milk. The vaccine group showed reduced clinical signs and viral shedding compared to the adjuvant-only group.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence of the model's utility in studying H5N1 pathogenesis and immune response, highlighting its potential for vaccine development and efficacy testing.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of vaccines and the understanding of H5N1 transmission in livestock, which is critical for preventing zoonotic spread and ensuring food safety.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its small sample size and the use of a single animal species, but the results are supported by direct observations and validated protocols, providing moderate confidence in the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study developed a caprine mammary infection model to investigate the pathogenesis and immune response to highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1. Seven goats were acclimated and divided into vaccinated and adjuvant-only groups. Inoculation with HPAI H5N1 genotypes D1.1 and B3.13 resulted in acute mastitis, decreased milk yield, and high virus shedding. The vaccinated group showed reduced clinical signs and viral shedding. The model's utility for vaccine development and efficacy testing was highlighted, though its small sample size and limited host scope may affect generalizability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to direct observations and validated methods.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在开发山羊乳腺感染模型,以研究高致病性禽流感 H5N1 的 传播 和 免疫应答,满足对相关动物模型研究病毒 传播 和牲畜疾病进展的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及七只山羊,经过 7 天的适应,其中三只山羊在颈部皮下注射疫苗,三只只接受佐剂。每只接种疫苗和未接种疫苗的 队列研究 都有一台挤奶机,所有程序均在 CL3 实验室进行。
elements_zh.methods: 山羊接种 HPAI H5N1 基因型 D1.1 和 B3.13,并使用 TCID50 测定法测量病毒载量。收集血清和乳汁样本进行病毒中和和 ELISA 测试,并根据直肠温度和呼吸、抑郁和乳腺炎体征进行临床评分。
elements_zh.main_results: 乳房内接种 HPAI H5N1 基因型 D1.1 和 B3.13 会导致急性乳腺炎、产奶量下降和牛奶中病毒大量脱落。与仅使用佐剂的组相比,疫苗 组的临床症状和病毒脱落有所减少。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为该模型在研究 H5N1 发病机制 和 免疫应答 中的实用性的证据,强调了其在 疫苗 开发和功效测试中的潜力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 疫苗 的开发和对牲畜中 H5N1 传播 的理解提供了信息,这对于防止人畜共患传播和确保食品安全至关重要。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和使用单一动物物种的限制,但结果得到了直接观察和经过验证的方案的支持,为研究结果提供了适度的可信度。

analysis_zh.main_results: 乳房内接种 HPAI H5N1 基因型 D1.1 和 B3.13 会导致急性乳腺炎、产奶量下降和牛奶中病毒大量脱落。与仅使用佐剂的组相比,疫苗 组的临床症状和病毒脱落有所减少。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为该模型在研究 H5N1 发病机制 和 免疫应答 中的实用性的证据,强调了其在 疫苗 开发和功效测试中的潜力。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 疫苗 的开发和对牲畜中 H5N1 传播 的理解提供了信息,这对于防止人畜共患传播和确保食品安全至关重要。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到样本量小和使用单一动物物种的限制,但结果得到了直接观察和经过验证的方案的支持,为研究结果提供了适度的可信度。

papers.full_text: AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity. These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. MATERIALS AND METHODSCollection and purification of LCTG-001SIgA was purified and pooled from the breast milk of 120 lactating individuals, as described previously (13). Briefly, frozen human milk was thawed and clarified through centrifugation and dialyzed in PBS. The supernatant was loaded onto a CaptureSelect IgA Affinity Matrix resin, and IgA was isolated as previously described (13). Pooled elution fractions were dialyzed in PBS and filtered. The final concentration was determined using a spectrophotometer.SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresisTwo micrograms of LCTG-001 was mixed with 4× lithium dodecyl sulfate loading dye and β-mercaptoethanol at 95°C for 10 min. Sample was loaded onto a 4 to 12% bis-tris gel (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and ran at 100 V for 90 min with Bolt Mops SDS running buffer (Invitrogen). The gel was stained with Coomassie blue for 30 min at room temperature and destained using 40% methanol and 10% acetic acid in water.Neutrophil isolationNeutrophils were isolated from peripheral blood of consenting healthy male and female donors as described previously, using density gradient centrifugation (29, 30). Studies were approved by the Hamilton Integrated Research Ethics Board. Briefly, blood was collected into EDTA-coated tubes via venipuncture. Three milliliters of Histopaque 1119 and 3 ml of Histopaque 1077 were layered in a 15-ml Falcon tube, followed by 6 ml of blood. Samples were centrifuged at 2000 rpm for 30 min at room temperature with no deceleration in an Allegra X-12R centrifuge (Beckman Coulter). The neutrophil layer was collected between the Histopaque layers and red blood cells (RBCs). Neutrophils were diluted in 50 ml of cold polymorphonuclear cell (PMN) buffer [0.5% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.3 mM EDTA (Invitrogen) in Hank’s balanced salt solution (Gibco)]. Diluted cells were centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The supernatant was discarded, the pellet was resuspended, and RBCs were lysed using ammonium-chloride-potassium (ACK) lysis buffer [NH4Cl (8.3 g/liter), KHCO3 (1 g/liter), and 0.05 mM EDTA, in sterile distilled H2O]. Cells were incubated with ACK lysis buffer for 5 min with agitation every 30 s. Following incubation, cells were diluted in 50 ml of PMN buffer and centrifuged at 1400 rpm for 5 min at room temperature, followed by an additional wash with PMN buffer. Cells were resuspended in a final volume of 1 ml in PMN buffer.Cells and virusesHuman adenocarcinoma alveolar basal epithelial (A549) cells [American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)] and human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (ATCC) were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells (ATCC) were maintained in Earle’s minimal essential medium (MEM Earles) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, 1% of 1 M sodium pyruvate, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Hep-2 cells (ATCC) were maintained in minimum essential medium (MEM) containing 10% FBS (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX supplement (Gibco), 1% of 1 M Hepes, and penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/ml; Gibco) at 37°C and 5% CO2. Expi293 cells (Gibco) were maintained at 37°C and 8% CO2 with regular agitation (150 rpm) in Expi293 expression medium (Gibco).A/Netherlands/602/2009 H1N1 (NL/09) and X-31 (gifts from P. Palese, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, NY) were propagated in 10-day-old embryonated chicken eggs as per standard protocols (24). X-31 is a reassortant virus with the internal genes of A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 H1N1 (PR8) and the HA and NA of A/Hong Kong/1/1968 H3N2 (HK/68). A/California/04/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09) (gift from P. Palese) and A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 (clade 2.3.4.4b) (gift from Y. Berhane, CFIA, MB) were grown in MDCK cells. Cells were infected at 70% viability at a multiplicity of infection of 0.1 and incubated for 1 hour at 37°C. Following incubation, virus was removed and replaced with 1× infection media [1× MEM (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.6% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1× MEM amino acids (Gibco), 1× MEM vitamin solution (Gibco), 1× GlutaMAX (Gibco), 1× penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), 0.6% sodium bicarbonate, 1× Hepes, and tolylsulfonyl phenylalanyl chloromethyl ketone (TPCK)–treated trypsin (1 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich)]. The supernatant was collected 48 hours following infection by centrifugation at 500g for 5 min. RSV A2 expressing green fluorescent protein (GFP; ViraTree) was grown in Hep-2 cells. E1/E3-deleted HuAd serotype 5 expressing GFP was a gift from Z. Xing (McMaster University, ON).H5N1 2.3.4.4b VLP productionPlasmids encoding the HA and NA from A/seal/QC/FAV869-3/2022 H5N1 were a gift from M. Côté (University of Ottawa, ON). HEK 293T cells were seeded in T150 flasks and transfected with HA and NA plasmids using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 240 μl of lipofectamine was incubated with 8 ml of Opti-MEM (Gibco) for 7.5 min. During the incubation, 32 μg of each plasmid was diluted with 8 ml of Opti-MEM. Lipofectamine and plasmid mixtures were combined and incubated at room temperature for 25 min. After the incubation, 10 ml of supplemented DMEM (2% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% GlutaMAX, and 1% Hepes) was added to the transfection mixture and incubated on cells overnight at 37°C and 5% CO2. The next day, media was replaced with DMEM containing 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX. The cell supernatant was collected 4 days posttransfection and centrifuged at 3000g for 2 min. The pellet was removed, and the supernatant was stored at −80°C.Transmission electron microscopyA 3-μl drop of sample was applied to a formvar-coated copper grid stabilized with a 5-nm carbon film and left for 10 min to allow for the VLPs to settle on the grid. Excess sample was blotted off with filter paper. The grids were then briefly rinsed by immersion in deionized water and blotted dry with filter paper. Then, 3 μl of 1% (aq) uranyl acetate was applied to the grid surface and left for 1 min. Excess stain was removed by blotting with filter paper, and the grid was allowed to dry completely. Imaging of the grids was performed using a TALOS L120C transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operating at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. Images were acquired with a 4K CETA complementary metal-oxide semiconductor camera.Influenza A virus purificationClarified supernatants from IAV-infected MDCK cells or allantoic fluid from embryonated chicken eggs were layered on top of 8 ml of 20% sucrose in NTE [0.5 M NaCl, 10 mM tris HCl, and 1 mM EDTA (pH 7.5)] buffer in Ultra-Clear Ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 2 hours at 4°C at 76650g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Clarified supernatants from VLP-transfected 293T cells were layered on top of 3 ml of 20% glycerol in PBS in Ultra-Clear Ultracentrifuge tubes (Beckman Coulter). Samples were spun for 4 hours at 4°C at 135,000g inside a SW 32i rotor using an Optima L-90K Ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Purified viruses and VLPs were quantified using a bicinchoninic acid assay Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.Recombinant antigenscH6/1 HA was a gift from P. Palese (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, NY). cH6/1 is composed of the H6 HA head domain from A/mallard/Sweden/81/02 H6N1 and H1 HA stalk domain from PR8. HK/68 HA was made using the Expi293 expression system. Expi293 cells (Gibco) were transfected with plasmid encoding HK/68 HA (gift from A. McDermott, NIAID, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Proteins were purified by Ni resin affinity chromatography. RSV A2 fusion protein (RSV-F), Cal/09 HA, A/American wigeon/South Carolina/AH0195145/2021 (H5N1) HA, and A/Texas/37/2024 (H5N1) NA were purchased from SinoBiological. Lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells was a gift from Z. Xing (McMaster University, ON).Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assaysThe 96-well NUNC-MaxiSorp plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4°C with purified soluble Cal/09 HA, HK/68 HA, cH6/1 HA, H5 HA, N1 NA, RSV-F recombinant protein, or purified 2.3.4.4b H5N1 VLPs, diluted to 2 μg/ml in bicarbonate-carbonate coating buffer (pH 9.4). For HuAd5 ELISAs, plates were coated with 50 μl of Ad-5–infected HeLa cell lysate (100 μg/ml) in PBS. Plates were blocked for 1 hour at 37°C with reagent diluent [0.5% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.02% sodium azide, in 1× tris-Tween buffer]. LCTG-001 was serially diluted 1:2 across each row. For in vivo biodistribution studies, homogenized lung tissue or BAL fluid was serially diluted 1:2 across each row. Following a 1-hour incubation at 37°C, plates were washed three times with 1× tris-Tween wash buffer. After washing, goat anti-human-biotin IgA (Southern Biotech) was diluted 1:2000 in reagent diluent and added to all wells. Plates were again incubated for 1 hour at 37°C, followed by three washes with 1× tris-Tween buffer. A streptavidin-alkaline phosphatase secondary antibody (1:2000, Southern Biotech) was added to all wells for 1 hour at 37°C. Plates were subsequently washed three times before addition of pNPP one component microwell substrate solution (Southern Biotech) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume 3 N sodium hydroxide. The optical density (OD) at 405 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of control wells with no sample.MNT assays Human adenovirus MNT The day before infection, 96-well plates of A549 cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 105 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Cells were subsequently incubated with serial dilutions of LCTG-001 and an E1/E3-deleted HuAd serotype 5 expressing GFP (gift from Z. Xing, McMaster University, Hamilton, ON, Canada) (1.6 × 106 PFU per well) for 24 hours at 37°C and 5% CO2 in α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco). Postincubation, fluorescence (GFP) was read using Cytation 5 (Agilent, Biotek). Neutralization titer was determined as the highest antibody dilution that achieved a 50% reduction in fluorescence compared to the virus control wells. Respiratory syncytial virus MNT The day before infection, Hep-2 cells were seeded at a density of 2.5 × 104 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Cells were subsequently incubated with serial dilutions of LCTG-001 and RSV GFP (ViraTree) (4 × 103 PFU per well) for 1 hour at 37°C, 5% CO2. The antibody/virus mixture was removed and replenished with fresh DMEM supplemented with 2% FBS, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% Hepes (pH 7.3), and 1% GlutaMAX for 24 hours at 37°C, 5% CO2. Postincubation, fluorescence (GFP) was read using Cytation 5 (Agilent, Biotek). Neutralization titer was determined as the highest antibody dilution that achieved a 50% reduction in fluorescence compared to the virus control wells. Influenza A virus MNT The day before infection, 96-well plates of MDCK cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 104 cells per well in clear flat-bottom TC-treated 96-well plates (Corning). Serial dilution of LCTG-001 and viruses (3600 PFU Cal/09 or 24500 PFU X-31) were preincubated for 30 min at 37°C and 5% CO2 in DMEM supplemented with 0.3% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich), 0.1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), and TPCK (1 μg/ml)–treated trypsin (Sigma-Aldrich). Following incubation, MDCK cells were infected with the LCTG-001–virus mixture for 1 hour at 37°C and 5% CO2. After the 1-hour infection, the infectious media was replaced with fresh supplemented DMEM. Plates were incubated for 18 hours and then fixed with 80% acetone for 20 min at −20°C before blocking with 5% nonfat milk in PBS for 30 min at room temperature, followed by an incubation in 3% hydrogen peroxide for 20 min at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before a 1-hour incubation at room temperature with a 1:2000 dilution of biotin-conjugated mouse anti-NP (Millipore) in 5% nonfat milk. Following incubation, plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer and incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with a secondary horseradish peroxidase (HRP)–conjugated streptavidin (1:5000, Millipore). Plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before the addition of SigmaFast OPD (Sigma-Aldrich) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume of 3 M hydrochloric acid. The OD at 490 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of uninfected control wells, and percent neutralization was calculated on the basis of the ratio between the sample OD value to infected control values.Enzyme-linked lectin assaysThe 96-well NUNC-MaxiSorp plates (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were coated overnight at 4°C with fetuin (25 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in 1× KPL coating buffer (SeraCare). In a separate plate, LCTG-001 was serially diluted in sample diluent [MES (Life Technologies) (pH 6.5), 20 mM CaCl2, 1% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5% Tween 20]. Virus (Cal/09, X-31, or H5N1 VLPs) was diluted to 90% of the max OD (predetermined) in sample diluent. Fetuin-coated plates were washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer, and LCTG-001 dilutions and virus were transferred to the fetuin-coated plate. Plates were incubated overnight at 37°C. Following incubation, plates were washed six times with PBS-Tween wash buffer. Peanut agglutinin (PNA)–HRP (1 mg/ml) was diluted 1:500 in PNA-HRP diluent [MES (pH 6.5), 20 mM CaCl2, and 1% BSA] and added to all wells for 2 hours at room temperature. Plates were then washed three times with PBS-Tween wash buffer before the addition of SigmaFast OPD (Sigma-Aldrich) to each well. Plates were developed for 10 min, and the reaction was quenched with an equal volume of 3 M hydrochloric acid. The OD at 490 nm was read on a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent). OD values were normalized on the basis of control wells without virus, and percent inhibition was calculated on the basis of the ratio between the sample OD value to control values with virus only.Luminol assaysLuminol assays were performed as previously described (30). Briefly, immune complexes were formed by incubating 2.5 μg of virus with 5 μg of LCTG-001 in 50 μl for 30 min at room temperature. Luminol (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to all wells. Following isolation, 5 × 105 cells of human neutrophils were added to each well. Kinetic measurements of luminescence [in relative light units (RLU)] were taken at 1-min intervals for 1 hour using a Biotek Synergy H1 (Agilent).MiceEight- to 12-week-old female BALB/c mice were purchased from Charles River Laboratories (Saint Constant, QC, Canada). B cell–deficient mice C.Cg-Igh-Jtm1Dhu of BALB/c background were purchased from Taconic Biosciences (Germantown, NY, USA). Animals were housed under specific pathogen–free conditions at McMaster University, Hamilton, ON. All animal protocols were reviewed and approved by the institutional Animal Research and Ethics Board (Animal Utilization Protocol 23-62).Antibody administration and IAV infectionAnimals received LCTG-001, PBS, and NL/09 intranasally as previously described (70). For antibody administration, animals were anesthetized with isoflurane and received a single bolus of 40 μl containing either 1 mg of LCTG-001 diluted in PBS or PBS as a negative control. Mice were infected with 450 PFU of NL/09, administered intranasally in a final volume of 40 μl diluted in PBS. Mice were monitored for weight loss and clinical signs daily, including huddling, lack of grooming, and lethargy. A reduction to 80% of initial weight was considered humane endpoint in accordance with institutional guidelines.Lung isolation and preparation for histologyMice were euthanized by exsanguination. Whole lungs were isolated as previously described (70), with some modifications. Briefly, lungs were removed from the mice and cannulated. full_text_sections.results: RESULTSAssessment of broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogensUnlike IgG in conventional IVIG or convalescent plasma, which is peripherally sourced from the circulation, SIgA is exclusively found at mucosal sites. Sourcing from the respiratory mucosa is not feasible due to procedural complexities and limited antibody yield. To circumvent these limitations, we explored breast milk as an alternative source of mucosal SIgA. Breast milk is a scalable and sustainable source of mucosal SIgA, and donations of extra breast milk are already collected by over 700 human milk banks worldwide. To produce purified SIgA, breast milk samples were collected from 120 lactating donors through collaborations with milk banks in Indianapolis and Pittsburgh. Initial sample shipments included 85 donor contributions received on 11 October 2022, followed by an additional 35 samples on 29 November 2022. The samples, collected throughout 2022, were pooled to yield a total volume of 15,585 ml. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. The purity of LCTG-001 was confirmed by Coomassie staining (fig. S1) and was consistent with previous reports (13). The donor cohort was not screened for recent infection or vaccination status, thereby aligning with conventional IVIG collection practices in which donors are not selected on the basis of prior antigenic exposures (3, 14).We next evaluated whether the polyclonal SIgA pool, LCTG-001, could recognize and neutralize a panel of respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human adenovirus (HuAd), and IAV. Representative strains and serotypes were selected for each virus to assess LCTG-001’s binding and neutralizing potency. To assess LCTG-001’s antiviral activity, we performed enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) to evaluate antibody binding, alongside microneutralization (MNT) assays to measure functional neutralization.We first assessed binding of LCTG-001 to RSV fusion protein (RSV-F), the antigen used in licensed RSV vaccines (15). LCTG-001 demonstrated robust binding to RSV-F (AUC = 62.02 ± 1.273; Fig. 1A), and these antibodies were able to neutralize RSV at physiologically relevant concentrations [median inhibitory concentration (IC50) = 320 μg/ml; Fig. 1B].Fig. 1.LCTG-001 has broad antiviral activity against a panel of common respiratory viral pathogens.(A, C, and E) LCTG-001 binding responses to RSV-F (A), HuAd5 lysate (C), and Cal/09 HA (E). (B, D, and F) LCTG-001 neutralizing antibody responses to RSV (B), HuAd5 (D), and Cal/09 (F), measured by percent (%) neutralization using MNT assays. Data presented in (A) to (F) represent mean ± SEM. Data presented in (A), (C), and (E) represent three technical replicates. Data presented in (B), (D), and (F) are from three independent experiments.We next assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against adenovirus, focusing on HuAd type 5 (HuAd5), one of the most prevalent HuAd serotypes (16, 17). ELISAs were performed using the lysate from HuAd5-infected HeLa cells as a source of antigen (18). Again, LCTG-001 demonstrated specific binding to the lysate of infected cells (AUC = 62.28 ± 2.309; Fig. 1C) and neutralized HuAd5 with considerable potency (IC50 = 180 μg/ml; Fig. 1D).Last, we assessed the antiviral activity of LCTG-001 against IAV. IAV is a respiratory virus responsible for both seasonal epidemics and sporadic pandemics, with five pandemics in the last century (19). We first investigated the ability of LCTG-001 to recognize and neutralize A/California/07/2009 H1N1 (Cal/09). Cal/09 (H1N1) is an isolate from the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which then circulated seasonally and was a recommended seasonal influenza vaccine strain for more than 5 years in North America. Hence, most of the population has been exposed through infection and/or vaccination. Similar to RSV and HuAd5, LCTG-001 showed specific binding to Cal/09 (H1N1) hemagglutinin (HA) (AUC = 54.76 ± 4.886; Fig. 1E) and neutralization activity (IC50 = 670 μg/ml; Fig. 1F). full_text_sections.discussion: DISCUSSIONIn this study, we evaluated the antiviral activity and protective efficacy of LCTG-001, a polyclonal SIgA product derived from pooled human breast milk, as a novel mucosal passive immunization strategy that can address the inherent limitations associated with conventional intravenous, IgG-based treatments. IVIG and monoclonal antibody passive immunization strategies, while standard of care in the field for conferring prophylactic and/or therapeutic protection against respiratory pathogens, often have limited transudation to the respiratory mucosa (36–39). These therapies are also logistically burdensome due to the need for parenteral administration in health care settings and are associated with a variety of side effects, including infusion-related reactions (40).In contrast to the periphery, the predominant antibody isotype found in the respiratory mucosa is SIgA. SIgA is actively transported across epithelial barriers and is highly resistant to proteolytic degradation, making it well suited for conferring protection within the respiratory mucosa (41). Moreover, SIgA is naturally localized to mucosa through polymeric immunoglobulin receptor–mediated epithelial transport, depositing IgA into the lumen where respiratory viruses establish infection, a targeted delivery that serum-derived IgG achieves only sparingly (11, 39, 41, 42).Our results demonstrate that LCTG-001 has broad-spectrum antiviral activity mediated by multiple mechanisms. This polyclonal SIgA neutralized diverse respiratory viruses, including RSV, adenovirus, and representatives of both circulating human group 1 and group 2 IAV subtypes, including those with pandemic potential, thereby highlighting its exceptionally broad reactivity. Similarly, polyclonal SIgA compositions administered via the intranasal and intratracheal route were able to neutralize SARS-CoV-2 in K18+ hACE2 transgenic mice (13). This breadth of activity likely arises from the rich and diverse pool of SIgA isolated from pooled breast milk, capturing a wide array of antibodies with varying specificities within a single product.Notably, LCTG-001 not only inhibited IAV viral entry in vitro but also exhibited robust NA inhibition. While NA antibodies may not be potently neutralizing, they can limit viral spread and have been shown to correlate with protection in influenza infection (43–45). Both HA stalk binding and NA-specific antibodies can contribute to NAI activity, the former through steric hindrance of the NA binding site and the latter by directly binding near the enzymatic site of the protein (26, 27). The presence of NAI activity suggests that LCTG-001 can impair virion release, even in the context of strains for which conventional neutralizing antibodies are absent. Furthermore, LCTG-001 induced Fc-dependent activation of neutrophils, as evidenced by a luminol-based assay. In humans, IgA is known to engage FcαRI (CD89) on myeloid cells, triggering processes like phagocytosis, respiratory burst, and NETosis (29, 30). Our data confirm that a complex SIgA pool from breast milk can harness this pathway. Thus, beyond classical neutralization, LCTG-001 is capable of activating innate immune cells to facilitate pathogen clearance. The ability of SIgA to activate neutrophils has important implications for mucosal defense. IgA is often viewed as a non-inflammatory “shield” that blocks pathogen entry. Here, we show that SIgA can also engage innate immunity, further facilitating pathogen clearance. This FcαRI-dependent mechanism adds a crucial layer of protection at mucosal surfaces.Our use of a polyclonal human SIgA pool from breast milk reveals the breadth of Fc-mediated activity of LCTG-001 in the context of IAV. Prior studies have mostly examined serum-derived or engineered monomeric IgA (29, 30, 46). SIgA can engage the FcαR on cells; however, this interaction requires accessory molecules such as MAC-1 and results in a lower affinity compared to cross-linked monomeric IgA (47–49). Hence, the ability of SIgA to engage Fc-mediated neutrophil effector functions in an IAV antigen–specific context has not been fully examined. We demonstrated that the polyclonal SIgA which comprises LCTG-001 retains the ability to engage Fc effector functions on neutrophils, triggering a potent effector response against three different strains of IAV. This novel finding further broadens the paradigm of how SIgA contributes to antiviral immunity, indicating that SIgA-based interventions could actively modulate the innate immune milieu in the airways during respiratory viral infection.Another notable aspect of LCTG-001’s efficacy is its breadth of antiviral activities against IAVs. Our data suggest that this polyclonal mixture appears to target multiple viral proteins and life cycle steps: We detected antibodies likely directed against the conserved HA stalk, those capable of inhibiting NA (mediating NAI), and antibodies capable of stimulating Fc-dependent effector functions. These modes of action are complementary, and the interplay between Fab-mediated and Fc-mediated functions is evident in our data. In essence, LCTG-001 may not rely on a single mechanism of action but rather uses a variety of effector functions to mediate protection against viral pathogens. This was evident after H1N1 challenge, where there was incomplete neutralization at the highest concentration of antibody tested. Despite this, we observed high binding activity to Cal/09 (H1N1) HA. The robust protection may be partially explained by the high level of NA inhibition and Fc-mediated neutrophil activity against Cal/09 (H1N1), which suggests the presence of antibodies with potent anti-IAV activity that may not demonstrate traditional neutralization in vitro. These diverse activities may be especially valuable for highly mutable viruses like IAV, where complete protection often requires neutralizing the virus as well as containing infection through immune effector mechanisms (3, 50–52).The cross-reactivity of LCTG-001 against an H5N1 avian influenza strain (clade 2.3.4.4b), despite no known exposure of donors to this strain, was particularly encouraging. These antibodies appear to be directed against the conserved group 1 HA stalk of H5 and to the N1 protein. This result suggests that the pool of human donor SIgA contains antibodies recognizing conserved epitopes shared with emerging avian viruses. VLPs were used to allow for work to be completed under standard biosafety level 2 conditions. Although VLPs generally preserve many of the structural and antigenic features of the wild-type virus, differences in particle assembly, glycosylation patterns, protein stoichiometry, and membrane composition can alter the presentation and accessibility of antigenic epitopes (53). Still, likely candidates for such cross-reactive targets are the HA stalk and NA (54, 55), as was confirmed by the observed binding activity of LCTG-001 to both recombinant HA and NA from 2.3.4.4b (H5N1). Through repeated infections or vaccinations with common IAV strains, antibodies likely accumulate in the breast milk that recognize conserved elements of potential pandemic viruses, in agreement with studies reporting cross-reactive serum IgG in humans (54, 56, 57). While these cross-reactive antibodies may not potently neutralize a novel strain, they can contribute to protection via secondary mechanisms such as by inhibiting the NA activity of the virus or by engaging Fc receptors for virus clearance. LCTG-001 could serve as a readily deployable passive immunization strategy in the face of an emerging influenza pandemic by providing immediate partial immunity while strain-specific vaccines or monoclonals are being developed. Even partial protection, by constricting viral replication or dampening undesired inflammation, could be life-saving during an outbreak of a novel virus, especially for immunocompromised individuals. full_text_sections.other: INTRODUCTIONImmunoglobulin replacement therapy, which can take the form of intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or subcutaneous immunoglobulin, is essential for mitigating infectious diseases and is especially critical in treating primary immunodeficiencies such as common variable immunodeficiency (CVID). CVID is characterized by impaired antibody production, manifesting as reduced levels of immunoglobulin G (IgG), IgA, and/or IgM (1, 2). Regular IVIG infusions are administered to patients with CVID to replenish immunoglobulin levels, thereby reducing infection frequency and severity (3). Despite its effectiveness, IVIG therapy is costly, invasive, and requires frequent medically assisted administration (1, 4).Beyond management of immunoglobulin immunodeficiencies, IVIG and convalescent plasma have also been used as passive immunization strategies to protect populations against viral infections, including in pandemic settings where vaccines are either unavailable or in limited supply. This was exemplified during the 1918 and 2009 influenza A virus (IAV) pandemics, as well as during the initial stages of COVID-19 (5–8). However, these strategies require intravenous administration of antibodies derived from the circulation, which are rich in IgG and monomeric IgA but differ markedly from the predominantly dimeric and secretory IgA (SIgA) present at mucosal surfaces (9). Thus, these approaches do not fully recapitulate the protective immune landscape of the respiratory mucosa found in healthy individuals (4, 10). In addition, antibodies administered intravenously must transudate from the circulation to the mucosal surfaces to exert their protective effects, which limits availability at respiratory surfaces (11). This limitation highlights the need for mucosally delivered passive immunization strategies which can deliver antibodies directly to the site of pathogen entry.Sourcing SIgA from human biospecimens, such as those found in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluids, is not practical due to the invasiveness of the procedures and the limited yield of antibodies. In contrast, breast milk is a more attractive source that is more plentiful, accessible, and rich in mucosal SIgA (12). Previous work has demonstrated that breast milk–derived SIgA has antiviral activity against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) and is a viable prophylactic strategy in preclinical models (13). This study used breast milk from human milk donors post–SARS-CoV-2 infection, thereby enriching the antibody pool for anti–SARS-CoV-2 antibodies. Building on these observations, we hypothesized that purifying IgA from a large sample of donors without screening milk samples for neutralizing antibodies against any particular pathogen would yield a polyclonal SIgA product with broad antiviral activity against a diverse array of respiratory pathogens due to varied donor exposures to infections and/or vaccinations, akin to IVIG.Here, we investigate a polyclonal, breast milk–derived SIgA product, LCTG-001. Our findings demonstrate that LCTG-001 exhibits broad antiviral activity in vitro against a panel of respiratory pathogens. We further demonstrate that LCTG-001 has neutralizing and nonneutralizing activity against both group 1 and group 2 IAVs, in addition to activity against emerging zoonotic strains. Last, we demonstrate that when delivered directly to the respiratory mucosa, LCTG-001 was protective in vivo against IAV challenge in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. Collectively, these results highlight mucosal delivery of breast milk–derived IgA as a passive immunization strategy capable of addressing limitations inherent in traditional intravenous antibody therapies, offering potential protection against both endemic and pandemic respiratory infections. papers.full_text_excerpt: These findings highlight the potential of breast milk–derived secretory IgA as a scalable, mucosa-targeted passive immunization strategy capable of addressing both endemic and emerging respiratory viral threats. Approximately 1 liter of this pooled milk was processed using a previously validated and patented purification method (13) to yield a polyclonal SIgA product, designated LCTG-001. AbstractPassive immunization is an important tool for protecting individuals with primary immune deficiencies from infectious diseases and offers a rapid response strategy for protecting vulnerable populations, particularly during the interval between pathogen emergence and vaccine deployment. Current approaches rely on intravenous delivery of IgG-enriched plasma or monoclonal antibodies, which limits accessibility, scalability, and effectiveness at mucosal surfaces, the primary entry point for respiratory viruses. Here, we tested LCTG-001, a polyclonal secretory IgA preparation derived from pooled human breast milk, to address these limitations. LCTG-001 demonstrated broad antiviral activity against clinically relevant respiratory viruses, including respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, and influenza A virus. LCTG-001 effectively recognized both group 1 and group 2 influenza A subtypes, including the highly pathogenic H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b, and engaged nonneutralizing effector mechanisms such as neuraminidase inhibition and neutrophil activation. When administered intranasally, LCTG-001 conferred complete protection against influenza A challenge in both immunocompetent and antibody-deficient murine models, preventing morbidity and mortality through a transient early reduction in viral burden followed by sustained improvements in lung pathology and lung barrier integrity.
