papers.title_original: Shifts in acute respiratory pathogen epidemiology: an 8-year surveillance study in Hangzhou, China (2018–2025)

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens among acute respiratory tract infection (ARTI) cases in Hangzhou and evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a retrospective surveillance study conducted in Hangzhou, China, from 2018 to 2025, analyzing 81,974 patients with ARTI. Cases were tested for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP).
analysis.methods: Positivity criteria followed the manufacturers' instructions for each respective assay. The co-infection rate was calculated, and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.
analysis.main_results: Among 81,974 patients, 33,350 tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positivity rate of 40.68%. The positivity rates of FluA, FluB, and MP were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic period (2020–2022) and then rebounded sharply in the post-pandemic period (2023–2025). In contrast, RSV, ADV, and CP showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers than before the pandemic.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings reveal a dynamic shift in the epidemiology of respiratory pathogens, with FluA, FluB, and MP exhibiting a "revenge rebound" after the pandemic, while RSV, ADV, and CP remained inhibited but increased in absolute numbers. This pattern highlights the complex interplay between the pandemic and seasonal respiratory pathogens.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results suggest the need for a dynamic monitoring system to track changes in pathogen prevalence and implement targeted prevention and control measures during high-incidence seasons, particularly for FluA, FluB, and MP.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a retrospective design, which may introduce bias, and the observed changes in positivity rates could be influenced by external factors such as public health interventions. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study analyzed the epidemiology of six respiratory pathogens, including seasonal influenza viruses, in Hangzhou, China, over an 8-year period from 2018 to 2025. It found that the positivity rates of influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), and Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) were significantly suppressed during the COVID-19 pandemic but rebounded sharply afterward, forming a "revenge rebound" pattern. In contrast, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP) showed persistent inhibition but had higher absolute case numbers. The study highlights the need for dynamic monitoring and targeted prevention strategies during high-incidence seasons. However, the retrospective design and potential external influences limit the confidence in the findings, resulting in a moderate evidence assessment.

Cases with positive test results were analyzed for influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP), and statistical analysis was performed according to the pandemic stage, age, sex, season, and co-infection status.ResultsAmong 81,974 patients, a total of 33,350 cases tested positive for pathogens, with an overall positive rate of 40.68%. The research results suggest that a dynamic monitoring system needs to be established, and targeted prevention and control measures should be implemented for key individuals and pathogens during high-incidence seasons.Keywords: Acute Respiratory Tract Infection, epidemiological characteristics, Hangzhou, influenza virus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, pathogen spectrum 2.Materials and methods2.1.Study populationThis study aimed to systematically characterize the epidemiological features of six key respiratory pathogens—influenza A virus (FluA), influenza B virus (FluB), RSV, adenovirus (ADV), Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP), and Chlamydia pneumoniae (CP)—among ARTI cases in Hangzhou, and to evaluate the long-term impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on local pathogen dynamics. Data from 81,974 ARTI cases from seven medical institutions in Hangzhou City between January 2018 and December 2025 were collected. MP (19.56%) and FluA (16.93%) were the most prevalent pathogens. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在系统地描述杭州市急性呼吸道感染(ARTI)病例中六种主要呼吸道病原体的流行病学特征,并评估COVID-19大流行对当地病原体动态的长期影响。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项回顾性 监测 研究,于 2018 年至 2025 年在中国杭州进行,分析了 81,974 名 ARTI 患者。对病例进行了甲型流感病毒(FluA)、乙型流感病毒(FluB)、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)、腺病毒(ADV)、肺炎支原体(MP)和肺炎衣原体(CP)检测。
analysis_zh.methods: 阳性标准遵循制造商针对每种检测的说明。计算合并感染率,并根据流行阶段、年龄、性别、季节、合并感染状况进行统计分析。
analysis_zh.main_results: 81974例患者中,病原体检测呈阳性33350例,总体阳性率为40.68%。FluA、FluB和MP的阳性率在COVID-19大流行期间(2020-2022年)显着受到抑制,然后在大流行后时期(2023-2025年)急剧反弹。相比之下,RSV、ADV 和 CP 显示出持续的抑制作用,但绝对病例数比大流行前更高。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果揭示了呼吸道病原体流行病学的动态变化,FluA、FluB和MP在大流行后表现出“报复性反弹”,而RSV、ADV和CP仍然受到抑制,但绝对数量有所增加。这种模式凸显了大流行和季节性呼吸道病原体之间复杂的相互作用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果表明,需要建立动态监测系统来跟踪病原体发病率的变化,并在发病率高发季节实施有针对性的预防和控制措施,特别是针对A型流感、B型流感和MP。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于回顾性设计,可能会引入偏差,并且观察到的阳性率变化可能受到公共卫生干预等外部因素的影响。由于这些限制,证据是中等的。

papers.title: Exploration of the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus

source_records.title: Exploration of the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: IntroductionScutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb widely used for its heat-clearing and detoxifying properties, has shown broad-spectrum antiviral potential. However, its anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.MethodsIn this study, the anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms of S. barbata extract were investigated using H1N1-infected MDCK cells and BALB/c mice. Transcriptomic analysis followed by mRNA and protein-level validation was performed to characterize its molecular effects, while UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS was used to identify blood-absorbed constituents. Potential active compounds were subsequently screened by integrating the absorbed constituents with network pharmacology and further validated in vitro and in vivo.ResultsS. barbata extract markedly inhibited H1N1 replication in MDCK cells (IC50 = 42.87 μg/mL; CC50 > 500 μg/mL) and reduced viral burden and pulmonary inflammation in infected mice. Mechanistically, S. barbata treatment suppressed the Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, and chemokine signaling pathways, suggesting coordinated regulation of antiviral and inflammatory responses. Among the blood-absorbed constituents, baicalein and chrysoeriol were identified as key candidate active compounds and exhibited potent anti-H1N1 activity in vitro and in vivo (IC50 = 13.80 and 11.10 μM, respectively).DiscussionCollectively, these findings demonstrate that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 effects through a combination of direct inhibition of viral replication and modulation of excessive inflammatory responses, with baicalein and chrysoeriol representing important contributors to its antiviral activity. Materials and methodsMaterialsChrysoeriol (C861251) was obtained from Macklin (Shanghai, China), and baicalein (B20571) was purchased from Yuan Ye Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, 812207), fetal bovine serum (FBS, 10270-106), 0.25% trypsin–EDTA (2323363), phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, BYHC1713), and Opti-MEM medium (31985070) were all supplied by Gibco (Massachusetts, USA). MDCK cells (as a host of H1N1) and IA V [A/Puerto Rico/8/1934(H1N1)] were provided by the Shandong Academy of Medical Sciences (Jinan, China). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits for TNF-α (JL10484), IL-1β (JL18442), IL-6 (JL20268), IL-2 (JL20256), IFN-γ (JL10967), and IL-4 (JL20266) were obtained from Shanghai Jianglai Biotechnology Co., Ltd., (Shanghai, China). The anti-influenza A virus nucleoprotein antibody (ab20343) was purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies, including FITC anti-mouse CD4 (116004), PE anti-mouse IL-4 (504104), APC anti-mouse IFN-γ (505809), and APC anti-mouse CD8b (Ly-3) (126614), were supplied by BioLegend (California, USA).Sample preparationThe extract of S. barbata was prepared using a water extraction method. Briefly, 100 g of dried herb powder was mixed with 1,000 mL of deionized water and subjected to ultrasonic-assisted extraction at 250 W for 1 h. The resulting extract was filtered, concentrated under reduced pressure, and lyophilized to yield a dry powder. For subsequent experiments, the lyophilized extract was reconstituted according to its experimental application: dissolved in Opti-MEM medium for in vitro cellular assays and in PBS buffer for in vivo animal studies. Both solutions were further diluted to the required working concentrations for pharmacodynamic evaluation.Study on anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vitroMDCK cells were treated with varying concentrations of S. barbata extract and oseltamivir phosphate (OP) for 48 h. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay to determine the 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50) for both agents. The highest tested concentration that maintained cell viability above 90% was defined as the non-cytotoxic concentration for subsequent experiments. For viral infection studies, MDCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells/mL (100 μL per well) and cultured for 24 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. Following incubation, the culture medium was removed, and cell monolayers were washed twice with PBS. Cells were then infected with H1N1 virus (100 TCID50/well) in Opti-MEM medium supplemented with 1,000 U/mL penicillin, 100 μg/mL streptomycin, and 2 μg/mL TPCK-trypsin, while simultaneously being treated with different concentrations of either S. barbata extract or OP. After 48 h of incubation, cell viability was measured using the MTT assay. The half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values for S. barbata and OP against H1N1 viral infection were calculated according to the Reed-Muench method (Chen et al., 2010; Geng et al., 2019).MDCK cells were seeded in 12-well plates at a density of 8 × 104 cells per well and cultured until full confluence was reached. The cell monolayers were then washed twice with PBS and replenished with fresh Opti-MEM medium. Subsequently, the cells were treated with either S. barbata extract or OP, followed by immediate infection with H1N1 virus at a dose of 100 TCID50 per well. The infected cells were maintained at 37 °C under 5% CO2 for 24 h. To quantify viral gene expression, cells subjected to the above treatment were harvested after three freeze-thaw cycles, and the supernatant was collected following centrifugation. The mRNA expression level of the H1N1 NP gene in the supernatant was detected by Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). For the analysis of viral protein expression, MDCK cells grown on coverslips in 12-well plates were treated and infected under identical conditions as described above. After 24 h of infection, the coverslips were collected, and the expression level of H1N1 NP protein in MDCK cells was determined by immunofluorescence assay.Study on the anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vivoAll animal experiments were reviewed and approved by the Laboratory Animal Care and Use Committee of Shandong University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (approval no. SDUTCM20220415022). Specific pathogen-free (SPF) female BALB/c mice (6 weeks old, 15–18 g) were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology Co., Ltd., [Animal production license no. SCXK (Jing) 2021-0006; animal use license no. SYXK (Lu) 2017-0022]. Mice were housed in an individually ventilated cage (IVC) system under controlled environmental conditions (temperature 20 °C–24 °C) with free access to standard chow and water, and were acclimatized for 3 days prior to experimentation.The mice were randomly divided into five groups: control group, model group, OP group (20 mg⋅kg–1), S. barbata (390 mg⋅kg–1) group, and S. barbata (78 mg⋅kg–1) group. Following anesthesia with a small-animal anesthesia system (RWD Life Science, China), mice were intranasally inoculated with 20 μL 0.8 LD50 H1N1 virus. Two hours post-infection, drug administration was initiated by oral gavage once daily for five consecutive days. At the end of the experiment, peripheral blood samples were collected from the mice under light anesthesia. Then, mice were euthanized by overdose of isoflurane anesthesia (5% isoflurane delivered at 2 L/min for 10 min), and death was confirmed before tissue collection. Lung, spleen, and thymus tissues were immediately collected for subsequent analyses.QRT-PCRViral RNA was extracted using the TIANamp Virus RNA Kit (Tiangen, China), and total RNA from lung tissues was isolated using the RNA Easy Fast Tissue/Cell Kit (Tiangen, China). Reverse transcription and quantitative PCR amplification were performed using the BeyoFastTM SYBR Green One-Step qRT-PCR Kit (Beyotime, China). The specific primer sequences are listed in Table 1. The thermal cycling conditions were as follows: reverse transcription at 50 °C for 15 min; initial denaturation at 95 °C for 2 min; followed by 40 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 15 s and annealing/extension at 60 °C for 30 s. GAPDH was used as the internal reference gene, and the relative expression levels of the viral NP gene were calculated using the 2–ΔΔCt method.TABLE 1Primer sequences for quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction.GeneDirectionNucleotide sequence (5′→ 3) (H1N1)FORTCCGTCCATTCAATCCAGAGGHA (H1N1)REVGATCCGCTGCATAGCCTGATIL-6FORTTCCATCCAGTTGCCTTCTTGIL-6REVAATTAAGCCTCCGACTTGTGAAM2 (H1N1)FORGCAACGGTTCAAGTGATCCTCM2 (H1N1)REVACCATCGTCAGCATCCACAGMyd88FORACCTGTGTCTGGTCCATTGCMyd88REVGGAATCAGTCGCTTCTGTTGGNA (H1N1)FORGGCTGGCTAACAATCGGAATTNA (H1N1)REVACACAGGCACATTCAGACTCTNP (H1N1)FORGTATGGACCTGCCGTAGCNP (H1N1) analysisMDCK cells were seeded onto glass coverslips placed in 12-well plates (Beyotime, China) and subjected to viral infection and drug treatment according to the experimental design. Following treatment, the cells were washed three times with pre-cooled PBS, fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde at room temperature for 20 min, and permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 for 15 min. After blocking with 2% BSA for 30 min, cells were incubated overnight at 4 °C with an anti-influenza A virus NP monoclonal antibody, followed by incubation with AF488-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (Bioss, China) at room temperature for 1 h in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (Beyotime, China) for 5 min. Fluorescence images were captured using an Olympus fluorescence microscope (Olympus, Japan).Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)The concentrations of TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-2, IFN-γ, and IL-4 in lung tissue homogenates were quantified using commercial ELISA kits (Jianglai, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.Histopathological examinationLung tissues were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 48 h, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned at 4 μm thickness. Hematoxylin–eosin (H&E) and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining were performed. For H&E staining, sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin to assess inflammatory cell infiltration and pathological alterations. For IHC staining, sections underwent antigen retrieval and 5% BSA blocking, followed by incubation with primary antibodies against TLR4 and RelA at 4 °C overnight, and then with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies at room temperature for 30 min. Color development was performed using DAB, nuclei were counterstained with hematoxylin, and slides were mounted with neutral resin for microscopic observation.Transcriptomic analysisTotal RNA extraction and RNA-seq of lung tissues were conducted by BGI Tech Solutions Co., Ltd., (Wuhan, China). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified with |log2(fold change)| > 1 and adjusted p < 0.05. Overlapping DEGs between the control and model groups, and between the treatment and model groups, were subjected to hierarchical clustering, Gene Ontology (GO) annotation, and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis.Flow cytometry analysisSpleens were gently ground through a 200-mesh stainless steel sieve to obtain single-cell suspensions. After red blood cell lysis, cells were resuspended in flow cytometry buffer (PBS containing 1% FBS). For Th1/Th2 analysis, cells were stimulated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (50 ng/mL), ionomycin (1 μg/mL), and brefeldin A (10 μg/mL) at 37 °C for 4 h, followed by surface staining with CD4-FITC, fixation/permeabilization, and intracellular staining with IFN-γ-APC and IL-4-PE. For T cell subset analysis, cells were stained with PE-CD3, APC-CD4, and FITC-CD8 antibodies. Data were acquired on a BD flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, USA) and analyzed using FlowJo software.Analysis of blood-absorbed componentsTwelve BALB/c mice were randomly divided into model and treatment groups. H1N1 infection was established as described previously. The treatment group received S. barbata extract (3.9 g⋅kg–1, ten times the effective dose) via oral gavage, while the model group received an equal volume of PBS for six consecutive days. Peripheral blood samples were collected from the orbital venous plexus of mice under light anesthesia at 10 min, 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 h after the final administration. Blood samples were collected into heparinized tubes and centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C to obtain plasma. Each 200 μL plasma sample was mixed with 20 μL of 20% ascorbic acid and 800 μL of methanol, vortexed, and centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 10 min. The supernatant was analyzed using UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) with an Ultimate 3,000 UHPLC system coupled to a Q ExactiveTM quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer. Chromatographic separation was achieved at 45 °C using a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min and an injection volume of 5 μL. The mobile phases consisted of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) with the following gradient: 0–2 min (95% A), 2–4 min (95%–70% A), 4–8 min (70%–50% A), 8–10 min (50%–20% A), 10–14 min (20%–0% A), and 14–15 min (0% A). The MS parameters were as follows: negative ion mode spray voltage, 3200 V; positive ion mode, 3,800 V; capillary temperature, 320 °C; full-scan resolution, 60,000; MS/MS resolution, 15,000; scan range, m/z 100–1,500; stepped collision energy, 10/20/40 eV. Data were processed using Xcalibur 3.0 software. The structures of the compounds were determined through analysis of fragmentation patterns, and confirmed by comparison with both reference standards and database information (MassBank, FooDB), as well as supporting literature.Network pharmacology analysis of potential active componentsPotential targets of blood-absorbed compounds were identified using the PubChem and SwissTargetPrediction databases (Daina et al., 2019; Hao et al., 2013). In PubChem, the search parameters were set to “active” for activity and “9606” for taxids. In SwissTargetPrediction, the filter “homospines” and a probability threshold of >0.05 were applied. The combined target lists were standardized to gene symbols using the UniProt database (Piñero et al., 2021; Stelzer et al., 2016). DEGs (n = 1,907) that significantly differed between both the treatment vs. model and control vs. model groups were defined as disease-associated targets. The intersection between drug and disease targets was identified using Venny 2.1. KEGG enrichment analysis was performed on overlapping targets using the Metascape platform. The compound–target–pathway–disease interaction network was visualized using Cytoscape 3.6.0.Validation of monomer compound activityStandard compounds of chrysoeriol and baicalein were accurately weighed, dissolved in DMSO, and diluted with Opti-MEM medium containing 2 μg/mL TPCK-treated trypsin. The antiviral and cytotoxicity assays were performed following the same procedures described for in “Study on anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vitro.” Mice were randomly assigned to the control, model, OP (20 mg/kg), chrysoeriol (20 or 4 mg/kg), and baicalein (20 or 4 mg/kg) groups. full_text_sections.abstract: IntroductionScutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata), a traditional Chinese medicinal herb widely used for its heat-clearing and detoxifying properties, has shown broad-spectrum antiviral potential. However, its anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated.MethodsIn this study, the anti-H1N1 activity and underlying mechanisms of S. barbata extract were investigated using H1N1-infected MDCK cells and BALB/c mice. Transcriptomic analysis followed by mRNA and protein-level validation was performed to characterize its molecular effects, while UPLC-Q-Orbitrap-MS was used to identify blood-absorbed constituents. Potential active compounds were subsequently screened by integrating the absorbed constituents with network pharmacology and further validated in vitro and in vivo.ResultsS. barbata extract markedly inhibited H1N1 replication in MDCK cells (IC50 = 42.87 μg/mL; CC50 > 500 μg/mL) and reduced viral burden and pulmonary inflammation in infected mice. Mechanistically, S. barbata treatment suppressed the Toll-like receptor, NF-κB, and chemokine signaling pathways, suggesting coordinated regulation of antiviral and inflammatory responses. Among the blood-absorbed constituents, baicalein and chrysoeriol were identified as key candidate active compounds and exhibited potent anti-H1N1 activity in vitro and in vivo (IC50 = 13.80 and 11.10 μM, respectively).DiscussionCollectively, these findings demonstrate that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 effects through a combination of direct inhibition of viral replication and modulation of excessive inflammatory responses, with baicalein and chrysoeriol representing important contributors to its antiviral activity.

The anti-influenza A virus nucleoprotein antibody (ab20343) was purchased from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies, including FITC anti-mouse CD4 (116004), PE anti-mouse IL-4 (504104), APC anti-mouse IFN-γ (505809), and APC anti-mouse CD8b (Ly-3) (126614), were supplied by BioLegend (California, USA).Sample preparationThe extract of S. barbata was prepared using a water extraction method. Briefly, 100 g of dried herb powder was mixed with 1,000 mL of deionized water and subjected to ultrasonic-assisted extraction at 250 W for 1 h. The resulting extract was filtered, concentrated under reduced pressure, and lyophilized to yield a dry powder. For subsequent experiments, the lyophilized extract was reconstituted according to its experimental application: dissolved in Opti-MEM medium for in vitro cellular assays and in PBS buffer for in vivo animal studies. Both solutions were further diluted to the required working concentrations for pharmacodynamic evaluation.Study on anti-H1N1 activity of S. barbata in vitroMDCK cells were treated with varying concentrations of S. barbata extract and oseltamivir phosphate (OP) for 48 h. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay to determine the 50% cytotoxic concentration (CC50) for both agents. The highest tested concentration that maintained cell viability above 90% was defined as the non-cytotoxic concentration for subsequent experiments. For viral infection studies, MDCK cells were seeded in 96-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells/mL (100 μL per well) and cultured for 24 h at 37 °C with 5% CO2. The infected cells were maintained at 37 °C under 5% CO2 for 24 h. full_text_sections.results: ResultsIn vitro antiviral activity of S. barbataIn vitro assays demonstrated that S. barbata and OP exhibited dose-dependent inhibitory effects against H1N1 infection in MDCK cells (Figures 1A, B). Panel C is a scatter plot comparing relative expression of H1N1 NP mRNA across five treatment groups, with significant differences marked by asterisks. These effects were notably alleviated in the S. barbata and OP treatment groups (Figure 2A). On day 6 post-infection, mice were euthanized, and the lung, spleen, and thymus were collected and weighed to calculate organ indices. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionDirect and indirect anti-H1N1 effects of S. barbataThe antiviral activity of S. barbata extract against H1N1 infection was first evaluated in an MDCK cell model. The extract exhibited a IC50 of 42.87 μg/mL against H1N1, while showing negligible cytotoxicity toward MDCK cells (CC50 > 500 μg/mL). Within the non-cytotoxic concentration range (100 and 200 μg/mL), S. barbata treatment markedly reduced viral titers in the supernatant and decreased the intracellular expression level of the viral NP. Consistent with the in vitro findings, S. barbata also demonstrated significant protective efficacy against H1N1 infection in vivo. Direct antiviral effects are generally defined as interference with viral proliferation processes, including adsorption, penetration, replication, assembly, or release, or by damaging viral structural proteins. HA and NA are characteristic surface glycoproteins of H1N1, while NP and matrix protein M2 serve as core structural proteins. RT-qPCR analysis revealed that S. barbata significantly downregulated the mRNA expression of HA, NA, NP, and M2 in mouse lung tissues, showing a consistent inhibitory trend across all four genes. These results suggest that S. barbata exerts a direct inhibitory effect on H1N1 viral replication.In addition to direct antiviral action, S. barbata also exerts indirect effects by alleviating virus-induced tissue injury and modulating host immune responses. Following H1N1 invasion, infected mice typically exhibit pulmonary congestion, edema, and increased lung mass. The lung index serves as a key indicator of pulmonary inflammation and is widely used to evaluate the anti-H1N1 efficacy of candidate drugs. Moreover, the developmental state of immune organs such as the spleen and thymus reflects the overall immune competence of the host. H1N1 infection generally reduces the spleen and thymus indices due to excessive immune cell consumption. S. barbata administration significantly decreased the lung index while restoring the spleen and thymus indices, indicating that the extract protects the host through immunoregulatory mechanisms.Upon influenza virus infection, the host immune system releases a variety of cytokines to inhibit viral replication and regulate immunity. However, excessive cytokine secretion can trigger uncontrolled inflammation and tissue injury, a phenomenon often referred to as a “cytokine storm.” Thus, suppressing hyperinflammatory cytokine release is critical for mitigating H1N1-induced lung damage. Overexpression of IL-1β promotes excessive recruitment and activation of neutrophils and macrophages, while IL-6 facilitates neutrophil chemotaxis and local infiltration. TNF-α induces leukocyte migration and promotes degranulation of granulocytes, amplifying the inflammatory cascade. Elevated levels of IL-1β, IFN-γ, IL-6, and TNF-α have been correlated with the severity of H1N1 infection in clinical cases. In our study, S. barbata significantly reduced the levels of these pro-inflammatory cytokines in lung homogenates, consistent with histopathological findings showing alleviated pulmonary injury. IL-2 is a key cytokine that promotes the differentiation of CD8+ T cells into cytotoxic T lymphocytes during viral infection (Zhou et al., 2021). Our results showed that S. barbata treatment significantly decreased IL-2 levels in the lungs of H1N1-infected mice. Therefore, we further explored its regulatory effects on CD4+ and CD8+ T cell populations. CD8+ T cells play a direct role in killing infected cells, whereas CD4+ T cells enhance the effector functions of innate immune cells and B cells. An imbalance in the CD4+/CD8+ ratio has been associated with increased severity of H1N1-induced pneumonia. Flow cytometry revealed that S. barbata decreased the proportion of CD4+ T cells in the spleen without significantly affecting CD8+ T cells, suggesting that the extract may suppress overactivation of CD4+ T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, S. barbata partially restored the Th1/Th2 balance by increasing both Th1 and Th2 subpopulations, indicating a bidirectional regulatory effect. Interestingly, despite the overall increase in CD4+ T cell proportion in the model group, both Th1 and Th2 subsets were reduced, implying expansion of other CD4+ subpopulations–a phenomenon warranting further investigation.Molecular mechanisms underlying the anti-H1N1 effects of S. barbataTranscriptomic analysis provided deeper insight into the molecular basis of S. barbata’s anti-H1N1 activity. GO enrichment analysis indicated that the DEGs after S. barbata treatment were mainly involved in biological processes such as regulation of inflammatory responses, positive regulation of innate immunity, and leukocyte migration. The enriched cellular components included “ficolin-1-rich granule” and “ficolin-1-rich granule lumen.” Ficolin-1-rich granules store and release Ficolin-1 upon stimulation; Ficolin-1 functions as a soluble pattern recognition receptor that recognizes pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and activates the complement system via the lectin pathway, thereby participating in innate immune signaling.Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes pathway enrichment further revealed that the toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathway was the most significantly modulated pathway following S. barbata treatment. During IAV infection, viral RNA within airway and alveolar epithelial cells activates TLRs, leading to the induction of interferon regulatory factors and type I interferons (IFN-α/β). This activation can subsequently trigger the NF-κB pathway, promoting the expression of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines. While these responses are essential for viral clearance, excessive activation results in tissue injury. Our data indicate that S. barbata alleviates H1N1-induced pathology by suppressing the overactivation of the TLR and NF-κB pathways. These findings were further validated by RT-qPCR and immunohistochemical analyses, which confirmed the downregulation of key genes in the TLR and chemokine signaling pathways.Identification and validation of the active compounds responsible for the anti-H1N1 activityFollowing oral administration, most herbal components undergo absorption, distribution, and metabolism before reaching their target tissues. Pharmacological activity is generally mediated by prototype or metabolized compounds that enter systemic circulation. Using UPLC-MS, we identified 122 blood-absorbed constituents of S. barbata. By integrating network pharmacology and transcriptomic analyses, we intersected the predicted targets of these compounds with DEGs identified in the transcriptomic data, constructing a “S. barbata–compound–target–pathway–H1N1” interaction network. Among these, baicalein and chrysoeriol exhibited the highest degree values in the network, indicating their central regulatory roles. These two flavonoids were associated with multiple antiviral and immune-related pathways, including the influenza A pathway, chemokine signaling pathway, toll-like receptor signaling pathway, and downstream NF-κB pathway. Subsequent in vitro and in vivo experiments confirmed that both baicalein and chrysoeriol possessed potent inhibitory effects against H1N1 infection, validating the network-based predictions.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionInfluenza A virus (IAV), a member of the genus Influenza virus within the family Orthomyxoviridae, is an enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA virus (Zeng et al., 2016). Since the 20th century, IAV has caused multiple global pandemics, at least three of which were closely associated with the H1N1 subtype (Krammer et al., 2018). The most recent pandemic, the 2009 H1N1 “swine flu” outbreak, resulted in at least 16,000 deaths worldwide. In addition to pandemics, IAV exhibits a pronounced seasonal epidemic pattern. Although seasonal strains generally display lower pathogenicity than emerging pandemic variants, they can still lead to severe lower respiratory tract infections and extensive lung injury. According to estimates by Iuliano et al. (2018) seasonal influenza causes approximately 291,243–645,832 deaths globally each year; among 92 surveyed countries, 9,243–105,690 annual deaths in children under 5 years of age were attributed to IAV infection (Iuliano et al., 2018). Furthermore, Wang et al. (2020) reported that in 2018, around 10 million children under 5 years old worldwide developed influenza-associated acute lower respiratory tract infections, resulting in approximately 870,000 hospitalizations and 35,000 deaths.Following IAV infection, the host’s innate immune system is rapidly activated. Infected host cells recognize viral pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through various pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), thereby initiating innate immune signaling pathways. Once viral RNA enters the cytoplasm, it activates three principal intracellular immune pathways: the retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) pathway, the toll-like receptor (TLR) pathway, and the inflammasome pathway, all of which contribute to antiviral innate immunity. During the early phase of IAV infection, immune responses occur primarily in infected airway and alveolar epithelial cells. Viral RNA activates the TLR signaling pathway, inducing the expression of key signaling molecules that promote the activation of interferon regulatory factors (IRFs) and enhance the transcription of type I interferons (IFN-α/β). Moreover, activation of this pathway can further stimulate the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling cascade, leading to the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. The combined effects of type I interferons, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and the activation and differentiation of cytotoxic T cells ultimately contribute to viral clearance (Jagger et al., 2012).Although traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) does not include the concept of “virus,” antiviral therapy within TCM dates back to the Han dynasty, notably to Zhang Zhongjing’s Treatise on Cold Damage and Miscellaneous Diseases. According to TCM theory, IAV infection belongs to the category of “Warm Diseases” and is closely related to pulmonary disorders caused by “external heat pathogens” (Cao et al., 2009; Wise et al., 2009). TCM herbal medicines are characterized by multi-component, multi-target, and multi-pathway mechanisms. Their active extracts can inhibit viral replication, disrupt viral structure, regulate immune balance, and maintain systemic homeostasis, reflecting the holistic regulatory principles of TCM (Zhang et al., 2013).In our previous screening of herbal medicines with anti-H1N1 activity, the aqueous extract of Scutellaria barbata D. Don (S. barbata) exhibited significant antiviral potential. S. barbata, a member of the Lamiaceae family and the genus S. barbata is the dried whole herb traditionally used for its heat-clearing, detoxifying, blood-stasis-resolving, hemostatic, diuretic, and anti-edematous properties. Modern pharmacological studies have demonstrated that heat-clearing and detoxifying herbs generally possess strong antiviral potential. Extracts of S. barbata have been shown to alleviate SARS-CoV-2–induced acute lung injury by inhibiting viral replication and modulating immune responses (Ran et al., 2025); its combined extract with Hedyotis diffusa suppresses hepatitis B virus–related hepatocellular carcinoma growth by regulating circular RNA (circRNA) expression (Yang et al., 2021); diterpenoids isolated from S. barbata display inhibitory activity against Epstein–Barr virus lytic replication (Wu et al., 2015); and its total flavonoid fraction exhibits anti-parainfluenza virus activity (Shan-Shan et al., 2009).Based on these findings, the present study established H1N1-infected MDCK cell and BALB/c mouse models to systematically evaluate the inhibitory effects of S. barbata extract against IAV (H1N1 subtype). The results demonstrated that S. barbata exerts anti-H1N1 activity by directly suppressing viral replication and modulating anti-inflammatory and immune-related signaling pathways. Baicalein and chrysoeriol were confirmed to be key constituents responsible for the antiviral activity of S. barbata. After 48 h of incubation, cell viability was measured using the MTT assay. papers.title_original: Exploration of the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus, addressing the need for understanding its antiviral properties and potential therapeutic applications.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved in vitro assays using MDCK cells and in vivo experiments on mice, with the latter divided into control, model, and treatment groups. The treatment group received Scutellaria barbata extract, while the model group was exposed to the virus.
analysis.methods: The study used enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits to measure cytokine levels, MTT assay to assess cytotoxicity, and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) to detect viral gene expression. Immunofluorescence assays and histopathological examination were also employed to analyze viral protein expression and tissue changes.
analysis.main_results: In vitro assays demonstrated that Scutellaria barbata suppressed viral gene expression and reduced inflammatory cytokine levels. The treatment also showed effects on the expression of antiviral and inflammatory pathways in infected cells.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that Scutellaria barbata may modulate antiviral and inflammatory responses through suppression of key signaling pathways, offering a novel perspective on its potential therapeutic use against influenza A (H1N1) virus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the mechanisms of Scutellaria barbata's antiviral activity, which could inform future research on natural compounds for influenza treatment and support the development of targeted therapies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on in vitro and in vivo models, which may not fully represent human influenza dynamics. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on experimental findings without direct clinical outcomes.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the mechanisms and active compounds of Scutellaria barbata D. Don against influenza A (H1N1) virus. It employs in vitro and in vivo models to assess the antiviral and anti-inflammatory effects of the extract. The results indicate that Scutellaria barbata suppresses viral gene expression and modulates inflammatory pathways. These findings suggest potential therapeutic applications but are based on experimental models, limiting their direct clinical relevance. The study contributes to understanding natural antiviral agents but lacks human data, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及使用 MDCK 细胞进行的体外测定和小鼠体内实验,后者分为对照组、模型组和 治疗 组。治疗组接受半枝莲提取物,而模型组则暴露于病毒。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用酶联免疫吸附测定(ELISA)试剂盒测量细胞因子水平,使用MTT测定评估细胞毒性,并使用定量实时PCR(qRT-PCR)检测病毒基因表达。还采用免疫荧光测定和组织病理学检查来分析病毒蛋白表达和组织变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 体外试验表明半枝莲可抑制病毒基因表达并降低炎症细胞因子水平。治疗 还显示出对感染细胞中 抗病毒药物 表达和炎症途径的影响。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,半枝莲可能通过抑制关键信号通路来调节 抗病毒药物 和炎症反应,为其对抗甲型 H1N1 流感病毒的潜在治疗用途提供了新的视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果提供了对半枝莲 抗病毒药物 活性机制的深入了解,这可以为未来针对流感 治疗 的天然化合物的研究提供信息,并支持靶向治疗的开发。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖体外和体内模型而受到限制,这些模型可能无法完全代表人类流感动态。证据是中等的,因为它基于没有直接临床结果的实验​​结果。

papers.title: Clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis

source_records.title: Clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: AbstractObjectiveThe aim of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics of severe viral encephalitis (SVE) in children and to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, thereby providing preliminary evidence to facilitate early risk stratification and reduce SVE-related disability and mortality.MethodsA retrospective study was conducted in 75 children diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, including 50 mild cases and 25 SVE cases. Demographic data, clinical manifestations, and laboratory parameters (peripheral white blood cell count (WBC), serum sodium, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocyte and protein levels, serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), electroencephalography (EEG), neuroimaging findings, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores) were collected and compared between groups. Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses, with enteroviruses (EVs) being the predominant type, accounting for 7 cases, followed by herpes zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases. In the SVE group, 9 out of 25 cases (36%) were found to have pathogens, with influenza A virus (4 cases) and herpes simplex virus (2 cases) being the main ones. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality (primary outcome) within the SVE subgroup.ResultsAmong the 25 children with SVE (15 males, mean age 7.74 ± 2.2 years), fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common; four patients died (16%). Compared with children with mild encephalitis, the SVE group exhibited significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences in CSF leukocytes, CSF protein, blood leukocytes, or serum sodium. In univariate Firth-corrected logistic regression, neuroimaging abnormalities (P = 0.007), seizures (P = 0.011), EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018), lower GCS score (per 1-point decrease, P < 0.001), and higher serum NSE (per 10 ng/mL increment, P = 0.018) were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality.ConclusionPediatric SVE presents with nonspecific early symptoms and substantial mortality. Seizures, EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality. However, given the small sample size and single-center design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center prospective cohorts. Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment.Keywords: children, clinical characteristics, exploratory factors, in-hospital mortality, severe viral encephalitis 2.Subjects and methods2.1.Study subjectsAll cases were derived from pediatric inpatients diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital from January 2023 to December 2025. All enrolled children fulfilled comprehensive diagnostic criteria for viral encephalitis as follows: (1) Acute onset of neurological symptoms and signs; (2) CSF examination showing an elevated WBC count (> 10 × 106/L) with a predominance of lymphocytes, and/or a mild increase in protein; (3) Electroencephalogram and/or cranial imaging showing changes consistent with viral encephalitis; (4) Other central nervous system diseases such as purulent meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and autoimmune encephalitis were excluded. Pediatric GCS scores were independently assigned and cross-validated by two assessors (physicians and nurses). All assessors had passed the standardized training and assessment within the department. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractObjectiveThe aim of this study was to describe the clinical characteristics of severe viral encephalitis (SVE) in children and to identify exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality, thereby providing preliminary evidence to facilitate early risk stratification and reduce SVE-related disability and mortality.MethodsA retrospective study was conducted in 75 children diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, including 50 mild cases and 25 SVE cases. Demographic data, clinical manifestations, and laboratory parameters (peripheral white blood cell count (WBC), serum sodium, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leukocyte and protein levels, serum neuron-specific enolase (NSE), electroencephalography (EEG), neuroimaging findings, and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores) were collected and compared between groups. Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses, with enteroviruses (EVs) being the predominant type, accounting for 7 cases, followed by herpes zoster virus (VZV) and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases. In the SVE group, 9 out of 25 cases (36%) were found to have pathogens, with influenza A virus (4 cases) and herpes simplex virus (2 cases) being the main ones. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality (primary outcome) within the SVE subgroup.ResultsAmong the 25 children with SVE (15 males, mean age 7.74 ± 2.2 years), fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common; four patients died (16%). Compared with children with mild encephalitis, the SVE group exhibited significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05). However, there were no significant differences in CSF leukocytes, CSF protein, blood leukocytes, or serum sodium. In univariate Firth-corrected logistic regression, neuroimaging abnormalities (P = 0.007), seizures (P = 0.011), EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018), lower GCS score (per 1-point decrease, P < 0.001), and higher serum NSE (per 10 ng/mL increment, P = 0.018) were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality.ConclusionPediatric SVE presents with nonspecific early symptoms and substantial mortality. Seizures, EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality. However, given the small sample size and single-center design, these findings are hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger multi-center prospective cohorts. Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment.Keywords: children, clinical characteristics, exploratory factors, in-hospital mortality, severe viral encephalitis

full_text_sections.results: 2.2.2.Routine laboratory indicators (initial test results)1) Peripheral blood test: White blood cell (WBC) count—a significantly elevated or decreased count may indicate severe disease. 2) Serum sodium: hyponatremia, especially < 130 mmol/L, strongly suggests possible syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), which is a marker of increased intracranial pressure and disease worsening. 3) Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis: WBC count—a high count does not necessarily indicate more severe disease; Protein content—a significant elevation (> 1 g/L) indicates severe disruption of the blood-brain barrier. 3.Results3.1.General characteristicsAmong the 50 children with mild viral encephalitis, there were 27 males and 23 females, with a mean age of 5.8 ± 2.2 years. Mild cases occurred year-round; 21 (42%) presented in winter-spring (December-May) and 29 (58%) in summer-autumn (June-November). Among the 25 SVE patients, there were 15 males and 10 females, with a mean age of 7.74 ± 2.2 years. SVE also occurred throughout the year, with 17 cases (68%) in winter-spring and 8 cases (32%) in summer-autumn. Acute onset (≤ 7 days) was observed in 23 cases (92%), and subacute onset (> 7 days) in 2 cases (8%). Compared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05), while the incidence of fever was not significantly different between the two groups (P > 0.05). See Table 1.All 75 children (50 mild, 25 SVE) underwent blood and CSF sampling for pathogen detection using multiplex PCR and/or serum virus IgM antibody tests. Additionally, throat swabs for respiratory virus PCR were collected for all patients. In the mild encephalitis group, 14 out of 50 cases (28%) were found to be infected with specific viruses. Among them, 7 cases were infected with enteroviruses (EVs), followed by VZV and human herpesvirus type 6 (HHV-6), each with 2 cases; 1 case of influenza A virus; 1 case of parainfluenza virus; and 1 case of EBV. Among the 25 SVE patients, 4 were infected with influenza A, 2 with HSV, 1 with SARS-CoV-2, 1 with human parainfluenza, 1 with adenovirus, and the remaining cases had no specific virus identified (clinical diagnosis was accepted as per the criteria described in Methods).3.2.Clinical symptoms and signs (SVE)Fever was the most frequent clinical symptom, observed in 19 out of 25 patients (76%), followed by signs of elevated intracranial pressure (e.g., headache and vomiting) in 17 patients (68%). Neurological dysfunction, including limb shaking, unsteady gait, hemiplegia, or slurred speech, was the initial manifestation in 8 patients (32%). Respiratory symptoms occurred during the disease course in 15 patients (60%). Psychobehavioral abnormalities, mainly excitatory symptoms such as irritability and delirium, were present in 6 patients (24%). Altered consciousness was observed in 11 patients (44%), and cognitive impairment was noted in a small proportion of cases (8%). Seizures occurred in 14 patients, predominantly as generalized seizures.3.3.Comparison of laboratory indicators between pediatric SVE and mild viral encephalitisCompared with the mild viral encephalitis group, the SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher rates of seizures, and lower GCS scores (all P < 0.05). Regarding laboratory indicators, the SVE group showed significantly higher rates of EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, and serum NSE levels than the mild encephalitis group (all P < 0.05). Among the 25 patients with SVE, 22 underwent cranial MRI and 3 underwent cranial CT because of their clinical condition. Eleven patients (44%) had abnormal neuroimaging findings: 10 on MRI and 1 on CT. MRI abnormalities presented as single or multiple patchy or band-like long T1 and long T2 signals, and some were accompanied by inflammatory demyelination. The MRI lesions involved the unilateral insular lobe in 4 cases, the brainstem in 2, the cerebellum in 1, the bilateral frontal lobes in 4, and extensive brain parenchyma in 2. EEG was abnormal in 21 cases: 11 showed paroxysmal diffuse high-amplitude slow waves, and 10 had focal epileptic discharges. However, no significant differences were observed in CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, blood leukocyte count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.05). See Table 2.3.4.Univariate comparisons and firth-penalized logistic regression for factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVEThe primary outcome for this analysis was in-hospital mortality (death versus survival during hospitalization). Among continuous variables, the death group had significantly lower GCS scores (P = 0.001) and significantly higher serum NSE levels (P = 0.007) compared with the survival group. No significant differences were observed in length of fever, CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, peripheral blood WBC, or serum sodium between the two groups (all P > 0.05).Among the examined variables, neuroimaging abnormalities showed the strongest association with mortality (P = 0.007), followed by seizures (P = 0.011) and EEG abnormalities (P = 0.018). Similarly, each 10 ng/mL increment in serum NSE was associated with an increased in-hospital mortality risk (P = 0.018). The odds ratio for GCS is interpreted per 1-point decrease in the score (lower GCS → higher mortality risk). The odds ratio for NSE is interpreted per 10 ng/mL increment. No significant associations were found for length of fever, CSF leukocyte count, CSF protein, peripheral blood WBC count, or serum sodium (all P > 0.10). These differences reflect clinical judgment and severity at presentation rather than a randomized treatment effect. There were 2 cases of epilepsy and 1 case of decreased lower limb muscle strength among survivors; there were 4 deaths. full_text_sections.discussion: 4.DiscussionViral encephalitis arises from viral invasion of the intracranial compartment, triggering diffuse parenchymal brain inflammation. Early clinical manifestations are heterogeneous and may be limited to non-specific symptoms including fever, headache, fatigue, and myalgia (12). The incidence of viral encephalitis shows a seasonal pattern, with peaks from June to July and from December to January (13), which is similar to the pattern observed in this study. The winter-spring predominance in our cohort may reflect the circulation pattern of respiratory viruses such as influenza and adenovirus, which constituted the majority of identified pathogens in this study. Unlike the classic predominance of enteroviruses reported in other pediatric encephalitis cohorts (14), our findings suggest that respiratory viruses may play a more prominent role in severe encephalitis cases during the winter-spring season in our region. Furthermore, we found that the age of children with severe encephalitis in Anqing was slightly older than that of those with mild conditions. In the present cohort, the pathogen detection rate among patients with SVE reached 36% (9/25). Influenza-A virus was the most frequently identified pathogen (4/25, 16%), followed by herpes simplex virus (2/25, 8%). This distribution was different from the classic pattern reported in the literature. It is possible that during this period, the enterovirus may not be the predominant circulating strain in this region. The sensitivity of viral nucleic acid testing is influenced by various factors such as sampling time, primer design, and viral load, approximately 40% to 60% of clinical cases of viral encephalitis have no identifiable pathogen, as documented in the literature (14).In recent years, the onset of viral encephalitis has shown a trend toward younger age groups, with increased incidence in neonates and infants (15). If not diagnosed and treated promptly, children may develop severe neurological complications (16); therefore, early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for improving prognosis. In most cases, mild viral encephalitis has a good prognosis after active treatment, whereas severe viral encephalitis progresses rapidly, is more likely to cause other CNS symptoms, leads to sequelae, and can even result in death (7). Clinically, brain failure is common in severe viral encephalitis and is an important cause of death in pediatric intensive care units. In the acute phase of pediatric SVE, various symptoms may occur, including agitation, drowsiness, coma, neurological dysfunction, convulsions, and psychobehavioral abnormalities. The most common clinical symptoms of SVE are headache, decreased consciousness, and convulsions, and in most cases the viral etiology remains unknown (3, 12), which is consistent with the clinical presentation of SVE patients in this study. The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a rapid indicator of the severity of brain injury and plays an important role in determining patient prognosis. In the present study, univariate analyses demonstrated that children with SVE who died exhibited significantly lower GCS scores and higher serum NSE concentrations compared with survivors. Neuroimaging abnormalities were also markedly more prevalent among non-survivors. These observations align with prior reports demonstrating that the magnitude of brain injury reflected by GCS, NSE, and neuroimaging is tightly associated with prognosis in viral encephalitis (7, 17). Pratamastuti D et al. found that the median serum NSE level in the acute encephalitis syndrome was significantly higher than that of the non-acute encephalitis syndrome group, these results indicate that serum NSE was a good indicator of neuronal brain injury (18). Similarly, in our study, serum NSE levels were higher in children with SVE than in those with mild viral encephalitis, and elevated serum NSE was identified as an exploratory factor associated with in-hospital mortality. Abnormal EEG and neuroimaging findings, as well as high NSE levels, reflect the extent of brain tissue injury and help assess patient prognosis.In the present study, most children with SVE received combined corticosteroid and immunoglobulin therapy, and the overall recovery rate was relatively high. In this cohort, immunomodulatory therapy was more frequently used in patients with more severe clinical presentations. The observational nature precludes causal inference, but our data provide a real-world snapshot of current management practices for pediatric SVE. In recent years, researchers have increasingly focused on exploring prognosis-associated factors in patients with established SVE, attempting to construct prediction models using clinical symptoms, laboratory indicators, and other parameters (16, 19). Gao et al. found that convulsive status epilepticus, stress-induced hyperglycemia, and miR-125b are exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE (20). Song et al. reported that levels of soluble interleukin-2 receptor (SIL-2R), endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), and CD93 in CSF and serum are significantly elevated in children with viral encephalitis and are closely associated with disease progression and prognosis, suggesting their potential value as early warning biomarkers (21). However, current research in this field is still in a preliminary stage, and a unified early warning indicator system with standardized cutoff values has not yet been established, limiting its clinical application and generalization. The key challenge in the clinical management of SVE is the mismatch between the therapeutic time window and the assessment of disease severity. This study demonstrated that seizures, EEG abnormalities, neuroimaging abnormalities, low GCS score, and elevated serum NSE level were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE. However, due to the small sample size (particularly the small number of deaths, n = 4), we were unable to perform multivariable adjustment for potential confounders. Therefore, these associations should be regarded as exploratory and preliminary rather than confirmatory. The extremely wide confidence intervals for categorical variables further reflect the statistical instability inherent in small-sample analyses. Larger multicenter studies with sufficient sample sizes are urgently needed to establish independent exploratory factors and to develop reliable risk stratification tools for pediatric SVE.Treatment modalities for SVE include antiviral drugs, osmotic agents to reduce intracranial pressure, corticosteroid and immunoglobulins, antiepileptic drugs, brain protection, and brain metabolism-enhancing agents. Studies have reported that early use of hemoperfusion combined with continuous veno-venous hemodiafiltration may improve the prognosis of pediatric SVE more than hemoperfusion alone (22). The timing of therapy initiation was within 24–48 h of diagnosis, and the indications were based on clinical judgment (rapid neurological deterioration, brain edema on imaging, or refractory seizures). In this cohort, the majority of SVE patients received corticosteroids and/or IVIG, and 84% survived to discharge. However, the observational nature of this study precludes causal inference regarding treatment efficacy. Treatment allocation was based on clinical judgment and disease severity, and differences in treatment between survivors and non-survivors likely reflect confounding by indication. Therefore, the observed association between immunotherapy and survival should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment benefit. Prospective randomized studies are needed to evaluate the efficacy of immunomodulatory therapies in pediatric SVE. The role of immunotherapy in pediatric SVE remains an area of ongoing investigation (23).Several limitations of this study must be acknowledged. full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionThe burden of pediatric SVE remains substantial. Early clinical symptoms are non-specific; specific clinical markers and sensitive early-warning tools are lacking, and clinical prognosis is often unfavorable. Convulsive seizures, abnormal EEG findings, neuroimaging abnormalities, elevated serum NSE concentrations, and low Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores represent potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality and merit further validation for mortality-risk stratification among children with SVE. Based on the above background, this study describes the clinical characteristics (including demographics, symptoms, signs, laboratory findings, EEG and neuroimaging features) of children with SVE in Anqing City of China, and compares the clinical and laboratory profiles between SVE and mild viral encephalitis. Finally, we identified potential factors associated with in-hospital mortality in children with SVE using univariate analysis. The ultimate goal is to provide preliminary regional data that may help clinicians recognize SVE early and guide risk stratification, while acknowledging the exploratory nature of the findings.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionViral encephalitis is one of the most common central nervous system (CNS) infectious diseases in children. The disease progresses rapidly with diverse manifestations; severe cases often have poor outcomes (1). The incidence of viral encephalitis in children is significantly higher than in adults. Based on data from Henan Province during 2012–2023, approximately 4.5% of pediatric viral encephalitis cases progress to severe viral encephalitis (SVE), which was defined in that study as cases requiring pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admission or presenting with altered consciousness or status epilepticus (2). SVE is characterized by acute onset, rapid progression, and high mortality (up to 8.4%) (3); some patients may evolve into acute necrotizing encephalopathy (4). Among survivors, about 20%–50% suffer from severe neurological sequelae (5), such as epilepsy, cognitive impairment, motor dysfunction, and behavioral abnormalities, which impose a long-term and heavy economic and psychological burden on families and society. Similar findings were reported by Gupta et al. in a retrospective study of pediatric acute encephalitis syndrome from eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, where a substantial proportion of survivors experienced long-term disability, including motor impairment and cognitive deficits (6). Qun Li et al. found that the incidence of sequelae, the number of patients receiving ICU treatment, and the number of deaths in the severe VE group were all significantly higher than those in the mild VE group (7). At present, the diagnosis of pediatric SVE mainly relies on clinical manifestations, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination, and neuroimaging (8), but these methods have certain limitations. Therefore, early identification of SVE and understanding of exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality are crucial for timely and aggressive treatment. In the present study, we analyzed the clinical characteristics and ancillary examination findings of children with SVE to identify potential exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality using univariate analyses (with Firth-penalized-likelihood estimation to address complete separation), with the aim of improving clinicians’ understanding of pediatric SVE and reducing SVE-related mortality and disability. 2.1.Study subjectsAll cases were derived from pediatric inpatients diagnosed with viral encephalitis at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital from January 2023 to December 2025. All enrolled children fulfilled comprehensive diagnostic criteria for viral encephalitis as follows: (1) Acute onset of neurological symptoms and signs; (2) CSF examination showing an elevated WBC count (> 10 × 106/L) with a predominance of lymphocytes, and/or a mild increase in protein; (3) Electroencephalogram and/or cranial imaging showing changes consistent with viral encephalitis; (4) Other central nervous system diseases such as purulent meningitis, tuberculous meningitis, cryptococcal meningitis, and autoimmune encephalitis were excluded. Alternative central nervous system infections were excluded according to the following criteria: 1) Bacterial purulent meningitis: excluded based on CSF profiles (predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes, low glucose, elevated protein), negative bacterial culture, and absence of clinical response to empirical antibiotic therapy. 2) Tuberculous meningitis: Excluded by CSF findings (lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein, decreased glucose), negative Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR, and clinical response to antiviral therapy rather than anti-tuberculous therapy. 3) Cryptococcal meningitis: Excluded by negative India ink stain and negative cryptococcal antigen test in CSF. 4) Autoimmune encephalitis: Excluded by negative testing for anti-neuronal antibodies (anti-NMDA, anti-LGI1, anti-CASPR2, anti-GAD) in both serum and CSF.In terms of pathogen detection, all children provided blood and CSF samples that were tested using multiplex PCR method or serum virus IgM antibody detection to detect viruses: herpes simplex virus 1/2 type, varicella-zoster virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), human herpesvirus 6 type; at the same time, throat swabs were collected for respiratory virus PCR detection (including influenza virus A/B, human parainfluenza virus, SARS-CoV-2). Pathogen detection in CSF and blood was performed using the Multiplex PCR Kit (Anhui Ranchi Biotechnology Co., Ltd., China), which detects HSV-1/2, VZV, and HHV-6. Respiratory viruses were detected from throat swabs using the Respiratory Virus PCR Kit (Guojun Group Anqing Co., Ltd., China), which includes influenza A/B, human parainfluenza virus, adenovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, and SARS-CoV-2. Serum virus-specific IgM antibodies were measured using commercial ELISA kits (Hefei Anmeson Medical Devices Co., Ltd., China). Notably, pathogen detection rates are influenced by multiple factors, including sampling timing, viral load, and primer design. A negative pathogen assay result does not exclude a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis (9). In cases where pathogen testing was negative, a clinical diagnosis of viral encephalitis was accepted based on the comprehensive criteria described above (acute neurological symptoms, CSF pleocytosis with lymphocytic predominance, compatible EEG/neuroimaging findings, and exclusion of other CNS diseases).The patients were divided into two groups: a mild viral encephalitis group (n = 50) and an SVE group (n = 25). All patients met the diagnostic criteria for pediatric severe viral encephalitis as defined by a practical review on diagnostic approach and treatment. The diagnostic criteria for mild viral encephalitis were based on reference (10): All of the following clinical features must be met: 1) Consciousness state: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≥ 13 points (drowsy or agitated, but able to be awakened, and able to follow commands); 2) Seizure episodes: No seizures, or only single, brief convulsive episodes; 3) Focal signs: No obvious limb paralysis, cranial nerve palsy, or ataxia (or extremely mild and short-term recovery); 4) Intracranial hypertension: No severe headache, projectile vomiting, papilledema, and normal fundus examination; 5) Vital signs: Stable respiration, heart rate, and blood pressure, no need for ventilator support; 6) Daily abilities: Can eat independently, with basic life skills retained. The diagnostic criteria for SVE were adopted without modification from reference (7) and included at least one of the following conditions: (1) Frequent convulsions or status epilepticus; (2) Consciousness disturbance with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 8; (3) Limb paralysis or neurobehavioral abnormalities; (4) Brainstem symptoms; (5) Severe or persistent intracranial hypertension; (6) Multiple organ impairment progressing to failure. Because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their associations with mortality within the SVE subgroup should be interpreted as severity markers rather than independent predictors. This study was approved by the ethics committee of Anqing Municipal Hospital (2024-94).Grouping based on GCS and seizures introduces definition-dependent differences between mild and severe cases; thus, comparisons serve only to describe clinical profiles, not to validate diagnostic values. In the prognostic regression analysis, whose primary outcome is in-hospital mortality within the SVE group, these variables are included as potential exploratory factors. However, because seizures and low GCS are components of the SVE definition, their association with mortality should be interpreted with caution, as discussed in the discussion section. Discharge-level functional prognosis was evaluated using the Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS): 1 = death, 2 = persistent vegetative state, 3 = severe disability, 4 = moderate disability, 5 = good recovery. papers.title_original: Clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to identify clinical characteristics and exploratory factors associated with in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis, addressing the need to better understand risk factors for this condition.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was conducted at the Department of Pediatrics, Anqing Municipal Hospital, from January 2023 to December 2025, involving 25 children diagnosed with severe viral encephalitis (SVE) and 50 children with mild encephalitis.
analysis.methods: Pathogen detection was conducted through multiplex PCR and/or serum viral IgM antibody testing. Univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to explore factors associated with in-hospital mortality. Serum NSE was modeled as a continuous variable per 10 ng/mL increment. Neuroimaging and EEG were performed within 24 h of admission.
analysis.main_results: Among the 25 children with SVE, fever (76%), signs of elevated intracranial pressure (68%), and seizures (56%) were common, with four patients dying (16%). The SVE group had significantly longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, higher proportions of abnormal EEG and neuroimaging abnormalities, and elevated serum NSE (all P < 0.05).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Neuroimaging abnormalities, seizures, EEG abnormalities, lower GCS score, and higher serum NSE were significantly associated with in-hospital mortality in the SVE group. The study highlights the importance of these factors in predicting severe outcomes.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Early recognition of these factors may aid in clinical risk assessment and improve management strategies for children with severe viral encephalitis.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its retrospective design and potential for selection bias. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the study and the lack of randomized control.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates clinical characteristics and exploratory factors linked to in-hospital mortality in pediatric severe viral encephalitis (SVE). Conducted at Anqing Municipal Hospital from 2023 to 2025, it compares 25 SVE cases with 50 mild encephalitis cases. Pathogen detection involved multiplex PCR and IgM antibody testing, while univariate analyses and Firth-penalized logistic regression were used to assess risk factors. Results showed that fever, elevated intracranial pressure, and seizures were common in SVE, with four deaths (16%). The SVE group had longer hospital stays, higher seizure rates, lower GCS scores, and more abnormal EEG and neuroimaging findings. Neuroimaging abnormalities, seizures, EEG abnormalities, lower GCS scores, and higher serum NSE were significantly associated with mortality. The findings suggest these factors could aid in early risk assessment. However, the study's limitations include its retrospective design and potential selection bias, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在确定与住院 死亡率 儿童重症病毒性脑炎相关的临床特征和探索性因素,满足更好地了解这种情况的危险因素的需要。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究于2023年1月至2025年12月在安庆市立医院儿科进行,涉及25名确诊为重症病毒性脑炎(SVE)的儿童和50名轻度脑炎儿童。
analysis_zh.methods: 通过多重 PCR 和/或血清病毒 IgM 抗体检测进行病原体检测。采用单变量分析和 Firth 惩罚逻辑回归来探讨与住院 死亡率 相关的因素。血清 NSE 被建模为每 10 ng/mL 增量的连续变量。入院24小时内进行神经影像学和脑电图检查。
analysis_zh.main_results: 在 25 名 SVE 儿童中,发烧(76%)、颅内压升高(68%)和癫痫发作(56%)很常见,其中 4 名患者死亡(16%)。SVE组住院时间明显更长,癫痫发作率更高,GCS评分更低,脑电图和神经影像异常比例更高,血清NSE升高(均P < 0.05)。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 神经影像学异常、癫痫发作、脑电图异常、较低的 GCS 评分和较高的血清 NSE 与 SVE 组中的住院 死亡率 显着相关。该研究强调了这些因素在预测严重后果方面的重要性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 及早认识这些因素可能有助于临床风险评估并改善患有严重病毒性脑炎的儿童的管理策略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其回顾性设计和潜在的选择偏倚而受到限制。由于该研究的观察性质和缺乏随机对照,证据是中等的。

papers.title: Identifying the immunocompetence markers at weaning to predict long-term vaccine response and persistence in pigs
papers.abstract: Vaccination is a key strategy for controlling infectious disease in pigs, but the magnitude and persistence of vaccine-induced immunity vary among individuals. We investigated whether immune and physiological traits measured at weaning could predict long-term antibody (Ab) status and Ab persistence following vaccination against Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae (MH) and Influenza A virus (IAV), and whether predictive markers were shared between vaccines. Two vaccination trials were conducted in a cohort of 381 Large White pigs (MH, n=189; IAV, n=192). Animals were vaccinated at weaning (28 days of age) and received a booster 21 days later. Long-term Ab status was defined at 118 days post-vaccination (dpv) using assay-specific thresholds, while Ab persistence was defined as the decline from the individual peak response at 28 or 35 dpv to 118 dpv. A broad panel of immune and physiological traits measured at weaning was evaluated as candidate predictors. Sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (sPLS-DA) was used for variable selection, followed by PLS-DA classification models. Cross-validated accuracies ranged from 64.7% to 67.7%, indicating moderate predictive performance. Across vaccines, eight predictors were shared for long-term Ab status and twelve for Ab persistence. Hematocrit, IgG, platelet count, and plateletcrit (PCT) were associated with positive long-term Ab status for both vaccines, whereas mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC) and neutrophil percentage were associated with negative status. For persistence, higher vitamin D, -1 globulin concentration, platelet count, and PCT were consistently associated with persistent responses across vaccines, while MCHC and spectral absorbance traits were associated with non-persistence. These findings indicate that early-life immune and physiological traits measured at weaning are associated with immunocompetence traits that contribute to variation in subsequent long-term vaccine antibody outcomes and responsiveness. The identification of both shared and vaccine- or phenotype-specific predictors suggests that vaccine responsiveness reflects both general features of baseline immunocompetence and context-specific determinants.

papers.title: A prospective, comparative cohort analysis of influenza antibody waning in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation
papers.abstract: Background: Reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic prompted concern about waning of population immunity that could lead to subsequent surges in circulation. We compared longitudinal influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong, two regions with reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods: In two prospective cohort studies (HIVE, Michigan; EPI-HK, Hong Kong), we analyzed longitudinal serum samples collected from 2020 through 2023 from participants without influenza infection or vaccination. Sera were tested using hemagglutination inhibition assays (HAI) and microneutralization (MN) against vaccine strains. Two-year fold changes in titers were estimated using multivariable power-law models adjusted for age and baseline titer. Results: We analyzed 173 sera from 57 HIVE participants and 259 sera from 60 EPI-HK participants. Initial HAI geometric mean titers ranged from 12.3-123.4 in HIVE and 6.3-40.9 in EPI-HK. Among those with >1:40 baseline titers in HIVE, fold-change estimates indicated waning for H1N1 strains, including A/Brisbane (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86]), A/Idaho (0.40 [0.32,0.50]), and A/Michigan (0.43 [0.34,0.52]), while H3N2 and influenza B showed minimal or no waning. In EPI-HK, fold-change estimates demonstrated heterogeneous patterns by strain for H1N1, and waning for selected H3N2 strains, including A/Cambodia (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) and A/Singapore (0.48 [0.33,0.69]). MN results were consistent with HAI findings. Conclusion: Influenza antibody responses during the pandemic showed heterogeneous, strain-specific changes rather than uniform decline. These findings suggest that population immunity was maintained for many strains despite reduced viral circulation, with waning occurring in particular strains and varying by population.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the waning of influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation. It compares longitudinal data from two cohort studies, HIVE and EPI-HK, analyzing serum samples collected between 2020 and 2023. The results show strain-specific variations in antibody waning, with significant declines observed for certain H1N1 strains but minimal or no waning for H3N2 and influenza B.
