elements_zh.research_question_and_background: COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 的减少引发了人们对人群免疫力减弱的担忧,这可能导致随后的流通量激增。我们比较了密歇根州和香港的纵向流感抗体滴度,这两个地区在 COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 有所降低。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 在两项前瞻性 队列研究 研究(密歇根州 HIVE;香港 EPI-HK)中,我们分析了 2020 年至 2023 年从未感染流感或 疫苗接种 的参与者收集的纵向血清样本。
elements_zh.methods: 使用针对 疫苗 菌株的血凝抑制测定 (HAI) 和微量中和 (MN) 测试血清。使用针对年龄和基线滴度进行调整的多变量幂律模型来估计滴度的两年倍数变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 我们分析了 57 名 HIVE 参与者的 173 份血清和 60 名 EPI-HK 参与者的 259 份血清。HIVE 中初始 HAI 几何平均滴度为 12.3-123.4,EPI-HK 为 6.3-40.9。在 HIVE 基线滴度 >1:40 的人群中,倍数变化估计表明 H1N1 毒株减弱,包括 A/布里斯班 (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86])、A/爱达荷 (0.40 [0.32,0.50]) 和 A/密歇根 (0.43 [0.34,0.52]),而 H3N2 和乙型流感表现出最小的减弱或没有减弱。在 EPI-HK 中,倍数变化估计显示了 H1N1 病毒株的异质模式,而选定的 H3N2 病毒株的变化则呈减弱趋势,包括 A/柬埔寨 (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) 和 A/新加坡 (0.48 [0.33,0.69])。MN 结果与 HAI 结果一致。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现表明,尽管病毒循环减少,但许多毒株的群体免疫力仍得以维持,但特定毒株的免疫力减弱,且因群体而异。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以通过强调抗体减弱的毒株特异性变异来为 监测 策略和 疫苗 开发提供信息,这可能会影响未来的流感 暴发 和公共卫生干预措施。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖于未感染流感或 疫苗接种 的参与者的血清样本而受到限制,并且由于 队列研究 研究的观察性质和潜在的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

papers.abstract_zh: 背景:COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 的减少引发了人们对人群免疫力减弱的担忧,这可能导致随后的流通量激增。我们比较了密歇根州和香港的纵向流感抗体滴度,这两个地区在 COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 有所降低。方法:在两项前瞻性 队列研究 研究(密歇根州 HIVE;香港 EPI-HK)中,我们分析了 2020 年至 2023 年从未感染流感或 疫苗接种 的参与者收集的纵向血清样本。使用针对 疫苗 菌株的血凝抑制测定 (HAI) 和微量中和 (MN) 测试血清。使用针对年龄和基线滴度进行调整的多变量幂律模型来估计滴度的两年倍数变化。结果:我们分析了 57 名 HIVE 参与者的 173 份血清和 60 名 EPI-HK 参与者的 259 份血清。HIVE 中初始 HAI 几何平均滴度为 12.3-123.4,EPI-HK 为 6.3-40.9。在 HIVE 基线滴度 >1:40 的人群中,倍数变化估计表明 H1N1 毒株减弱,包括 A/布里斯班 (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86])、A/爱达荷 (0.40 [0.32,0.50]) 和 A/密歇根 (0.43 [0.34,0.52]),而 H3N2 和乙型流感表现出最小的减弱或没有减弱。在 EPI-HK 中,倍数变化估计显示了 H1N1 病毒株的异质模式,而选定的 H3N2 病毒株的变化则呈减弱趋势,包括 A/柬埔寨 (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) 和 A/新加坡 (0.48 [0.33,0.69])。MN 结果与 HAI 结果一致。结论:大流行期间的流感抗体反应表现出异质性、毒株特异性变化,而不是统一下降。这些发现表明,尽管病毒循环减少,但许多毒株的群体免疫力仍得以维持,但特定毒株的免疫力减弱,且因群体而异。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 的减少引发了人们对人群免疫力减弱的担忧,这可能导致随后的流通量激增。我们比较了密歇根州和香港的纵向流感抗体滴度,这两个地区在 COVID-19 大流行期间流感 传播 有所降低。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 在两项前瞻性 队列研究 研究(密歇根州 HIVE;香港 EPI-HK)中,我们分析了 2020 年至 2023 年从未感染流感或 疫苗接种 的参与者收集的纵向血清样本。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用针对 疫苗 菌株的血凝抑制测定 (HAI) 和微量中和 (MN) 测试血清。使用针对年龄和基线滴度进行调整的多变量幂律模型来估计滴度的两年倍数变化。
analysis_zh.main_results: 我们分析了 57 名 HIVE 参与者的 173 份血清和 60 名 EPI-HK 参与者的 259 份血清。HIVE 中初始 HAI 几何平均滴度为 12.3-123.4,EPI-HK 为 6.3-40.9。在 HIVE 基线滴度 >1:40 的人群中,倍数变化估计表明 H1N1 毒株减弱,包括 A/布里斯班 (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86])、A/爱达荷 (0.40 [0.32,0.50]) 和 A/密歇根 (0.43 [0.34,0.52]),而 H3N2 和乙型流感表现出最小的减弱或没有减弱。在 EPI-HK 中,倍数变化估计显示了 H1N1 病毒株的异质模式,而选定的 H3N2 病毒株的变化则呈减弱趋势,包括 A/柬埔寨 (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) 和 A/新加坡 (0.48 [0.33,0.69])。MN 结果与 HAI 结果一致。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现表明,尽管病毒循环减少,但许多毒株的群体免疫力仍得以维持,但特定毒株的免疫力减弱,且因群体而异。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以通过强调抗体减弱的毒株特异性变异来为 监测 策略和 疫苗 开发提供信息,这可能会影响未来的流感 暴发 和公共卫生干预措施。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其依赖于未感染流感或 疫苗接种 的参与者的血清样本而受到限制,并且由于 队列研究 研究的观察性质和潜在的混杂因素,证据是中等的。

news.content_title: National flu and COVID-19 surveillance report: 15 October 2026 (week 42)
news.content: This publication is licensed under the terms of the Open Government Licence v3.0 except where otherwise stated. To view this licence, visit nationalarchives.gov.uk/doc/open-government-licence/version/3 or write to the Information Policy Team, The National Archives, Kew, London TW9 4DU, or email: psi@nationalarchives.gov.uk . Where we have identified any third party copyright information you will need to obtain permission from the copyright holders concerned. This publication is available at https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-reports-2026-to-2027-season/national-flu-and-covid-19-surveillance-report-15-october-2026-week-42 This report summarises the information from the surveillance systems which are used to monitor COVID-19 (caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 or SARS-CoV-2), influenza, respiratory syncytial virus ( RSV ) and diseases caused by other seasonal respiratory viruses in England. The report is based on data up to week 41 of 2026 between 5 October and 11 October 2026. The main messages of this report are: Annual reports for the 2025 to 2026 season: Influenza in the UK, annual epidemiological report: winter 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Epidemiology of COVID-19 in England (published 25 June 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in all GP patients: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in school-aged children: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Seasonal influenza vaccine uptake in frontline healthcare workers: annual report 2025 to 2026 (published 28 May 2026) Influenza activity remained stable and is circulating at baseline levels, some indicators showed decreased activity among young adults. Emergency department ( ED ) attendances for influenza-like-illness ( ILI ) remained stable and above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection ( ARI ) incidents in the community decreased compared with the previous week. Weekly influenza vaccine uptake for the 2026 to 2027 season was reported for the first time in the week 41 report. Some pharmacy vaccination data remained unavailable or incomplete at the time of analysis (week 42). Consequently, results for those aged 65 years and over and those aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups have been excluded from this report. This is to prevent misleading conclusions being drawn from incomplete data. Data for pregnant women and children aged 2 and 3 years is included, but should be interpreted with caution as it may also be affected by incomplete pharmacy data. The impact on these groups is expected to be smaller because it is likely that fewer vaccinations are given in pharmacies to them. All cohorts will be reinstated and statistics revised once additional data becomes available. COVID-19 activity showed mixed trends and is circulating at low levels. ED attendances for COVID-19-like illness remained stable. The number of COVID-19 confirmed acute respiratory infections ( ARI ) incidents increased compared with the previous week. By the end of week 41 2026 (week ending 11 October 2026) 23.0% of all people aged 75 years and over, and 9.9% of all people aged under 75 years with a weakened immune system, had been vaccinated with an autumn 2026 dose since 1 October 2026. RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. ED attendances for acute bronchiolitis remained stable and below seasonally expected levels. Note 1: these indicators use the moving epidemic method ( MEM ) and the mean standard deviation method ( MSD ) to define thresholds to determine their respective levels of activity. Further information on these methods can be found in Influenza surveillance in Europe: establishing epidemic thresholds by the Moving Epidemic Method and Setting thresholds to determine COVID-19 activity levels using the mean standard deviation ( MSD ) method, England, 2022 to 2024 . The MEM approach is well-established for some influenza surveillance indicators, however, for other indicators both the MEM and MSD are experimental and may be subject to future revision. Influenza laboratory surveillance and GP swabbing positivity have transitioned from using MEM to using MSD . These approaches will be considered alongside expert opinion and triangulation of other data sources. The Second Generation Surveillance System ( SGSS ) captures test result information for notifiable infectious diseases, including COVID-19 and influenza, from laboratories in England. The unified sample dataset ( USD ) stores all SARS-CoV-2 test results reported to SGSS , Respiratory DataMart and UKHSA laboratories, and is used to calculate the percentage of tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 among all SARS-CoV-2 tests conducted. analysis.brief_en: The National Flu and COVID-19 Surveillance Report for 15 October 2026 (week 42) provides an update on influenza and respiratory virus activity in England. The report indicates that influenza activity remained stable and at baseline levels, with some indicators showing decreased activity among young adults. Emergency department attendances for influenza-like-illness (ILI) remained stable and above seasonally expected levels. The number of influenza-confirmed acute respiratory infection (ARI) incidents in the community decreased compared to the previous week. However, some pharmacy vaccination data was incomplete, leading to the exclusion of results for individuals aged 65 years and over, as well as those aged 6 months to under 65 years in clinical risk groups. The report also notes that RSV activity increased and is circulating at baseline levels. OffOn Stream on FDA approves Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine Moderna was seeking approval for the vaccine's use in adults over 50. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Mary Kekatos, and Eric M. Strauss August 6, 2026, 3:59 AM Share The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. The vaccine, mFLUSIVA, is expected to be available for people 50 and older for the 2026-2027 respiratory illness season. "Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFLUSIVA provides an important new option for America's seniors. This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation," Stéphane Bancel, Chief Executive Officer of Moderna, said in a statement. In this Dec. 15, 2020, file photo, the Moderna, Inc. headquarters is shown in Cambridge, Mass. Elise Amendola/AP, FILE In a clinical trial for people aged 50 to 64, the mRNA vaccine led to 27% fewer confirmed flu cases than the current standard vaccine. The safety profile for Moderna’s vaccine and the current standard was about the same, but more people taking the mRNA vaccine reported side effects; those were mostly mild and lasted two days or less. For people 65 and older, a high-dose vaccine is currently recommended. Moderna said it will keep data this winter on how mFlusiva does compared to the current high-dose vaccine and submit that to the FDA to see if the vaccine remains approved for that population. Earlier this year, the FDA announced it would not review Moderna's application for the vaccine. Strauss August 6, 2026, 3:59 AM Share The Food and Drug Administration approved Moderna's mRNA seasonal flu vaccine on Wednesday. The vaccine, mFLUSIVA, is expected to be available for people 50 and older for the 2026-2027 respiratory illness season. "Flu remains a significant public health challenge, and mFLUSIVA provides an important new option for America's seniors. This approval also reflects the ongoing potential of our mRNA platform to help address important public health challenges through continued scientific innovation," Stéphane Bancel, Chief Executive Officer of Moderna, said in a statement. In this Dec. 15, 2020, file photo, the Moderna, Inc. headquarters is shown in Cambridge, Mass. Elise Amendola/AP, FILE In a clinical trial for people aged 50 to 64, the mRNA vaccine led to 27% fewer confirmed flu cases than the current standard vaccine. The safety profile for Moderna’s vaccine and the current standard was about the same, but more people taking the mRNA vaccine reported side effects; those were mostly mild and lasted two days or less. For people 65 and older, a high-dose vaccine is currently recommended. Moderna said it will keep data this winter on how mFlusiva does compared to the current high-dose vaccine and submit that to the FDA to see if the vaccine remains approved for that population. Earlier this year, the FDA announced it would not review Moderna's application for the vaccine. However, the agency backtracked and agreed to review the shot after Moderna promised to conduct another study after the shot became available on the market. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In January 2026, health authorities in Burundi confronted a familiar and unsettling scenario. A secondary school in Bujumbura reported a sharp increase in respiratory illness among its students, and the immediate suspicion fell on SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. The prospect of a resurgence in a densely populated school setting was a serious concern for the national public health system. Yet when symptomatic students were tested for SARS-CoV-2, the results came back negative, leaving clinicians and epidemiologists with a cluster of unexplained severe acute respiratory infections and no identified cause. That diagnostic dead end is precisely where the investigation described in a study published in BMC Infectious Diseases begins. A team led by Néhémie Nzoyikorera of the National Reference Laboratory at the National Public Health Institute in Burundi, working with colleagues at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam and partners across East Africa, Morocco, and Germany, applied targeted viral enrichment sequencing to nasopharyngeal samples collected from symptomatic students. The approach was designed to cast a wide net: rather than testing for one pathogen at a time, the method enriches and sequences viral genetic material present in a sample, allowing researchers to identify whatever viruses are there, known or unknown. The technical foundation of the investigation rests on the Illumina Viral Surveillance Panel version 2, run on the compact iSeq 100 sequencing platform. Eight samples from SARS-CoV-2-negative students were processed through this targeted enrichment workflow. The panel uses probes designed to capture viral genomes across a broad range of respiratory and other viruses, concentrating scarce viral nucleic acid against a background of human DNA and other genetic noise. After sequencing, the reads were quality-checked, screened for viral identification, and then assembled into genome sequences where coverage permitted. Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Symptoms Order DNA Kits Study Biology Track Outbreaks The results were decisive. Influenza A virus was detected in seven of the eight samples analyzed, and four of those samples yielded near-complete influenza A genomes of sufficient quality for detailed genomic characterization. When the researchers assigned clades to the reconstructed genomes, every characterized virus fell into the same category: Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K. This was the first genomic detection and characterization of that subclade in Burundi, a finding that carries significance well beyond the school gates because H3N2 subclade K has been drawing attention internationally as an emerging variant of the seasonal influenza virus. Influenza A(H3N2) is one of the seasonal influenza A subtypes that circulates in human populations and is notorious for its capacity to evolve rapidly. The hemagglutinin protein, the HA of H3N2, is the primary target of protective antibodies, and mutations accumulating in the HA gene allow the virus to escape immunity built up through previous infections and vaccination. Clade and subclade designations, such as subclade K, are assigned on the basis of characteristic amino acid signatures in HA, and they help global surveillance laboratories track which genetic variants are spreading, which are vaccine-matched, and which signal a need for updated vaccine composition. Phylogenetic analysis of the Burundian sequences added a layer of complexity to the outbreak picture. The sequences did not form a single tight cluster. Instead, they split into two distinct groups on the phylogenetic tree, suggesting that at least two separate viral lineages of H3N2 subclade K were circulating during the outbreak. This observation matters for outbreak interpretation. A single introduction followed by onward transmission would typically produce a compact cluster of closely related genomes, whereas the presence of divergent lineages points to multiple introductions or to undetected circulation in the community before the school cluster was recognized. Genomic analysis was therefore able to reveal structure in the outbreak that routine testing alone could not. The researchers also examined the neuraminidase sequences for markers associated with resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors, the class of antiviral drugs that includes oseltamivir. No resistance-associated markers were detected, an important clinical finding because it indicates that antiviral treatment would be expected to remain effective against the circulating viruses if severe cases required it. The absence of resistance markers also provides reassurance for national treatment guidelines and for any future response to H3N2 subclade K in the region. Discover more Genomic genomic Bioengineering News Subscription Bioengineering careers guide Bioengineering Career Guide To ensure the findings contributed to the global picture, the influenza genome sequences were shared through GISAID, the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data, which serves as the central repository for influenza sequence data used by the World Health Organization and surveillance laboratories worldwide. Sharing genomes from Burundi addresses a longstanding gap in global influenza surveillance, which has historically been dominated by data from high-income countries in temperate regions. Sequences from African settings, particularly from outbreaks identified through unexplained severe acute respiratory infection surveillance, help clarify how subclade K and other variants move between regions and how they evolve in different population contexts. The study also underscores the value of severe acute respiratory infection surveillance as a pillar of emerging disease preparedness. The samples in this investigation had been collected initially for SARI surveillance, and the national ethics framework, including approval by the National Ethics Committee of Burundi with a consent waiver, allowed their use for pathogen identification. When the initial hypothesis of a COVID-19 resurgence collapsed, the surveillance infrastructure and the stored samples provided the raw material for a rapid pivot to unbiased pathogen detection. The Burundi Public Health Emergency Operation Center supported the epidemiological investigations, and reagents were provided through the East African Community Secretariat’s Mobile Lab Project, illustrating how regional cooperation underpins laboratory response capacity. The broader lesson from the Bujumbura school outbreak is that targeted viral enrichment sequencing is a practical tool for investigating acute respiratory outbreaks when the cause is unknown, particularly when initial testing is negative and routine testing for other respiratory viruses is limited. In settings where multiplex PCR panels are expensive or unavailable, a single sequencing run can identify the pathogen, characterize its genome, assign its clade, screen for resistance markers, and place it in a global phylogenetic context. The first genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K in Burundi demonstrates that genomic surveillance capacity, strengthened through projects such as GREAT-LIFE at the national public health institute, can deliver actionable findings from a modest number of samples, and that the identification of distinct viral lineages within a single school outbreak highlights the value of genomic approaches to complement routine laboratory testing and support respiratory pathogen surveillance in Burundi and across the region. The genomic analysis showed that the sequences split into two distinct groups on the phylogenetic tree, suggesting multiple introductions or community circulation of the virus. This finding highlights the value of genomic surveillance in identifying and understanding outbreaks, especially when initial tests are inconclusive. The study also underscores the importance of severe acute respiratory infection surveillance as a tool for emerging disease preparedness.

news.title_zh: 基因组测序揭示布隆迪一所中学中隐藏的流感甲型H3N2流感病毒亚系K学校暴发 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: In January 2026, a secondary school in Bujumbura, Burundi, experienced a sharp increase in respiratory illness among students, initially suspected to be caused by SARS-CoV-2. However, testing for SARS-CoV-2 came back negative, leading to a diagnostic dead end. A study published on October 17, 2026, in BMC Infectious Diseases used targeted viral enrichment sequencing to analyze eight samples from the students. The results revealed that Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K was responsible for the outbreak, with seven of the eight samples testing positive. Four of these samples provided near-complete genomes, allowing for detailed characterization. The genomic analysis showed that the sequences split into two distinct groups on the phylogenetic tree, suggesting multiple introductions or community circulation of the virus. This finding highlights the value of genomic surveillance in identifying and understanding outbreaks, especially when initial tests are inconclusive. The study also underscores the importance of severe acute respiratory infection surveillance as a tool for emerging disease preparedness.
news.content_zh: 2026年1月,布隆迪布琼布拉的一所中学出现学生呼吸道疾病病例急剧上升的情况,最初疑似由SARS-CoV-2引起。然而,SARS-CoV-2检测结果为阴性,导致诊断陷入僵局。2026年10月17日发表在《BMC Infectious Diseases》上的研究使用靶向病毒富集测序技术分析了来自学生的八份样本。结果显示,流感甲型H3N2流感病毒亚系K是导致暴发的原因,其中八份样本中有七份检测呈阳性。这四份样本提供了接近完整的基因组,从而能够进行详细特征分析。基因组分析表明,序列在系统发育树上分为两个明显不同的组,提示病毒可能存在多次引入或在社区内循环传播。这一发现突显了基因组监测在识别和理解暴发中的价值,尤其是在初始检测结果不明确的情况下。该研究还强调了严重急性呼吸道感染监测作为新兴疾病应对工具的重要性。

news.content: CHAIRMAN: DR. KHALID BIN THANI AL THANI EDITOR-IN-CHIEF: PROF. KHALID MUBARAK AL-SHAFI News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook Qatar Health General Education Government Weather Transport Culture How To? World Gulf Middle East Asia Europe Africa Americas Business Qatar Business Middle East Business World Business Stock Market Energy Sports Qatar Sport Football Formula One NBA Cricket Tennis Rally Athletics Motosports Golf Horse Racing Olympics Padel Cuesports Views Editor-in-Chief Opinion Editorial Doha Today Community Campus Souq Life Style Technology Motoring Feature & more Wellness Food Travel Fashion Science & Environment Entertainment Cinema Music In Focus Qatar 2022 Doha Expo Asian Cup IAAF Doha2019 Ramadan Qatar National Day World Cup 2026 News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook Qatar / Health Seasonal influenza vaccine available at health centres Published: 15 Oct 2026 - 08:36 am | Last Updated: 15 Oct 2026 - 12:02 pm Follow usnews Copy A+ A- The Peninsula Doha, Qatar: The seasonal influenza vaccine is available free of charge at Primary Health Care Corporation (PHCC) health centres across Qatar, as part of efforts to protect individuals and communities from infectious diseases. Vaccination remains a key pillar of disease prevention at every stage of life, from infancy to older adulthood. PHCC provides routine and seasonal vaccinations, as well as vaccines for travel, Hajj and Umrah, in accordance with the National Immunization Programme. Executive Director of Preventive Health Department at PHCC, Dr. Hamad Al Mudahka emphasised the importance of raising awareness about vaccination and its role in protecting individual and community health. He highlighted the department's commitment to promoting vaccine awareness through educational campaigns and outreach activities targeting all age groups. Manager of Health Protection at PHCC, Dr. Khalid Elawad stressed the importance of ensuring access to vaccination services and enhancing public awareness of their benefits. PHCC’s immunisation programme covers vaccines against several diseases, including measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, hepatitis B, human papillomavirus (HPV), pneumococcal disease, COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and meningococcal disease. Vaccine requirements depend on age, health status and approved recommendations. The seasonal influenza vaccine is particularly important during the respiratory virus season. PHCC recommends annual vaccination for everyone aged six months and older, with particular attention to groups at greater risk of complications, including young children, older adults, pregnant women, people with chronic diseases and healthcare workers. As influenza virus strains change from season to season, annual vaccination helps reduce the severity of illness, complications and hospital admissions. The vaccine is available free of charge at PHCC health centres, with access arrangements following the procedures announced by individual centres. PHCC emphasises that immunisation is not limited to childhood. While children must complete their recommended vaccination schedules, adolescents, adults, pregnant women and older people may also require vaccines according to their health conditions, risk factors, travel requirements and seasonal considerations. Children who miss scheduled vaccine doses can receive catch-up vaccinations based on their age and immunisation history. Delayed doses should not prevent parents from completing their children’s vaccination schedules. PHCC operates 31 health centres across Qatar, supporting access to healthcare and preventive services. Its vaccination arrangements also help ensure appropriate assessments and the timely administration of recommended doses. Vaccination efforts complement the work of PHCC’s Control of Communicable Diseases Team, which supports disease prevention, surveillance, awareness and healthcare professional training. These activities contribute to strengthening infection prevention and improving public understanding of communicable diseases. With the influenza season underway, PHCC encourages eligible individuals to receive their annual flu vaccine, particularly those most vulnerable to complications. Vaccination protects individuals while helping safeguard families and the wider community by reducing the risk of serious illness and transmission. KHALID MUBARAK AL-SHAFI News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook Qatar Health General Education Government Weather Transport Culture How To? World Gulf Middle East Asia Europe Africa Americas Business Qatar Business Middle East Business World Business Stock Market Energy Sports Qatar Sport Football Formula One NBA Cricket Tennis Rally Athletics Motosports Golf Horse Racing Olympics Padel Cuesports Views Editor-in-Chief Opinion Editorial Doha Today Community Campus Souq Life Style Technology Motoring Feature & more Wellness Food Travel Fashion Science & Environment Entertainment Cinema Music In Focus Qatar 2022 Doha Expo Asian Cup IAAF Doha2019 Ramadan Qatar National Day World Cup 2026 News Opinion Writers Videos Editorials Handbook Qatar / Health Seasonal influenza vaccine available at health centres Published: 15 Oct 2026 - 08:36 am | Last Updated: 15 Oct 2026 - 12:02 pm Follow usnews Copy A+ A- The Peninsula Doha, Qatar: The seasonal influenza vaccine is available free of charge at Primary Health Care Corporation (PHCC) health centres across Qatar, as part of efforts to protect individuals and communities from infectious diseases. Vaccination remains a key pillar of disease prevention at every stage of life, from infancy to older adulthood. PHCC provides routine and seasonal vaccinations, as well as vaccines for travel, Hajj and Umrah, in accordance with the National Immunization Programme. Executive Director of Preventive Health Department at PHCC, Dr. Hamad Al Mudahka emphasised the importance of raising awareness about vaccination and its role in protecting individual and community health. He highlighted the department's commitment to promoting vaccine awareness through educational campaigns and outreach activities targeting all age groups. Manager of Health Protection at PHCC, Dr. Khalid Elawad stressed the importance of ensuring access to vaccination services and enhancing public awareness of their benefits. PHCC’s immunisation programme covers vaccines against several diseases, including measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, hepatitis B, human papillomavirus (HPV), pneumococcal disease, COVID-19, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and meningococcal disease. Vaccine requirements depend on age, health status and approved recommendations. The seasonal influenza vaccine is particularly important during the respiratory virus season. PHCC recommends annual vaccination for everyone aged six months and older, with particular attention to groups at greater risk of complications, including young children, older adults, pregnant women, people with chronic diseases and healthcare workers. As influenza virus strains change from season to season, annual vaccination helps reduce the severity of illness, complications and hospital admissions. The vaccine is available free of charge at PHCC health centres, with access arrangements following the procedures announced by individual centres. PHCC emphasises that immunisation is not limited to childhood. While children must complete their recommended vaccination schedules, adolescents, adults, pregnant women and older people may also require vaccines according to their health conditions, risk factors, travel requirements and seasonal considerations. Children who miss scheduled vaccine doses can receive catch-up vaccinations based on their age and immunisation history. Delayed doses should not prevent parents from completing their children’s vaccination schedules. PHCC operates 31 health centres across Qatar, supporting access to healthcare and preventive services. Its vaccination arrangements also help ensure appropriate assessments and the timely administration of recommended doses. Vaccination efforts complement the work of PHCC’s Control of Communicable Diseases Team, which supports disease prevention, surveillance, awareness and healthcare professional training. These activities contribute to strengthening infection prevention and improving public understanding of communicable diseases. With the influenza season underway, PHCC encourages eligible individuals to receive their annual flu vaccine, particularly those most vulnerable to complications. Vaccination protects individuals while helping safeguard families and the wider community by reducing the risk of serious illness and transmission. news.content_zh: 半岛新闻社于2026年10月15日发布的卡塔尔报道指出,季节性流感 疫苗 在全国PHCC卫生中心均可获得。该疫苗 免费提供,建议所有6个月及以上年龄的人群接种,尤其是那些并发症风险较高的群体,如婴幼儿、老年人、孕妇、患有慢性病的人群以及医护人员。PHCC强调,疫苗接种不仅限于儿童时期,还包括针对多种疾病的疫苗,包括麻疹、腮腺炎、风疹、白喉、破伤风、百日咳、脊髓灰质炎、乙型肝炎、人乳头瘤病毒(HPV)、肺炎球菌病、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)和脑膜炎球菌病。在呼吸道病毒高发季节,季节性流感 疫苗 尤其重要,因为它有助于减轻疾病严重程度、减少并发症和住院人数。PHCC的疫苗接种安排支持适当的评估和推荐剂量的及时接种,补充其传染病控制团队在疾病预防、监测、意识提升和培训方面的工作。该报道强调了疫苗接种在保护个人、保障家庭及更广泛社区方面的重要性,通过降低严重疾病和传播的风险来实现这一目标。

Add Weather to your Google feeds Photo: AP 315.000 doses of free vaccines against seasonal flu have been provided in Serbia Copied 315.000 doses of free vaccines against seasonal flu have been provided in Serbia. Doctors especially recommend immunization for people over 65 years old, chronically ill, pregnant women and other people with an increased risk of complications Vaccination against seasonal flu it started in Serbia. Doctors advise persons at particular risk of severe forms and complications of the flu to be vaccinated. There are two vaccines available, which are free. What vaccines are available Sa "Batut" Institute it was announced that a total of 315.000 doses of flu vaccines were planned and contracted for the upcoming season. Two vaccines are available to patients. Photo: Tanjug/Miloš Milivojević Vaccination against seasonal flu has started throughout Serbia In question are 288.000 doses of the trivalent vaccine "Torvaxflu" produced by the Institute for Virology, Vaccines and Serums "Torlak" and 27.000 doses of trivalent "Vaksigrip" manufactured by Sanofi Pasteur. As stated, Torlak's vaccine contains three strains, two strains of type A and one of type B, in accordance with the recommendation of the World Health Organization. This vaccine is intended for adults. In addition to adults, children older than six months and pregnant women can also receive Vaxigrip. Photo: TANJUG/MINISTRY OF HEALTH/A. ANGELOVSKI/bs One of the free vaccines was made in Torlak Flu symptoms are high fever, headache, malaise, severe muscle and throat pain, cough, etc. Doctor's recommendations Doctor Mira Alimpijević from the Belgrade Health Center tells Nova.rs that it is recommended to receive one dose of the flu vaccine every year, because the strains circulating in the population change every year, and the composition of the vaccines is different. Photo: Tanjug/Ana Paunković Doctors especially recommend immunization for people over 65 years old, chronically ill, pregnant women and other people with an increased risk of complications "That is why citizens are recommended to get a flu vaccine every year, in order to protect themselves, but also their family members, people with chronic and malignant diseases or people with immunodeficiencies. As a result of greater vaccination coverage, collective immunity is created in the population and thus the spread of the epidemic is prevented," she points out for Nova. She adds that the flu season begins in December, and that the epidemic reaches its peak in January and February. He recommends that the vaccination be done in November, because it takes two to three weeks to achieve immunity. Who should get vaccinated? Vaccination is carried out before the flu season, and is especially recommended for people with chronic diseases, people over 65, pregnant women and other groups with an increased risk of more serious complications. Photo: Pexels/Polina Tankilevitch Fever is one of the symptoms of flu "The recommendation of the World Health Organization is that active immunization should be carried out in persons at special risk. These include persons with malignant diseases regardless of the current therapeutic status, renal dysfunction, hemoglobinopathy, chronic neurological disorders, immunosuppression, extremely obese persons..." explains the doctor. When asked why it is desirable to vaccinate healthy people, the answer is that the vaccine is least effective in those for whom it is most important, and thus prevents the transmission of the virus. According to the doctor, pregnant women in the first trimester of pregnancy, people allergic to eggs, people who had an allergic reaction to the flu vaccine and people who currently have an infection, have a fever, cough, sneeze, etc. are never vaccinated. analysis.time: Vaccination against seasonal flu has started on October 16, 2026, at 10:04 p.m. The flu season is expected to begin in December and peak in January and February (N17).
analysis.location_and_population: The vaccination campaign is taking place in Serbia (N2). It is especially recommended for people over 65 years old, chronically ill, pregnant women, and other high-risk groups (N3, N15).
analysis.event: Vaccination against seasonal flu has started in Serbia (N1, N8). Doctors recommend annual vaccination due to changing strains (N14).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: A total of 315,000 doses of free vaccines against seasonal flu have been provided in Serbia (N2). The vaccines are intended to prevent severe complications and reduce the spread of the virus (N16).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The vaccination campaign is ongoing, with two vaccines available: Torvaxflu and Vaksigrip (N8, N7). The World Health Organization recommends the vaccine composition (N9). The campaign is part of public health efforts to prepare for the flu season (N18).

analysis.brief_en: Vaccination against seasonal flu has begun in Serbia on October 16, 2026, with 315,000 free doses provided. The campaign targets high-risk groups such as individuals over 65, those with chronic illnesses, pregnant women, and others prone to severe complications. Doctors emphasize the importance of annual vaccination due to the changing strains of the virus, as recommended by the World Health Organization. Two vaccines, Torvaxflu and Vaksigrip, are available, with the former intended for adults and the latter for children over six months and pregnant women. The flu season is expected to start in December and peak in January and February, so vaccination is advised in November to allow time for immunity to develop. This initiative aims to create collective immunity and prevent the spread of the virus.

news.source_body_en: Vaccination against seasonal flu has begun in Serbia on October 16, 2026, with 315,000 free doses provided. The campaign targets high-risk groups such as individuals over 65, those with chronic illnesses, pregnant women, and others prone to severe complications. Doctors emphasize the importance of annual vaccination due to the changing strains of the virus, as recommended by the World Health Organization. Two vaccines, Torvaxflu and Vaksigrip, are available, with the former intended for adults and the latter for children over six months and pregnant women. The flu season is expected to start in December and peak in January and February, so vaccination is advised in November to allow time for immunity to develop. This initiative aims to create collective immunity and prevent the spread of the virus.

news.content_title: Osivax Reports Phase 2b Results for OVX836 and Advances Combination Strategy for Next-Generation Seasonal Influenza Vaccines
news.content: My Markets Watchlist Markets News Search Business Strategy Economy Finance Retail Advertising Careers Law Media Real Estate Small Business The Better Work Project Personal Finance Tech Science AI Enterprise Transportation Startups Innovation Markets News Stocks Indices Commodities Crypto Currencies ETFs Lifestyle Entertainment Culture Travel Food Health Education Parenting Military & Defense Politics Reviews Home Kitchen Style Streaming Pets Tech Deals Gifts Tickets Video Big Business So Expensive View From Above Small Business Authorized Account Risky Business Boot Camp Still Standing How Crime Works Life Lessons Level Up Community Games Boxed Pipeline Knighthop Tally Osivax Reports Phase 2b Results for OVX836 and Advances Combination Strategy for Next-Generation Seasonal Influenza Vaccines PRESS RELEASE GlobeNewswire Oct. 15, 2026, 05:30 AM Phase 2b study provides first consistent efficacy signal for a monovalent nucleoprotein-based influenza vaccine across both major influenza A subtypes OVX836 did not meet its pre-specified primary endpoint of 50% vaccine efficacy Results support development of OVX836 in combination with traditional seasonal influenza vaccines to provide a complementary layer of protection Strategic collaborations with GC Biopharma and a second, undisclosed global pharmaceutical partner enable next phase of combination vaccine development Lyon, France and Liège, Belgium - 15 October 2026 - Osivax, a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing differentiated influenza vaccines designed to generate broad-spectrum immune responses, today announced results from its sponsored Phase 2b field efficacy trial of OVX836 and outlined the next phase of development for its next-generation seasonal influenza vaccine strategy. The Phase 2b field efficacy trial evaluated the efficacy, safety and immunogenicity of OVX836 (480 μg) versus placebo in 2,850 healthy adults in Europe. The trial did not achieve its pre-specified primary endpoint of 50% vaccine efficacy (VE), while a point estimate VE of 24% (not statistically significant) was reported. Secondary endpoints of VE, such as the CDC-defined influenza-like illness and the strain-specific VE showed an emerging pattern for a preliminary VE signal with VE point estimates of 28% (CDC), 27% (A/H3) and 25% (A/H1N1pdm09), respectively. The vaccine also demonstrated a favorable safety profile consistent with previous clinical trials and induced robust NP-specific antibody and T-cell responses. To Osivax’s knowledge, these findings represent the first consistent efficacy signal for a monovalent nucleoprotein-based influenza vaccine across both major influenza A subtypes in a field efficacy trial. In parallel to the development of OVX836 as a standalone vaccine candidate, Osivax has been advancing a combination strategy to harness the potential synergistic effects of influenza vaccines targeting different influenza antigens. The Phase 2b results further support this strategy, which combines the broad cellular immunity induced by OVX836 with the strain-specific protection provided by established seasonal influenza vaccines. Recently established collaborations with GC Biopharma and a second, undisclosed global pharmaceutical partner will enable the development of combination vaccine candidates in a single injection. This approach has the potential to substantially improve overall vaccine efficacy. “Large efficacy studies are designed not only to evaluate clinical benefit, but also to deepen our understanding of novel immune mechanisms under real-world conditions," said Dr Nicola Groth, Chief Medical Officer of Osivax. "While the study did not meet its primary endpoint, the consistency of the efficacy signal across influenza A subtypes, together with the observed immunogenicity and favourable safety profile, reinforces our confidence that nucleoprotein-targeted immunity can provide a complementary mechanism of protection alongside conventional seasonal influenza vaccines.” “These results provide a clear direction for the future development of OVX836. Rather than replacing existing seasonal influenza vaccines, we believe the greatest opportunity lies in complementing them” said Alexandre Le Vert, CEO and Co-Founder of Osivax.“By combining strain-specific antibody protection with the broad cellular immunity induced by OVX836, we aim to develop next-generation influenza vaccines capable of delivering broader and more durable protection against seasonal influenza.” The two collaborations provide access to established seasonal influenza vaccines for the development of combination vaccine candidates. Securing distinct agreements with two established leaders in influenza vaccines represents a significant milestone for Osivax and a strong external validation of its combination strategy. The first Phase 1/2 combination study is anticipated in Q4 2027. About OVX836 OVX836 is a first-in-class influenza A vaccine candidate that targets the nucleoprotein (NP), a highly conserved internal antigen. Unlike surface antigens, the NP is much less likely to mutate, providing a broader and more universal immune response. Osivax’ oligoDOMTM technology enables the design and production of a recombinant version of the NP, which self-assembles into a nanoparticle, thus triggering powerful T- and B-cell immune responses. OVX836 has been tested in 7 clinical trials with over 4,000 participants so far, and has shown promising safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy read-outs. About OXV836-005 – Asuniva Asuniva is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter Phase 2b trial conducted in Belgium, France, Finland and Germany, to assess the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of a single intramuscular dose of OVX836 (480 μg) in 2,850 participants aged 18–59 years. Asuniva is the first large, field efficacy study with OVX836 which generated the clinical evidence needed to advance the vaccine toward late-stage development. Further information can be found at clinicaltrials.gov. About Osivax Osivax is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing a portfolio of differentiated influenza vaccines generating superior T-cell responses in addition to strong and sustained B-cell responses, thanks to its novel, self-assembling nanoparticle platform technology, oligoDOMTM. The company’s lead candidate, OVX836, is a broad-spectrum influenza A vaccine candidate currently in Phase 2b clinical trials with over 4,000 volunteers tested and encouraging first signal of vaccine efficacy data. By combining OVX836 with standard flu vaccines, Osivax is advancing toward a best-in-class seasonal flu vaccine to prevent all strains of influenza. news.content_original: My Markets Watchlist Markets News Search Business Strategy Economy Finance Retail Advertising Careers Law Media Real Estate Small Business The Better Work Project Personal Finance Tech Science AI Enterprise Transportation Startups Innovation Markets News Stocks Indices Commodities Crypto Currencies ETFs Lifestyle Entertainment Culture Travel Food Health Education Parenting Military & Defense Politics Reviews Home Kitchen Style Streaming Pets Tech Deals Gifts Tickets Video Big Business So Expensive View From Above Small Business Authorized Account Risky Business Boot Camp Still Standing How Crime Works Life Lessons Level Up Community Games Boxed Pipeline Knighthop Tally Osivax Reports Phase 2b Results for OVX836 and Advances Combination Strategy for Next-Generation Seasonal Influenza Vaccines PRESS RELEASE GlobeNewswire Oct. 15, 2026, 05:30 AM Phase 2b study provides first consistent efficacy signal for a monovalent nucleoprotein-based influenza vaccine across both major influenza A subtypes OVX836 did not meet its pre-specified primary endpoint of 50% vaccine efficacy Results support development of OVX836 in combination with traditional seasonal influenza vaccines to provide a complementary layer of protection Strategic collaborations with GC Biopharma and a second, undisclosed global pharmaceutical partner enable next phase of combination vaccine development Lyon, France and Liège, Belgium - 15 October 2026 - Osivax, a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing differentiated influenza vaccines designed to generate broad-spectrum immune responses, today announced results from its sponsored Phase 2b field efficacy trial of OVX836 and outlined the next phase of development for its next-generation seasonal influenza vaccine strategy. The Phase 2b field efficacy trial evaluated the efficacy, safety and immunogenicity of OVX836 (480 μg) versus placebo in 2,850 healthy adults in Europe. The trial did not achieve its pre-specified primary endpoint of 50% vaccine efficacy (VE), while a point estimate VE of 24% (not statistically significant) was reported. Secondary endpoints of VE, such as the CDC-defined influenza-like illness and the strain-specific VE showed an emerging pattern for a preliminary VE signal with VE point estimates of 28% (CDC), 27% (A/H3) and 25% (A/H1N1pdm09), respectively. The vaccine also demonstrated a favorable safety profile consistent with previous clinical trials and induced robust NP-specific antibody and T-cell responses. To Osivax’s knowledge, these findings represent the first consistent efficacy signal for a monovalent nucleoprotein-based influenza vaccine across both major influenza A subtypes in a field efficacy trial. In parallel to the development of OVX836 as a standalone vaccine candidate, Osivax has been advancing a combination strategy to harness the potential synergistic effects of influenza vaccines targeting different influenza antigens. The Phase 2b results further support this strategy, which combines the broad cellular immunity induced by OVX836 with the strain-specific protection provided by established seasonal influenza vaccines. Recently established collaborations with GC Biopharma and a second, undisclosed global pharmaceutical partner will enable the development of combination vaccine candidates in a single injection. This approach has the potential to substantially improve overall vaccine efficacy. “Large efficacy studies are designed not only to evaluate clinical benefit, but also to deepen our understanding of novel immune mechanisms under real-world conditions," said Dr Nicola Groth, Chief Medical Officer of Osivax. "While the study did not meet its primary endpoint, the consistency of the efficacy signal across influenza A subtypes, together with the observed immunogenicity and favourable safety profile, reinforces our confidence that nucleoprotein-targeted immunity can provide a complementary mechanism of protection alongside conventional seasonal influenza vaccines.” “These results provide a clear direction for the future development of OVX836. Rather than replacing existing seasonal influenza vaccines, we believe the greatest opportunity lies in complementing them” said Alexandre Le Vert, CEO and Co-Founder of Osivax.“By combining strain-specific antibody protection with the broad cellular immunity induced by OVX836, we aim to develop next-generation influenza vaccines capable of delivering broader and more durable protection against seasonal influenza.” The two collaborations provide access to established seasonal influenza vaccines for the development of combination vaccine candidates. Securing distinct agreements with two established leaders in influenza vaccines represents a significant milestone for Osivax and a strong external validation of its combination strategy. The first Phase 1/2 combination study is anticipated in Q4 2027. About OVX836 OVX836 is a first-in-class influenza A vaccine candidate that targets the nucleoprotein (NP), a highly conserved internal antigen. Unlike surface antigens, the NP is much less likely to mutate, providing a broader and more universal immune response. Osivax’ oligoDOMTM technology enables the design and production of a recombinant version of the NP, which self-assembles into a nanoparticle, thus triggering powerful T- and B-cell immune responses. OVX836 has been tested in 7 clinical trials with over 4,000 participants so far, and has shown promising safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy read-outs. About OXV836-005 – Asuniva Asuniva is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter Phase 2b trial conducted in Belgium, France, Finland and Germany, to assess the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of a single intramuscular dose of OVX836 (480 μg) in 2,850 participants aged 18–59 years. Asuniva is the first large, field efficacy study with OVX836 which generated the clinical evidence needed to advance the vaccine toward late-stage development. Further information can be found at clinicaltrials.gov. About Osivax Osivax is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing a portfolio of differentiated influenza vaccines generating superior T-cell responses in addition to strong and sustained B-cell responses, thanks to its novel, self-assembling nanoparticle platform technology, oligoDOMTM. The company’s lead candidate, OVX836, is a broad-spectrum influenza A vaccine candidate currently in Phase 2b clinical trials with over 4,000 volunteers tested and encouraging first signal of vaccine efficacy data. By combining OVX836 with standard flu vaccines, Osivax is advancing toward a best-in-class seasonal flu vaccine to prevent all strains of influenza. Osivax collaborates with leading global health agencies, including US based BARDA and NIH, and European-based institutions and top-tier pharmaceutical companies, reinforcing its mission to prevent all types of seasonal and pandemic influenza. By: Arianita Hoti 15 October 2026 19:23 Share to: By: Arianita Hoti 15 October 2026 19:23 Share to: As the flu season approaches, the number of patients with flu symptoms has begun to increase at Family Medicine Centers, while citizens who are vaccinated every year still do not know when they will be able to receive the vaccine this season. Doctors say they expect an increased number of patients. The Main Family Medicine Center in the capital does not have information about when the vaccinations will begin. Citizens who are vaccinated every year against seasonal flu are still waiting for their vaccines, while they have no information on when they will be able to receive them this season. Adem Krasniqi says that vaccination helps him against the flu and that he is looking forward to getting it this year as well. "Yes, I've received it every year. Only this year I don't know if they'll start giving it or not, because I'm receiving them, they're really helping," said Krasniqi. Even Artan Sinanaj, who gets vaccinated every year, says he doesn't know when he will be able to get it. "I get the seasonal flu vaccines every year and I've had results, not just me, but my whole family, with parents, with children, with everyone. More or less, we think it's making things easier for us, normally, because we get them for that purpose too. Realistically, I haven't gotten them this year yet, maybe they haven't even arrived yet," he said. also Arberi October 1, 2026 Seasonal flu vaccines will arrive in Kosovo three weeks late Vaccination was scheduled to begin in early October, but the National Institute of Public Health has announced that the vaccines will arrive in Kosovo three weeks late. The Main Center for Family Medicine in Pristina said they are awaiting information about vaccination against seasonal flu. Family doctor, Rushit Ismajli, says that so far they have not received any notification from the National Institute of Public Health, neither about vaccines nor about the start of vaccination. "We still do not have any information from the National Institute of Public Health about the seasonal flu, but we are waiting to have both the information and the vaccine for this situation," Ismajli said. He stressed that in recent days, an increase in the number of patients seeking medical help for flu-like symptoms has been observed, although there have been no complicated cases. "We have had a slightly increased number of patients with flu-like symptoms, with cough, fever, runny nose, body aches, but these can also be related to other viruses, not necessarily to seasonal flu. They can be related to a nasal virus, which we call rhinovirus. We also expect to have an increased number of patients this season, so we are also prepared as staff to deal with these situations," said Ismajli. According to the National Institute of Public Health, the delay in the arrival of vaccines is related to changes in the influenza virus strains recommended for this season. also Arberi 10 o. më parë Hoti: Seasonal flu vaccines arrive in Kosovo this week "This year, the international influenza vaccine production process has been affected by changes in the composition of the recommended strains for the northern hemisphere vaccine. These changes have affected production and supply deadlines at the global level, as well as the supply of countries in the region, including the Republic of Kosovo, where the vaccines are expected to arrive 21 days later than planned. Seasonal influenza vaccines for the 2026/2027 season are expected to arrive in the Republic of Kosovo on October 21, 2026," the announcement made earlier by the National Institute of Public Health (NIPHK) states. According to the National Institute of Public Health, 85 doses of the vaccine are expected to be delivered this season. The Ministry of Health has announced that the supply of the seasonal flu vaccine is being delayed due to problems with the manufacturer. According to the Ministry of Health, the economic operator with which it has an active contract notified the Ministry of the delays at the beginning of this month. "The Ministry of Health has taken all necessary actions in a timely manner to secure and supply the seasonal flu vaccine. However, the delays in this case were caused by the manufacturer itself, for which the Ministry was notified by the economic operator. For the delays caused in the supply, the Ministry of Health will take the necessary measures against the economic operator, in accordance with the terms of the contract and the legal provisions in force," the Ministry announced. Unlike Kosovo, the Ministry of Health and Social Protection in Albania has announced the launch of seasonal flu vaccination on September 30 and the provision of 280 doses, which will be available to priority groups. Last year, flu vaccination in Kosovo also began on October 1. also Arberi 21th of 2026 NIPHK: Vaccination against seasonal flu is expected to begin in October According to the NIPHK, about one billion cases of seasonal influenza are reported each year worldwide, while about 3 to 5 million of them present in severe forms. According to these data, about 99 percent of deaths in children under five years of age in developing countries are related to lower respiratory tract infections caused by influenza. #vaccination #Seasonal flu vaccine Similar articles Arberi 9th of 2026 Kosovo secures 85 thousand doses, flu vaccination starts on October 1 Lifestyle October 8, 2026 Expert advice for parents ahead of flu season Football. elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 国家公共卫生研究所和卫生部正在等待关于疫苗及其分发情况的进一步信息。延迟是由于病毒株变化和制造商问题所致。目前情况仍在调查中,卫生部表示将采取必要措施追究导致延迟的经济运营商责任。

analysis_en.time: The news report was published on 2026-10-15. The event date is not explicitly stated, but the vaccines are expected to arrive on October 21, 2026, and the flu season is approaching.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The event is related to the Republic of Kosovo, specifically mentioning the Main Family Medicine Center in the capital (Pristina) and the general population, including citizens who are vaccinated every year.
analysis_en.event: Seasonal flu vaccines have not yet been distributed in Kosovo, and the vaccination schedule has been delayed. The delay is attributed to changes in the influenza virus strains recommended for the season and issues with the manufacturer. The National Institute of Public Health (NIPHK) and the Ministry of Health have acknowledged the delay and are awaiting further information.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The delay in vaccine distribution has caused uncertainty among citizens who rely on annual vaccination. Doctors report an increased number of patients with flu-like symptoms, though these could be due to other viruses. The scale of impact is not quantified, but the delay is noted as affecting the entire population. The risk is not explicitly stated, but the situation is described as being under investigation.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The National Institute of Public Health and the Ministry of Health are awaiting information about the vaccine and its distribution. The delay is due to changes in virus strains and manufacturer issues. The situation is under investigation, and the Ministry has stated it will take necessary measures against the economic operator responsible for the delay.

news.title_zh: 季节性流感疫苗尚未分发。- KOHA.net
news.source_body_en: The news report from KOHA.net, published on October 15, 2026, highlights that seasonal flu vaccines have not yet been distributed in Kosovo, with the expected arrival date pushed to October 21, 2026. This delay is attributed to changes in the recommended influenza virus strains for the 2026/2027 season and issues with the manufacturer. The Main Family Medicine Center in Pristina and other healthcare providers are awaiting further information about the vaccine's availability. Citizens who are vaccinated annually are expressing concern over the delay, as it affects their ability to receive protection. Doctors note an increase in patients with flu-like symptoms, though they caution that these could be caused by other viruses. The Ministry of Health has stated that it is taking necessary actions to address the delay and will hold the economic operator accountable. The situation remains under investigation, with no explicit risk level mentioned.

Explore Conditions Cardiovascular health Digestive health Endrocrine system Hearing Mental health Recent articles Guides More More Wellness Your body Conditions Guides Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Trending: Protein myths dietitians want to bust Cozy slippers that don't skimp on support The surprising link between food and sleep Hair-growth hype experts aren't buying Health Conditions Infectious Flu Everything you need to know about flu season 2026 An early start doesn’t necessarily mean disaster Scientific American Follow Claire Maldarelli Fri, October 16, 2026 at 4:00 PM UTC The beginning of fall and back-to-school time means cold virus season has arrived. Usually, colds hit as lesser-evil infections before influenza season takes over. But already, the flu is popping up early in pockets of the U.S. Here's why that might be and everything else you need to know as we head into the dreaded annual flu season. According to the Centers of Disease Control and Prevention's latest FluView report, released on October 9, flu activity has been climbing since early September. Flu season in the U.S. generally begins gaining momentum in the fall, with activity peaking between December and February. But surveillance indicators show that certain strains of influenza are rising fast. The CDC's latest data show a nationwide percent positivity rate for influenza—the percentage of all positive influenza tests—of 3.6 percent. That's a sixfold increase compared with this time in 2025, when the rate was 0.6 percent. Parts of the U.S. are showing much higher positive rates. The CDC splits the country up into regions, and Region 9, which includes Arizona, California, Hawaii and Nevada, had 9.5 percent positivity, according to the latest data. Experts say that is exceptionally high for this time of year. Advertisement Advertisement Sign up for Today in Science, a free daily newsletter from Scientific American and join a community of science-loving readers. "It's not unheard of to see things rising at this stage," says Andrew Pekosz, an immunologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. "But it's also something that we probably shouldn't be seeing until maybe November or December at the earliest." Flu can be caused by different types of influenza, including influenza A (and its subtypes) and influenza B. Usually, flu season brings a mix of types. Right now, in the areas of the country with the highest positivity rates, H1N1, a subtype of influenza A, is dominant. According to the CDC, the most recent weekly testing data showed that 98.4 percent of the positive tests indicated H1N1 and that 1.6 percent revealed H3N2, another influenza A subtype. Still, experts say it's too early to predict whether these spikes could signal a particularly severe winter flu season. Will this year's flu vaccines work well? One of the best ways to protect yourself from the flu is to get a flu vaccine. Every year experts reformulate these vaccines depending on what strains of the virus are circulating or predicted to circulate during the coming winter season. Advertisement Advertisement Whichever subtype dominates matters because it can help predict which groups will experience the greatest disease burden. It can also determine how well existing immunity will protect people, as well as how the year's flu vaccines will perform. H1N1 and H3N2 are both influenza A subtypes, but they are evolutionarily distinct and can affect people differently. H3N2-dominant seasons have historically been associated with particularly severe illness among older adults. H1N1, on the other hand, has had a greater effect on younger populations—but both can cause serious disease at any age. "The version [of H1N1] that's circulating seems to be a little bit different from the vaccine strain that we have and from H1N1 strains that have circulated before. It's what we call an antigenic drift," Pekosz says. That could be why the virus is emerging so early, he adds. If it can evade prior immunity, the pathogen will be easier to transmit. But it's still too early to know how that might influence the effectiveness of the current flu vaccines. When is the best time to get vaccinated? Trish Perl, a professor of internal medicine and a specialist in infectious disease at UT Southwestern Medical Center, says that right now is the best time to get a flu shot. Advertisement Advertisement "Immunity from the flu vaccine is strongest for about four to six months, and we usually expect flu to peak in December or January," Pekosz says. "So a September or October vaccination will get you through the worst part of the flu season." Perl agrees—she says that she often tells her people to, at the very least, get a flu vaccine before Thanksgiving. How bad will the upcoming flu season be?

The southern hemisphere’s flu season is ending now. What can it tell us about what to expect in the northern hemisphere this winter?

  • 14 October 2026
  • by Linda Geddes

At a glance

  • Based on observations of the southern hemisphere’s 2026 flu season, which has just ended, the upcoming season in the northern hemisphere is expected to be moderate, though predictions are difficult.
  • Scientists are watching the emergence of small changes in H1N1 influenza viruses that could potentially influence how the coming season unfolds.
  • Regardless of such changes, vaccination is expected to play a key role in reducing the toll of influenza in the coming months.

As the nights draw in and coughs and sniffles start to spread, perennial questions are emerging about how bad this year’s flu season might be, and how well vaccines are likely to protect us.

After a southern hemisphere flu season broadly in line with previous years, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is anticipating that its upcoming season there will be “moderate”, based on historic trends and expert opinion.

However, it cautions that severity is difficult to predict before the season begins, and vaccination remains a key defence against severe disease.

One development that scientists are closely monitoring is the emergence of small changes in H1N1 influenza viruses that could potentially influence how the coming season unfolds.

What can we learn from the southern hemisphere’s flu season?

Although influenza viruses circulate year-round, infections tend to peak during the winter months in temperate regions.

Monitoring influenza activity in southern hemisphere countries such as Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, where the flu season is just ending, can therefore offer early clues about which flu viruses are circulating and what the northern hemisphere might face. Its flu season usually begins in October and can last until May.

Even so, differences in population immunity, circulating flu strains and vaccination coverage mean the same patterns don’t necessarily repeat.

Overall, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported fewer influenza detections globally between February and August 2026 than during the same period last year.

My daughter and her schoolmates had been booked for HPV vaccine at Ntcheu District Hospital. Our homes were washed off and we ended up as refugees taking shelter in Lilongwe 160km away.

- Prof Nicola Lewis, Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre,Francis Crick Institute

The main viruses circulating were familiar forms of seasonal flu. These fall into two main groups: influenza A and the influenza B Victoria lineage. The former includes H1N1, a descendent of the virus that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic, and H3N2, which has circulated in humans since 1968.

Of these viruses, H3N2 was most common across the southern hemisphere, with a recently emerged subgroup known as subclade K accounting for the majority of H3N2 viruses analysed since February 2026.

When Subclade K was first detected at the tail end of the southern hemisphere’s 2025 flu season, its rapid accumulation of mutations initially sparked concerns that it might evade existing immunity and vaccines.

But despite the northern hemisphere’s 2025–2026 flu season starting unusually early in parts of Europe, its overall severity varied between countries, and wasn’t uniformly more severe than previous winters.

Nor does this year’s southern hemisphere flu season appear to have been unusually severe overall. “Within the variation of flu seasons, it wasn’t really anything to write home about,” said Dr Ruth Harvey, Deputy Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre at the Francis Crick Institute in London.

What could this mean for the northern hemisphere?

While the southern hemisphere’s experience offers some reassurance, it doesn’t guarantee that northern hemisphere countries will face a similar flu season.

Speaking at a WHO meeting on influenza vaccine composition in late September, Prof Nicola Lewis, Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre at the Francis Crick Institute, said: “In recent weeks, we’ve seen the continued circulation of influenza, perhaps to higher levels than we saw at the same time last year in 2025, and we’ve also continued to see both influenza A and influenza B.”

One development that scientists are watching is a recent increase in detections of H1N1 influenza viruses.

Last year influenza vaccines prevented an estimated 180,000 hospitalisations and thousands of deaths in the US alone.

Within a subgroup group of these viruses, known as D.3.1.1, researchers have identified small changes in the haemagglutinin protein found on the viruses’ surface.

Laboratory tests have suggested that antibodies may recognise some of these variants less well than the H1N1 virus targeted by this winter’s flu vaccine, although it is currently unclear whether this will translate into reduced protection.

Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute are currently running further tests using a technique that measures how well antibodies from large numbers of people with different infection and vaccination histories recognise emerging flu viruses.

This approach helped reveal that people had greater pre-existing immunity against last winter’s H3N2 subclade K variant that earlier laboratory studies had suggested, and that vaccination boosted these responses.

  • New study suggests severe flu can damage the heart
  • Why alcohol-based hand sanitiser doesn’t kill norovirus and five other winter illness myths

Should I get the seasonal flu vaccine?

Vaccination remains a key means of preventing serious flu-related illness, hospitalisation and death, particularly among people who are most vulnerable to complications.

Last year influenza vaccines prevented an estimated 180,000 hospitalisations and thousands of deaths in the US alone.

This year’s Northern Hemisphere flu vaccines target H1N1, H3N2 and influenza B viruses, and were updated earlier this year to better match recently circulating strains.

They are expected to play an important role in reducing the toll of influenza in the coming months, so it is worth taking up the offer of a seasonal flu vaccine if you’re eligible for one.

How bad will the upcoming flu season be?

The southern hemisphere’s flu season is ending now. What can it tell us about what to expect in the northern hemisphere this winter?

  • 14 October 2026
  • by Linda Geddes

At a glance

  • Based on observations of the southern hemisphere’s 2026 flu season, which has just ended, the upcoming season in the northern hemisphere is expected to be moderate, though predictions are difficult.
  • Scientists are watching the emergence of small changes in H1N1 influenza viruses that could potentially influence how the coming season unfolds.
  • Regardless of such changes, vaccination is expected to play a key role in reducing the toll of influenza in the coming months.

As the nights draw in and coughs and sniffles start to spread, perennial questions are emerging about how bad this year’s flu season might be, and how well vaccines are likely to protect us.

After a southern hemisphere flu season broadly in line with previous years, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is anticipating that its upcoming season there will be “moderate”, based on historic trends and expert opinion.

However, it cautions that severity is difficult to predict before the season begins, and vaccination remains a key defence against severe disease.

One development that scientists are closely monitoring is the emergence of small changes in H1N1 influenza viruses that could potentially influence how the coming season unfolds.

What can we learn from the southern hemisphere’s flu season?

Although influenza viruses circulate year-round, infections tend to peak during the winter months in temperate regions.

Monitoring influenza activity in southern hemisphere countries such as Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, where the flu season is just ending, can therefore offer early clues about which flu viruses are circulating and what the northern hemisphere might face. Its flu season usually begins in October and can last until May.

Even so, differences in population immunity, circulating flu strains and vaccination coverage mean the same patterns don’t necessarily repeat.

Overall, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported fewer influenza detections globally between February and August 2026 than during the same period last year.

My daughter and her schoolmates had been booked for HPV vaccine at Ntcheu District Hospital. Our homes were washed off and we ended up as refugees taking shelter in Lilongwe 160km away.

- Prof Nicola Lewis, Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre,Francis Crick Institute

The main viruses circulating were familiar forms of seasonal flu. These fall into two main groups: influenza A and the influenza B Victoria lineage. The former includes H1N1, a descendent of the virus that caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic, and H3N2, which has circulated in humans since 1968.

Of these viruses, H3N2 was most common across the southern hemisphere, with a recently emerged subgroup known as subclade K accounting for the majority of H3N2 viruses analysed since February 2026.

When Subclade K was first detected at the tail end of the southern hemisphere’s 2025 flu season, its rapid accumulation of mutations initially sparked concerns that it might evade existing immunity and vaccines.

But despite the northern hemisphere’s 2025–2026 flu season starting unusually early in parts of Europe, its overall severity varied between countries, and wasn’t uniformly more severe than previous winters.

Nor does this year’s southern hemisphere flu season appear to have been unusually severe overall. “Within the variation of flu seasons, it wasn’t really anything to write home about,” said Dr Ruth Harvey, Deputy Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre at the Francis Crick Institute in London.

What could this mean for the northern hemisphere?

While the southern hemisphere’s experience offers some reassurance, it doesn’t guarantee that northern hemisphere countries will face a similar flu season.

Speaking at a WHO meeting on influenza vaccine composition in late September, Prof Nicola Lewis, Director of the Worldwide Influenza Centre at the Francis Crick Institute, said: “In recent weeks, we’ve seen the continued circulation of influenza, perhaps to higher levels than we saw at the same time last year in 2025, and we’ve also continued to see both influenza A and influenza B.”

One development that scientists are watching is a recent increase in detections of H1N1 influenza viruses.

Last year influenza vaccines prevented an estimated 180,000 hospitalisations and thousands of deaths in the US alone.

Within a subgroup group of these viruses, known as D.3.1.1, researchers have identified small changes in the haemagglutinin protein found on the viruses’ surface.

Laboratory tests have suggested that antibodies may recognise some of these variants less well than the H1N1 virus targeted by this winter’s flu vaccine, although it is currently unclear whether this will translate into reduced protection.

Researchers at the Francis Crick Institute are currently running further tests using a technique that measures how well antibodies from large numbers of people with different infection and vaccination histories recognise emerging flu viruses.

This approach helped reveal that people had greater pre-existing immunity against last winter’s H3N2 subclade K variant that earlier laboratory studies had suggested, and that vaccination boosted these responses.

Have you read?

  • New study suggests severe flu can damage the heart
  • Why alcohol-based hand sanitiser doesn’t kill norovirus and five other winter illness myths

Should I get the seasonal flu vaccine?

Vaccination remains a key means of preventing serious flu-related illness, hospitalisation and death, particularly among people who are most vulnerable to complications.

Last year influenza vaccines prevented an estimated 180,000 hospitalisations and thousands of deaths in the US alone.

This year’s Northern Hemisphere flu vaccines target H1N1, H3N2 and influenza B viruses, and were updated earlier this year to better match recently circulating strains.

They are expected to play an important role in reducing the toll of influenza in the coming months, so it is worth taking up the offer of a seasonal flu vaccine if you’re eligible for one.
