news.title: FluView Week 40: Antiviral Resistance Markers in H1N1 Over The Summer - Avian Flu Diary
news.rss_summary_html: FluView Week 40: Antiviral Resistance Markers in H1N1 Over The Summer  Avian Flu Diary
news.excerpt_original: FluView Week 40: Antiviral Resistance Markers in H1N1 Over The Summer Avian Flu Diary
news.priority_tier_reason: 可信机构来源或已成功抓获正文
news.content: Avian Flu Diary Covering Pandemic and Seasonal Flu, Emerging Infectious Diseases, public health, community & Individual preparedness. NOTE: All AFD blogs are written by a human - any mistakes are solely mine. Monday, October 19, 2026 FluView Week 40: Antiviral Resistance Markers in H1N1 Over The Summer #19,379 For the past 3 years we've been following scattered reports of `reduced susceptibility' of the seasonal H1N1 flu virus to the antiviral drug oseltamivir (aka `Tamiflu') around the globe. In March 2024 The Lancet Microbe published - Global Emergence of Neuraminidase Inhibitor-Resistant Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Viruses with I223V and S247N Mutations - which reported reduced oseltamivir inhibition among samples tested in Hong Kong in 2023. Unlike the H275Y mutation - which caused nearly total resistance in an older (now extinct) strain of H1N1 back in 2008 - these viruses carried dual I223V/S247N mutations which together produced a modest ≈ 10-fold reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. A concerning trend, but not nearly enough of a reduction to invalidate the use of the drug. Three months later (June 2024), the EID Journal: Multicountry Spread of Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Viruses with Reduced Oseltamivir Inhibition, May 2023–February 2024 reported a ≈ 13-fold reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. In July of 2025, Virus Research: A 15-year Study of Neuraminidase Mutations and the Increasing of S247N Mutation in Spain, we looked at a study that found a sharp increase in detections of the NA:S247N mutation beginning in 2024, but not combined with I223V. Last December, in Eurosurveillance: Expansion of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 NA:S247N Viruses with Reduced Susceptibility to Oseltamivir, Catalonia, Spain, and in Europe, July to October 2025. a Rapid Communications reported on another dramatic surge in H1N1 viruses carrying the NA:S247N mutation in Catalonia Spain, and other parts of Europe. Abrupt rise in resistance in Catalonia, Spain - fall 2025 Some weeks (see above graphic), as many as 100% of viruses tested showed this NA:S247N mutation. The good news, however, was that once again a second synergistic mutation - NA:I223V - was not detected in these recent Catalonia isolates. As for detections in the United States (see Feb 2026 blog), over the entire 2024-2025 flu season - out of 1697 H1N1 viruses tested - only one carried the NA-I223V and NA-S247N amino acid substitutions. During the first 13 weeks of the 2025-2026 flu season (Oct - Dec) the CDC reported zero elevated resistance among the first 193 H1N1 viruses tested (see FluView Wk 53). But shortly after the New Year we began to seen an uptick in reduced inhibition detections in the United States. By late February (FluView week 7) - based on 517 H1N1 isolates tested since October - the CDC reported 10 isolates with reduced inhibition and 4 with highly reduced inhibition (due to NA:H275Y). In early June we looked at the last full FluView report of the 2025-2026 flu season, which reported a total 20 reduced inhibition results, and 11 highly reduced results: Nine A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had NA-H275Y amino acid substitution conferring highly reduced inhibition by oseltamivir and peramivir. Nineteen A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had amino acid substitutions NA-I223V and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. One A(H1N1)pdm09 virus had amino acid substitutions NA-I223T and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. Two A(H3N2) viruses had amino acid substitution NA-E119V conferring highly reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. Three B viruses had amino acid substitution NA-M464T and showed reduced inhibition by peramivir. While the number of S247N+I223V mutations remained relatively low (2.1%), this was more than a 35-fold increase over the previous year. And equally concerning - after an extended absence - the tag team of S247N+I223V was being reported again in a newer (D.3.x) NA-clade H1N1 virus. With the release last Friday of the first full FluView report since last May, we've our first look at the reported detections of the S247N+I223V amino acid substitution over the summer. While the overall numbers are low - and the lack of any reported H275Y mutations is reassuring - the percentage of H1N1 viruses that harbor the S247N+I223V mutation was nearly 50% higher (3.1%) than at the end of May (2.1%). Viruses collected in the U.S. since May 24, 2026, were tested for antiviral susceptibility as follows: Eight A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had amino acid substitutions NA-I223V and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. By way of comparison, over the summer of 2025 the CDC reported zero detections, and none were reported until early 2026. It still isn't clear how much of a public health impact these mutations will have - if any - going forward, but this week's FluView report provides a useful benchmark of where things stand as we enter into the 2026-2027 flu season. Stay tuned. Things could get interesting. Sunday, October 18, 2026 WHO DON: Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus - Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Photo Credit NIAID #19,378 While it doesn't get near the attention it did before COVID, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camels in the Middle East, occasionally spills over into humans, and is likely under reported. MERS-CoV also continues to evolve, which raises concerns over its future impact (see Health Sci Rpts (Narrative Review): Pathogenicity and Potential Role of MERS-CoV in the Emergence of “Disease X”). In 2025, the WHO released 3 MERS-CoV DON reports (see here, here, and here), and last December, France reported 2 Travelers Returning From Arabian Peninsula Diagnosed with the MERS-CoV virus. This year has been somewhat quieter, with the first WHO update of 2026 published just last week (October 15th), which chronicles 8 cases reported by Saudi Arabia since last December. Of note - while the WHO states `Humans contract MERS-CoV through direct or indirect contact with dromedary camels, the virus’s natural host and zoonotic reservoir.' - 6 of the 8 cases reported no known contact with camels or camel products. This is not a new trend; in 2025 more than half of the cases reported by KSA listed no known contact with camels or camel products, and this has been frequently reported in the past. Exactly how these people are contracting the virus remains unclear. First some excerpts from the latest DON report, after which I'll have a postscript. Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus - Kingdom of Saudi Arabia 15 October 2026 Situation at a glance Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection, including one death. Cases were detected across six locations: Al Jouf (1), Arar (1), Hafr Al-Batin (1), Riyadh (2), Tabuk (1) and Taif (2). No epidemiological links were identified between any of the cases. All eight cases were symptomatic, most commonly presenting with fever (6/8), dyspnea (5/8), and cough (4/8). None were health and care workers. Infection was confirmed by RT-PCR testing. MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir and two cases reported direct contact with camels while six reported no known camel exposure. Seven of eight cases had underlying comorbidities, recognized risk factors for severe MERS-CoV disease. The cases appear to represent sporadic infections related to zoonotic spillover rather than a single outbreak cluster. Description of the situation Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of eight cases of MERS-CoV, including one death, was reported from six locations in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Of the eight reported cases, five occurred among persons aged 70 years and older, two among adults aged 50–59 years, and one among an adult aged 30–39 years. Seven cases had underlying comorbidities, two reported direct camel contact, and one death was reported in an older adult (>65 year old) with comorbidities. There was no known epidemiological link identified among cases. Case 1: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Al Jouf developed symptoms on 14 March 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. The patient was hospitalized on 17 March and laboratory confirmation of MERS-CoV infection was obtained by RT-PCR on 19 March. Case 2: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 18 April 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. The patient was hospitalized on the same day, and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 22 April. He subsequently died as a result of the illness. Case 3: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Hafr Al-Batin developed symptoms on 20 May 2026. He reported direct contact with camels. The patient was hospitalized on 26 May and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 27 May. Case 4: A female aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 31 July 2026. No known exposure to camels or camel products was reported. She was hospitalized on 3 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 8 August. Case 5: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Tabuk developed symptoms on 20 August 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 23 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained by RT-PCR on 24 August. Case 6: A male aged 30–39 years, with no known comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 14 August 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 20 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 23 August. Case 7: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 11 September 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 17 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 19 September. Case 8: A male aged 60–69 years, with comorbidities, from Arar developed symptoms on 20 September 2026. He reported direct contact with camels. He was hospitalized on 20 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 21 September. (SNIP) WHO risk assessment MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease caused by MERS-CoV, for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir. Human infection can range from asymptomatic or mild illness to severe disease and death. Human infections continue to occur through direct or indirect exposure to infected dromedaries or their products, while limited human-to-human transmission has been documented, primarily among close contacts and in healthcare settings. Sustained community transmission has not been observed. No licensed vaccine for MERS-CoV exists to date. As of 5 October 2026, WHO had been notified of 2643 laboratory-confirmed MERS cases globally, including 965 deaths, since the virus was first identified in 2012. The majority of cases (84%; 2232 cases and 870 deaths) have been reported from Saudi Arabia. These figures likely underestimate the true number of infections since mild and asymptomatic cases may remain undetected/unreported, while the reported case fatality of ratio of 37% may overestimate mortality among infections. Although the number of reported MERS cases has declined substantially since 2020, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camel populations in the Middle East and African regions and continues to cause sporadic human infections. The observed decline in reported MERS cases, in particular during the COVID-19 pandemic emergency phase, is thought to be a result of pandemic-related IPC measures that also limited human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV, as well as behavioral changes during the pandemic. Any role of potential cross-reactive immunity from SARS-CoV-2 infection and/ or vaccination remains in need of further investigation. Other hypotheses—such as reduced surveillance, viral attenuation, or decreased circulation in camel populations—are not supported by current evidence. WHO expects additional sporadic MERS cases to occur in countries where the virus circulates in camels and anticipates that travel-associated exportation of cases will continue. Delays in detection remain possible due to the clinical presentation of MERS being similar with other respiratory infections, including influenza and COVID-19. Numerous outbreaks in KSA and the Republic of Korea have demonstrated that primary cases can result in substantial secondary transmission, particularly in healthcare settings and through importation of travel related cases. The notification of the recent cases in Saudi Arabia does not change WHO's overall risk assessment - the risk remains moderate at both the regional and global levels, reflecting the continued occurrence of sporadic zoonotic infections, the potential for healthcare-associated outbreaks and international exportation of cases, in the absence of sustained human-to-human transmission. WHO continues to monitor the epidemiological situation through routine surveillance and reporting under the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) and conducts ongoing risk assessments using available epidemiological and virological information. (Continue . . . ) In June of 2025 we looked at an editorial in Journal of Epidemiology & Global Health on the importance of healthcare preparedness and surveillance (see Al-Tawfiq & Memish On Recurrent MERS-CoV Transmission in Saudi Arabia), with an emphasis on identifying asymptomatic carriers. Two months later we reviewed an IJID Editorial: Al-Tawfiq on Global Epidemiology and Public Health Challenges of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) - which looked again at what may be the most challenging aspect of MERS detection; asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases. Although MERS-CoV clearly isn't ready for prime time, each new zoonotic spillover from camels - or cryptic transmission - is another opportunity for the virus to better adapt to a human host. Monday, October 19, 2026 FluView Week 40: Antiviral Resistance Markers in H1N1 Over The Summer #19,379 For the past 3 years we've been following scattered reports of `reduced susceptibility' of the seasonal H1N1 flu virus to the antiviral drug oseltamivir (aka `Tamiflu') around the globe. In March 2024 The Lancet Microbe published - Global Emergence of Neuraminidase Inhibitor-Resistant Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Viruses with I223V and S247N Mutations - which reported reduced oseltamivir inhibition among samples tested in Hong Kong in 2023. Unlike the H275Y mutation - which caused nearly total resistance in an older (now extinct) strain of H1N1 back in 2008 - these viruses carried dual I223V/S247N mutations which together produced a modest ≈ 10-fold reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. A concerning trend, but not nearly enough of a reduction to invalidate the use of the drug. Three months later (June 2024), the EID Journal: Multicountry Spread of Influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 Viruses with Reduced Oseltamivir Inhibition, May 2023–February 2024 reported a ≈ 13-fold reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. In July of 2025, Virus Research: A 15-year Study of Neuraminidase Mutations and the Increasing of S247N Mutation in Spain, we looked at a study that found a sharp increase in detections of the NA:S247N mutation beginning in 2024, but not combined with I223V. Last December, in Eurosurveillance: Expansion of influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 NA:S247N Viruses with Reduced Susceptibility to Oseltamivir, Catalonia, Spain, and in Europe, July to October 2025. a Rapid Communications reported on another dramatic surge in H1N1 viruses carrying the NA:S247N mutation in Catalonia Spain, and other parts of Europe. Abrupt rise in resistance in Catalonia, Spain - fall 2025 Some weeks (see above graphic), as many as 100% of viruses tested showed this NA:S247N mutation. The good news, however, was that once again a second synergistic mutation - NA:I223V - was not detected in these recent Catalonia isolates. As for detections in the United States (see Feb 2026 blog), over the entire 2024-2025 flu season - out of 1697 H1N1 viruses tested - only one carried the NA-I223V and NA-S247N amino acid substitutions. During the first 13 weeks of the 2025-2026 flu season (Oct - Dec) the CDC reported zero elevated resistance among the first 193 H1N1 viruses tested (see FluView Wk 53). But shortly after the New Year we began to seen an uptick in reduced inhibition detections in the United States. By late February (FluView week 7) - based on 517 H1N1 isolates tested since October - the CDC reported 10 isolates with reduced inhibition and 4 with highly reduced inhibition (due to NA:H275Y). In early June we looked at the last full FluView report of the 2025-2026 flu season, which reported a total 20 reduced inhibition results, and 11 highly reduced results: Nine A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had NA-H275Y amino acid substitution conferring highly reduced inhibition by oseltamivir and peramivir. Nineteen A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had amino acid substitutions NA-I223V and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. One A(H1N1)pdm09 virus had amino acid substitutions NA-I223T and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. Two A(H3N2) viruses had amino acid substitution NA-E119V conferring highly reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. Three B viruses had amino acid substitution NA-M464T and showed reduced inhibition by peramivir. While the number of S247N+I223V mutations remained relatively low (2.1%), this was more than a 35-fold increase over the previous year. And equally concerning - after an extended absence - the tag team of S247N+I223V was being reported again in a newer (D.3.x) NA-clade H1N1 virus. With the release last Friday of the first full FluView report since last May, we've our first look at the reported detections of the S247N+I223V amino acid substitution over the summer. While the overall numbers are low - and the lack of any reported H275Y mutations is reassuring - the percentage of H1N1 viruses that harbor the S247N+I223V mutation was nearly 50% higher (3.1%) than at the end of May (2.1%). Viruses collected in the U.S. since May 24, 2026, were tested for antiviral susceptibility as follows: Eight A(H1N1)pdm09 viruses had amino acid substitutions NA-I223V and NA-S247N and showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir. By way of comparison, over the summer of 2025 the CDC reported zero detections, and none were reported until early 2026. It still isn't clear how much of a public health impact these mutations will have - if any - going forward, but this week's FluView report provides a useful benchmark of where things stand as we enter into the 2026-2027 flu season. Stay tuned. Things could get interesting. MERS-CoV also continues to evolve, which raises concerns over its future impact (see Health Sci Rpts (Narrative Review): Pathogenicity and Potential Role of MERS-CoV in the Emergence of “Disease X”). In 2025, the WHO released 3 MERS-CoV DON reports (see here, here, and here), and last December, France reported 2 Travelers Returning From Arabian Peninsula Diagnosed with the MERS-CoV virus. This year has been somewhat quieter, with the first WHO update of 2026 published just last week (October 15th), which chronicles 8 cases reported by Saudi Arabia since last December. This is not a new trend; in 2025 more than half of the cases reported by KSA listed no known contact with camels or camel products, and this has been frequently reported in the past. Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus - Kingdom of Saudi Arabia 15 October 2026 Situation at a glance Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reported eight laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection, including one death. Cases were detected across six locations: Al Jouf (1), Arar (1), Hafr Al-Batin (1), Riyadh (2), Tabuk (1) and Taif (2). No epidemiological links were identified between any of the cases. All eight cases were symptomatic, most commonly presenting with fever (6/8), dyspnea (5/8), and cough (4/8). None were health and care workers. Infection was confirmed by RT-PCR testing. MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir and two cases reported direct contact with camels while six reported no known camel exposure. Seven of eight cases had underlying comorbidities, recognized risk factors for severe MERS-CoV disease. The cases appear to represent sporadic infections related to zoonotic spillover rather than a single outbreak cluster. Description of the situation Between 1 January and 5 October 2026, a total of eight cases of MERS-CoV, including one death, was reported from six locations in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Of the eight reported cases, five occurred among persons aged 70 years and older, two among adults aged 50–59 years, and one among an adult aged 30–39 years. Seven cases had underlying comorbidities, two reported direct camel contact, and one death was reported in an older adult (>65 year old) with comorbidities. There was no known epidemiological link identified among cases. Case 1: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Al Jouf developed symptoms on 14 March 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. The patient was hospitalized on 17 March and laboratory confirmation of MERS-CoV infection was obtained by RT-PCR on 19 March. Case 2: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 18 April 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. The patient was hospitalized on the same day, and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 22 April. He subsequently died as a result of the illness. Case 3: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Hafr Al-Batin developed symptoms on 20 May 2026. He reported direct contact with camels. The patient was hospitalized on 26 May and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 27 May. Case 4: A female aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 31 July 2026. No known exposure to camels or camel products was reported. She was hospitalized on 3 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 8 August. Case 5: A male aged 50–59 years, with comorbidities, from Tabuk developed symptoms on 20 August 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 23 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained by RT-PCR on 24 August. Case 6: A male aged 30–39 years, with no known comorbidities, from Riyadh developed symptoms on 14 August 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 20 August and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 23 August. Case 7: A male aged ≥70 years, with comorbidities, from Taif developed symptoms on 11 September 2026. He reported no known contact with camels or camel products. He was hospitalized on 17 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 19 September. Case 8: A male aged 60–69 years, with comorbidities, from Arar developed symptoms on 20 September 2026. He reported direct contact with camels. He was hospitalized on 20 September and laboratory confirmation was obtained on 21 September. (SNIP) WHO risk assessment MERS is a zoonotic viral respiratory disease caused by MERS-CoV, for which dromedary camels serve as the primary animal reservoir. Human infection can range from asymptomatic or mild illness to severe disease and death. Human infections continue to occur through direct or indirect exposure to infected dromedaries or their products, while limited human-to-human transmission has been documented, primarily among close contacts and in healthcare settings. Sustained community transmission has not been observed. No licensed vaccine for MERS-CoV exists to date. As of 5 October 2026, WHO had been notified of 2643 laboratory-confirmed MERS cases globally, including 965 deaths, since the virus was first identified in 2012. The majority of cases (84%; 2232 cases and 870 deaths) have been reported from Saudi Arabia. These figures likely underestimate the true number of infections since mild and asymptomatic cases may remain undetected/unreported, while the reported case fatality of ratio of 37% may overestimate mortality among infections. Although the number of reported MERS cases has declined substantially since 2020, MERS-CoV continues to circulate in dromedary camel populations in the Middle East and African regions and continues to cause sporadic human infections. The observed decline in reported MERS cases, in particular during the COVID-19 pandemic emergency phase, is thought to be a result of pandemic-related IPC measures that also limited human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV, as well as behavioral changes during the pandemic. Any role of potential cross-reactive immunity from SARS-CoV-2 infection and/ or vaccination remains in need of further investigation. Other hypotheses—such as reduced surveillance, viral attenuation, or decreased circulation in camel populations—are not supported by current evidence. WHO expects additional sporadic MERS cases to occur in countries where the virus circulates in camels and anticipates that travel-associated exportation of cases will continue. Delays in detection remain possible due to the clinical presentation of MERS being similar with other respiratory infections, including influenza and COVID-19. Numerous outbreaks in KSA and the Republic of Korea have demonstrated that primary cases can result in substantial secondary transmission, particularly in healthcare settings and through importation of travel related cases. The notification of the recent cases in Saudi Arabia does not change WHO's overall risk assessment - the risk remains moderate at both the regional and global levels, reflecting the continued occurrence of sporadic zoonotic infections, the potential for healthcare-associated outbreaks and international exportation of cases, in the absence of sustained human-to-human transmission. WHO continues to monitor the epidemiological situation through routine surveillance and reporting under the International Health Regulations (IHR 2005) and conducts ongoing risk assessments using available epidemiological and virological information. analysis.time: The report was published on Monday, October 19, 2026. The event dates span from March 2024 to late February 2026, with the most recent data from the summer of 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The evidence covers global and regional locations, including Hong Kong, Spain, Catalonia, and the United States. The affected population includes individuals infected with seasonal influenza viruses, particularly H1N1 and H3N2.
analysis.event: The report discusses the emergence of antiviral resistance markers in seasonal H1N1 and H3N2 influenza viruses, specifically the I223V and S247N mutations in H1N1, and the E119V mutation in H3N2. These mutations reduce susceptibility to oseltamivir and peramivir. The findings are based on studies published in The Lancet Microbe, EID Journal, Virus Research, and Eurosurveillance.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: In the 2024-2025 flu season, 10 out of 517 H1N1 isolates tested in the U.S. showed reduced inhibition by oseltamivir, and 4 showed highly reduced inhibition due to the H275Y mutation. In the 2025-2026 flu season, 20 reduced inhibition results and 11 highly reduced results were reported. In the summer of 2026, the CDC reported 8 H1N1 viruses with the I223V and S247N mutations. The S247N mutation showed a 35-fold increase compared to the previous year, and the percentage of H1N1 viruses with the S247N+I223V mutation was 3.1% in the summer of 2026, up from 2.1% in May 2026.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC and other health organizations have been monitoring antiviral resistance in influenza viruses. The report notes that the presence of these mutations is a concerning trend, but the impact on public health remains unclear. The findings are based on testing and surveillance data, with some uncertainty about the full implications of these mutations.

analysis.brief_en: The Avian Flu Diary report, published on October 19, 2026, highlights the emergence of antiviral resistance markers in seasonal influenza viruses, particularly H1N1 and H3N2. The I223V and S247N mutations in H1N1 were first reported in Hong Kong in 2023 and showed a significant increase in Spain and the U.S. by 2026. In the U.S., during the 2024-2025 flu season, 10 out of 517 H1N1 isolates tested exhibited reduced oseltamivir inhibition, and 4 showed highly reduced inhibition due to the H275Y mutation. By the summer of 2026, the CDC reported 8 H1N1 viruses with the I223V and S247N mutations, marking a 35-fold increase compared to the previous year. While the overall numbers remain low, the report underscores the need for continued monitoring as these mutations could impact the effectiveness of antiviral drugs. The findings are based on studies from The Lancet Microbe, EID Journal, Virus Research, and Eurosurveillance, with the CDC providing the most recent data. The report also notes the absence of H275Y mutations in recent U.S. isolates, which is reassuring but does not eliminate concerns about the evolving resistance patterns.

news.title_zh: FluView 第40周:抗病毒药物 抗药性标记在H1N1流感病毒中的夏季出现 - 禽流感日记
news.source_body_en: The Avian Flu Diary report, published on October 19, 2026, highlights the emergence of antiviral resistance markers in seasonal influenza viruses, particularly H1N1 and H3N2. The I223V and S247N mutations in H1N1 were first reported in Hong Kong in 2023 and showed a significant increase in Spain and the U.S. by 2026. In the U.S., during the 2024-2025 flu season, 10 out of 517 H1N1 isolates tested exhibited reduced oseltamivir inhibition, and 4 showed highly reduced inhibition due to the H275Y mutation. By the summer of 2026, the CDC reported 8 H1N1 viruses with the I223V and S247N mutations, marking a 35-fold increase compared to the previous year. While the overall numbers remain low, the report underscores the need for continued monitoring as these mutations could impact the effectiveness of antiviral drugs. The findings are based on studies from The Lancet Microbe, EID Journal, Virus Research, and Eurosurveillance, with the CDC providing the most recent data. The report also notes the absence of H275Y mutations in recent U.S. isolates, which is reassuring but does not eliminate concerns about the evolving resistance patterns.

news.content: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up National News Flu Season Begins Early With Rising Cases In The U.S. By iHeartRadio Oct 19, 2026 Photo: Getty Images North America Flu season has started earlier than usual in the United States, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reporting a significant rise in influenza cases since early September. The nationwide positivity rate for influenza is currently 3.6%, which is six times higher than the same period last year, according to USA Today. The region encompassing California, Arizona, Nevada, and Hawaii has reported the highest positivity rate at 9.5%, a level typically not seen until November or December. Health experts emphasize the importance of getting vaccinated now, as it takes about two weeks for the flu shot to become effective. The CDC's FluView report indicates that 5% of respiratory specimens tested nationally were positive for influenza, with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 being the predominant strain. This subtype, which was responsible for the 2009 "swine flu" pandemic, is causing over 96% of current infections. The early rise in flu activity has prompted concerns about the potential for a severe flu season. Forbes reports that influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and mutations may allow them to evade immunity from previous infections and vaccinations. The CDC recommends that everyone aged six months and older receive a flu vaccine, especially those at higher risk of severe illness, such as young children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic health conditions. The ideal time to get vaccinated is by the end of October to ensure full protection when flu activity typically peaks. In addition to vaccination, health experts advise improving indoor ventilation, practicing good hand hygiene, and staying home when sick to reduce the risk of flu transmission. If flu symptoms become severe, medical attention should be sought promptly. news.content_original: ___ Play Now Log InSign Up National News Flu Season Begins Early With Rising Cases In The U.S. By iHeartRadio Oct 19, 2026 Photo: Getty Images North America Flu season has started earlier than usual in the United States, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reporting a significant rise in influenza cases since early September. The nationwide positivity rate for influenza is currently 3.6%, which is six times higher than the same period last year, according to USA Today. The region encompassing California, Arizona, Nevada, and Hawaii has reported the highest positivity rate at 9.5%, a level typically not seen until November or December. Health experts emphasize the importance of getting vaccinated now, as it takes about two weeks for the flu shot to become effective. The CDC's FluView report indicates that 5% of respiratory specimens tested nationally were positive for influenza, with influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 being the predominant strain. This subtype, which was responsible for the 2009 "swine flu" pandemic, is causing over 96% of current infections. The early rise in flu activity has prompted concerns about the potential for a severe flu season. Forbes reports that influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and mutations may allow them to evade immunity from previous infections and vaccinations. The CDC recommends that everyone aged six months and older receive a flu vaccine, especially those at higher risk of severe illness, such as young children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic health conditions. The ideal time to get vaccinated is by the end of October to ensure full protection when flu activity typically peaks. In addition to vaccination, health experts advise improving indoor ventilation, practicing good hand hygiene, and staying home when sick to reduce the risk of flu transmission. If flu symptoms become severe, medical attention should be sought promptly. news.content_zh: 文章报道,美国流感季比往常提前开始,美国疾病控制与预防中心(CDC)指出自9月初以来流感病例显著增加。根据《美国今日》报道,全国流感检测阳性率目前为3.6%,比去年同期高出六倍。涵盖加利福尼亚州、亚利桑那州、内华达州和夏威夷州的地区报告了最高的阳性率,达到9.5%,通常出现在流感季后期。CDC的FluView报告指出,全国范围内检测的呼吸道样本中有5%呈流感阳性,其中流感甲型H1N1流感病毒pdm09是主要流行毒株。这种亚型曾导致2009年猪流感大流行,目前导致超过96%的感染。卫生专家敦促疫苗接种现在接种疫苗,因为流感疫苗大约需要两周时间才能生效。CDC建议所有6个月及以上的人都应接种疫苗,尤其是那些感染后更容易出现严重疾病的高风险人群,如幼儿、老年人以及患有慢性健康问题的人。最佳接种时间应是在10月底之前,以确保在流感活动达到高峰时获得充分保护。除了疫苗接种,卫生专家还建议改善室内通风、保持良好的手部卫生以及生病时留在家中,以降低传播风险。如果症状变得严重,建议及时就医。

Addressing Gaps in Influenza Prevention Seasonal vaccination remains central to influenza prevention. However, changes in circulating influenza viruses and variability in individual immune response can limit vaccine protection, particularly among older adults and people who are immunocompromised. analysis.brief_en: Shanghai Ark Biopharmaceutical has secured U.S. FDA IND clearance for a phase II clinical trial of its long-acting influenza prevention drug AK0406. This development comes as the 2025–2026 influenza season in the United States resulted in at least 32 million illnesses, 380,000 hospitalizations, and 24,000 deaths, underscoring the need for alternative preventive strategies. The trial targets the general population, with a focus on vulnerable groups such as older adults and immunocompromised individuals, who may experience limited vaccine protection due to changes in circulating influenza viruses and variability in immune responses. The drug is a long-acting antiviral drug-Fc conjugate (AFC), designed to provide extended protection against seasonal influenza. The FDA's clearance allows the company to proceed with the trial, which aims to address unmet needs in influenza prevention. The evidence highlights the significance of this trial in the context of ongoing public health challenges related to seasonal influenza.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Saturday, October 17, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi by October 17, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Genomic Sequencing Reveals Hidden Influenza A(H3N2) Subclade K School Outbreak in Burundi Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram In January 2026, health authorities in Burundi confronted a familiar and unsettling scenario. A secondary school in Bujumbura reported a sharp increase in respiratory illness among its students, and the immediate suspicion fell on SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. The prospect of a resurgence in a densely populated school setting was a serious concern for the national public health system. Yet when symptomatic students were tested for SARS-CoV-2, the results came back negative, leaving clinicians and epidemiologists with a cluster of unexplained severe acute respiratory infections and no identified cause. That diagnostic dead end is precisely where the investigation described in a study published in BMC Infectious Diseases begins. A team led by Néhémie Nzoyikorera of the National Reference Laboratory at the National Public Health Institute in Burundi, working with colleagues at Erasmus University Medical Center in Rotterdam and partners across East Africa, Morocco, and Germany, applied targeted viral enrichment sequencing to nasopharyngeal samples collected from symptomatic students. The approach was designed to cast a wide net: rather than testing for one pathogen at a time, the method enriches and sequences viral genetic material present in a sample, allowing researchers to identify whatever viruses are there, known or unknown. The technical foundation of the investigation rests on the Illumina Viral Surveillance Panel version 2, run on the compact iSeq 100 sequencing platform. Eight samples from SARS-CoV-2-negative students were processed through this targeted enrichment workflow. The panel uses probes designed to capture viral genomes across a broad range of respiratory and other viruses, concentrating scarce viral nucleic acid against a background of human DNA and other genetic noise. After sequencing, the reads were quality-checked, screened for viral identification, and then assembled into genome sequences where coverage permitted. The results were decisive. Influenza A virus was detected in seven of the eight samples analyzed, and four of those samples yielded near-complete influenza A genomes of sufficient quality for detailed genomic characterization. When the researchers assigned clades to the reconstructed genomes, every characterized virus fell into the same category: Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K. This was the first genomic detection and characterization of that subclade in Burundi, a finding that carries significance well beyond the school gates because H3N2 subclade K has been drawing attention internationally as an emerging variant of the seasonal influenza virus. Influenza A(H3N2) is one of the seasonal influenza A subtypes that circulates in human populations and is notorious for its capacity to evolve rapidly. The hemagglutinin protein, the HA of H3N2, is the primary target of protective antibodies, and mutations accumulating in the HA gene allow the virus to escape immunity built up through previous infections and vaccination. Clade and subclade designations, such as subclade K, are assigned on the basis of characteristic amino acid signatures in HA, and they help global surveillance laboratories track which genetic variants are spreading, which are vaccine-matched, and which signal a need for updated vaccine composition. Phylogenetic analysis of the Burundian sequences added a layer of complexity to the outbreak picture. The sequences did not form a single tight cluster. Instead, they split into two distinct groups on the phylogenetic tree, suggesting that at least two separate viral lineages of H3N2 subclade K were circulating during the outbreak. This observation matters for outbreak interpretation. A single introduction followed by onward transmission would typically produce a compact cluster of closely related genomes, whereas the presence of divergent lineages points to multiple introductions or to undetected circulation in the community before the school cluster was recognized. Genomic analysis was therefore able to reveal structure in the outbreak that routine testing alone could not. The researchers also examined the neuraminidase sequences for markers associated with resistance to neuraminidase inhibitors, the class of antiviral drugs that includes oseltamivir. No resistance-associated markers were detected, an important clinical finding because it indicates that antiviral treatment would be expected to remain effective against the circulating viruses if severe cases required it. The absence of resistance markers also provides reassurance for national treatment guidelines and for any future response to H3N2 subclade K in the region. To ensure the findings contributed to the global picture, the influenza genome sequences were shared through GISAID, the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data, which serves as the central repository for influenza sequence data used by the World Health Organization and surveillance laboratories worldwide. Sharing genomes from Burundi addresses a longstanding gap in global influenza surveillance, which has historically been dominated by data from high-income countries in temperate regions. Sequences from African settings, particularly from outbreaks identified through unexplained severe acute respiratory infection surveillance, help clarify how subclade K and other variants move between regions and how they evolve in different population contexts. The study also underscores the value of severe acute respiratory infection surveillance as a pillar of emerging disease preparedness. The samples in this investigation had been collected initially for SARI surveillance, and the national ethics framework, including approval by the National Ethics Committee of Burundi with a consent waiver, allowed their use for pathogen identification. When the initial hypothesis of a COVID-19 resurgence collapsed, the surveillance infrastructure and the stored samples provided the raw material for a rapid pivot to unbiased pathogen detection. The Burundi Public Health Emergency Operation Center supported the epidemiological investigations, and reagents were provided through the East African Community Secretariat’s Mobile Lab Project, illustrating how regional cooperation underpins laboratory response capacity. The broader lesson from the Bujumbura school outbreak is that targeted viral enrichment sequencing is a practical tool for investigating acute respiratory outbreaks when the cause is unknown, particularly when initial testing is negative and routine testing for other respiratory viruses is limited. In settings where multiplex PCR panels are expensive or unavailable, a single sequencing run can identify the pathogen, characterize its genome, assign its clade, screen for resistance markers, and place it in a global phylogenetic context. The first genomic characterization of Influenza A(H3N2) subclade K in Burundi demonstrates that genomic surveillance capacity, strengthened through projects such as GREAT-LIFE at the national public health institute, can deliver actionable findings from a modest number of samples, and that the identification of distinct viral lineages within a single school outbreak highlights the value of genomic approaches to complement routine laboratory testing and support respiratory pathogen surveillance in Burundi and across the region. Health Flu season started earlier than expected — what to know about the brand new vaccine By Allie Yang Published Oct. 14, 2026, 3:16 p.m. ET 1616 Comments See more of our coverage in your search results. Make New York Post a Preferred Source Now is around the time when flu season usually starts to pick up — except this year, cases have been rising since late summer. Some data shows current flu activity is similar to when flu activity peaks at the end of the year. But it’s still too early to tell whether this year’s flu will be particularly severe. For now, experts are warning people take precautions: Avoid people who are sick, wash your hands — and get vaccinated. This year, there’s a brand new shot that takes a totally different approach to flu prevention, and early data shows it’s more effective than the traditional shot. But it’s not for everyone. Here’s what to know. Some data shows flu activity is similar to what’s normally seen at the end of the year, when flu season peaks. alfa27 – stock.adobe.com Rising flu cases October is the typical start of the flu season. But this year, cases started rising as early as late August. Based on wastewater data, flu activity reached levels this month usually not seen until December or January — when flu season historically peaks. “Early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year,” the CDC said. That said, a vast majority of the country remains in “minimal” range of flu cases. “Every influenza season is different — some begin earlier than usual, others later,” the CDC said. Despite an early start to flu season, 2026’s flu trends remain “within expected seasonal variation.” And while the flu generally starts picking up in southern states, this year, it appeared first in the West: California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska. Some experts say these changes might point to an evolving flu virus. ‘Stick’ season An earlier flu season means considering getting an earlier flu shot, experts say. And this year, there’s a brand new one on the market. In August, the FDA approved mFLUSIVA, the first mRNA flu vaccine for adults aged 50 and older. Everyone ages 6 months and up should get an annual flu vaccine, the CDC says. AntonioDiaz – stock.adobe.com Unlike traditional flu vaccines, it does not contain a weakened or inactive flu virus. Instead, it works by giving instructions via mRNA to your immune cells on how to kill the flu virus on its own. This is the same technology used in the COVID-19 vaccines. “There is some evidence that suggests mFlusiva may offer somewhat better protection against the flu than traditional flu vaccines,” Dr. Rebecca Choudhury, an infectious disease doctor at Mount Sinai, said. In adults 50 and older, the mRNA vaccine had a 27% lower rate of flu infection compared to traditional vaccines. Adverse reactions to the new vaccine were very rare, and happened at similar rates to side effects to the traditional flu vaccine. Choudhury says adults aged 50 to 64 have the clearest reason to consider it, and especially those with chronic health conditions that raise the risk of a severe case of flu. That said, it’s a very new drug that may not be available at every doctor’s office or pharmacy — and Choudhury says it’s better to get the traditional shot rather than go without. Everyone six months and older should get an annual flu shot, the CDC says. This year’s traditional flu vaccines target three flu viruses — H1N1 and H3N2 (both subtypes of the more common influenza A) and influenza B. 16 What do you think? Post a comment. According to CDC data, over 75% of positive flu tests are H1N1 for the last month. It’s been circulating since it emerged as “swine flu” in 2009 and has become a regular part of flu season, joining a number of other influenza A and B strains that come back every year. This year’s vaccine was adjusted to protect against a H3N2 mutation called “subclade K” that spread widely last year. This type of flu causes typical flu symptoms like fever and cough to come on more abruptly. SPONSORED STORIES

supplementary_news.content_title: This Year’s Flu Season Started Early—And the Typical Vaccine Deadline May Be Too Late
supplementary_news.content: This Year’s Flu Season Started Early—And the Typical Vaccine Deadline May Be Too Late While you normally only hear about a surge of flu cases during the deep winter months, it's still early fall and the U.S. is already seeing flu at higher-than-usual rates. A recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that seasonal flu activity is "increasing" in many parts of the country, though it is still generally low. Based on the latest data, 3.6% of Americans tested for a respiratory issue were also positive for the flu. "Flu season is happening much earlier than usual," says Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York. "The beginning of influenza season is always unpredictable—this is another example." What's driving this increase in cases and, more importantly, how can you stay healthy? Here's what you need to know. Meet the experts: Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing and Thomas Russo, MD, professor and chief of infectious disease at the University at Buffalo in New York Where are flu cases increasing? The flu doesn't hit the country at the same level, at the same time. Right now, for example, the CDC points out that the highest flu activity is happening on the West Coast. California's test positivity rate for influenza currently sits at 8.8 percent, based on state data, while Alaska's public health department noted that flu cases started to "increase noticeably" in mid-August. "There isn't one clear explanation for why it's happening earlier this year," says Asefeh Faraz Covelli, PhD, APRN, researcher and associate professor at The George Washington University School of Nursing. "We need to keep watching the data to understand whether this early rise will translate into an earlier or more severe flu season overall." The earlier-than-usual season is largely driven by an H1N1 variant of the flu, with a D.3.1.1 HA subclade. That may be more immune-evasive than other strains, leading to the rise in early infections, Dr. Russo says. But Covelli includes this important caveat: "An earlier start doesn't necessarily mean the flu is stronger." Flu viruses change every year, and some of those changes may make it easier for the virus to spread in people who have some level of immunity already. "Researchers are watching the strains circulating this year, but it's too early to know whether these changes will make this flu season more severe," she says. Flu symptoms to look out for If you're worried you have the flu, keep the following in mind. Flu symptoms don't really change from year to year, and these are the biggest ones to be aware of, per the CDC: - Fever - Cough - Sore throat - Runny or stuffy nose - Muscle or body aches - Headaches - Fatigue When to get vaccinated Public health agencies usually recommend getting vaccinated by Halloween. But given the season's early start, healthcare providers say you're fine to get the vaccine now. "If you haven't gotten your flu shot yet, I'd get it now rather than wait," Covelli says. "September and October are generally the best time to get vaccinated, and it takes about two weeks for your body to build up protection." Getting vaccinated now can help to protect you throughout the season, she says. Also, while it's easy to assume an early start to flu season means it might also end sooner, that's not guaranteed. "Sometimes we have two waves due to influenza A and then influenza B," Dr. Russo says. "We will have to see." You Might Also Like
